nodes.heading: Criminal Procedure Act 2009
nodes.text: Criminal Procedure Act 2009

nodes.heading: Preliminary
nodes.text:
Authorised Version incorporating amendments as at
1 July 2026
The Parliament of Victoria enacts:

nodes.heading: Purposes
nodes.text: The purposes of this Act are—

to clarify, simplify and consolidate the laws
relating to criminal procedure in the
Magistrates' Court, the County Court and the
Supreme Court;

to provide new pre-trial disclosure
requirements for the prosecution;

to provide for the transfer to the County
Court or Supreme Court of summary
offences related to an offence to be tried on
indictment by the relevant court;

to abolish the procedure of indictment by
grand jury;

to clarify the tests relating to determination
of appeals by the Court of Appeal;

to provide for the stay of sentences on
appeal;

to amend the Sentencing Act 1991 to
provide for a maximum fine that may be
imposed for an indictable offence that is
heard and determined summarily;

to amend the Crimes Act 1958, the Crimes
(Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be
Tried) Act 1997, the Magistrates' Court
Act 1989, the Children, Youth and
Families Act 2005 and the Appeal Costs
Act 1998;

to repeal the Crimes (Criminal Trials)
Act 1999;

to make consequential and other
amendments.

This Chapter comes into operation on the day
after the day on which this Act receives the Royal
Assent.

Subject to subsection (4), the remaining
provisions of this Act come into operation on a
day or days to be proclaimed.

If a provision referred to in subsection (3) does
not come into operation before 1 January 2011, it
comes into operation on that day.

In this Act, sexual offence means any of the
following offences (other than an offence
excluded by subsection (2))—
an offence against—
a provision of Subdivision (8A), (8B),

, (8D), (8E), (8F), (8FAA) (except
section 53N) or (8FA) of Division 1 of
Part I of the Crimes Act 1958; or

section 327(2) (failure to disclose a
sexual offence committed against a
child under the age of 16 years) of
the Crimes Act 1958; or

section 5(1), 6(1), 7(1), 8(1), 9(1) or
11(1) of the Sex Work Act 1994
despite its repeal by the Sex Work
Decriminalisation Act 2022;
an intimate image offence;
an offence an element of which involves—

any person engaging in sexual activity;
or

any person taking part in a sexual act;
or
commercial sexual services; or
a sexual performance involving a child;
an offence an element of which involves—

soliciting, procuring, enabling or
threatening any of the conduct referred
to in paragraph (b); or

inducing or knowingly allowing a child
to enter or remain on premises so that
any of the conduct referred to in
paragraph (b) may occur;

an offence an element of which involves
child abuse material;

an offence an element of which involves
indecency;

an offence against section 49C(2) (failure
by person in authority to protect child from
sexual offence) of the Crimes Act 1958
as in force before the commencement of
section 16 of the Crimes Amendment
(Sexual Offences) Act 2016.

An offence against a provision of the Sex
Work Act 1994, despite its repeal by the Sex
Work Decriminalisation Act 2022, that is not
referred to in subsection (1)(a)(iii) is not a sexual
offence.

In determining whether an offence at common
law is a sexual offence, it does not matter that
the offence has since been abolished.

In determining whether an offence against an
enactment is a sexual offence, it does not matter
that the enactment has since been repealed.

In determining whether an offence is a sexual
offence, it does not matter that the offence is
described in this section—

differently from how it is described in the
enactment or common law that establishes
the offence; or

by reference to an enactment that was not in
operation on the date on which the offence is
alleged to have been committed.

Subdivision (13) of Division 1 of Part I of the Crimes
Act 1958 previously included offences involving child
pornography. That Subdivision has been repealed and
replaced by new offences that refer to child abuse material
rather than child pornography. Child pornography was
defined to include material of a certain kind, and child
abuse material is now defined as also including material
of that kind. An offence against a provision of repealed
Subdivision (13) is therefore a sexual offence under
subsection (1)(d).

In this section—
commercial sexual services has the meaning
given by section 35(1) of the Crimes
Act 1958;
sexual, in relation to an activity, has the
meaning given by section 35D of the
Crimes Act 1958;
sexual performance has the meaning given by
section 49Q(3) of the Crimes Act 1958;
taking part in a sexual act has the meaning given
by section 35C of the Crimes Act 1958.

nodes.heading: Ways in which a criminal proceeding is commenced
How a criminal proceeding is commenced
nodes.text: A criminal proceeding is commenced by—

history.raw: Note to s. 5 inserted by No. 48/2012 s. 10.

nodes.text:
filing or signing a charge-sheet in
accordance with section 6; or

filing a direct indictment in accordance with
section 159; or

a direction under section 415 that a person be
tried for perjury.

A proceeding may also be commenced under section 83AL of the
Sentencing Act 1991.

nodes.heading: Commencement of a criminal proceeding in the Magistrates' Court

nodes.text: A criminal proceeding is commenced—

history.raw: Note to s. 6(1) substituted as Notes by No. 32/2024 s. 812.

nodes.text:
by filing a charge-sheet containing a charge
in the Magistrates' Court; or

if the accused is arrested without a
warrant and is released on bail, by filing
a charge-sheet containing a charge with a
bail justice; or

if a summons is issued under section 14, at
the time the charge-sheet is signed.

A criminal proceeding against a child is commenced in
the same manner in the Children's Court: section 528 of
the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005.

In the case of a criminal proceeding for an alleged
offence by a child who was 12 or 13 years of age at the
time of the alleged commission of the offence, a record
of reasons must be filed with the charge-sheet.

If a charge-sheet is filed in accordance with the
method prescribed by the rules of court for
electronic filing, the requirements of section 8(1)
of the Electronic Transactions (Victoria)
Act 2000 are taken to have been met.
A charge-sheet must—
be in writing; and
be signed by the informant personally; and
comply with Schedule 1.

Section 18 requires an informant to nominate an address for
service of documents and other details. That information
may be included on a charge-sheet.

The informant may include a request for a
committal proceeding in a charge-sheet containing
a charge for an indictable offence that may be
heard and determined summarily.

nodes.heading: Time limits for filing a charge-sheet

nodes.text:
A proceeding for a summary offence must be
commenced within 12 months after the date on
which the offence is alleged to have been
committed except where—

otherwise provided by or under any other
Act; or

the accused gives written consent, and the
DPP or a Crown Prosecutor consent, to the
proceeding being commenced after the
expiry of that period.

See Part 5.1A of Chapter 5 of the Children, Youth and
Families Act 2005 for a shorter time limit in relation to
children.
A proceeding for an indictable offence—

may be commenced at any time, except
where otherwise provided by or under this or
any other Act; and

may be heard and determined summarily
even though the proceeding may have been
commenced more than 12 months after the
date on which the offence is alleged to have
been committed.

nodes.heading: Time limits on prosecuting certain former sexual offences removed

nodes.text:
Any immunity from prosecution arising because
of the time limit imposed by the following
repealed provisions on commencing a proceeding
for an offence is abolished—
section 47 of the Crimes Act 1928;
section 51 of the Crimes Act 1957;

section 48(6) of the Crimes Act 1958
(inserted by section 5 of the Crimes
(Sexual Offences) Act 1980 and repealed by
section 3 of the Crimes (Sexual Offences)
Act 1991);

section 49(6) of the Crimes Act 1958
(inserted by section 5 of the Crimes
(Sexual Offences) Act 1980 and repealed by
section 3 of the Crimes (Sexual Offences)
Act 1991).

Subsection (1) does not apply to an offence if the
conduct constituting it would not constitute an
offence under the law of Victoria immediately
before the day after the day on which the Jury
Directions Act 2015 receives the Royal Assent.

Without limiting any other defence available to a
person charged, because of subsection (1), with an
offence of a kind described in column 1 of the
Table in this subsection, the person may rely on a
defence described in column 2 of that Table in
relation to that offence.

7B Uncertainty about time when sexual offence
occurred
This section applies if—

conduct is alleged to have occurred at some
time during a period; and

there is uncertainty as to when, during that
period, the conduct allegedly occurred; and

because of a change in the law during that
period, the conduct, if proven, would
constitute one sexual offence before the
change and a different sexual offence after
the change.
A person may be charged with—

whichever of those sexual offences has the
lowest maximum penalty; or

if both of the sexual offences have the same
maximum penalty, the offence that the
conduct, if proven, would have constituted
before the change.

The means by which an offence may be charged
in accordance with subsection (2) include—

including a charge for that offence in a fresh
indictment within the meaning of
section 164; or

amending an indictment under section 165 so
that it includes a charge for that offence.

For the purposes of a proceeding that relates
(wholly or partly) to an offence that is charged in
accordance with subsection (2), the offence
charged is taken to have been in force when the
conduct allegedly occurred.

In any such proceeding, any requirement to prove
that the complainant was of a particular age is
satisfied if the prosecution proves that the
complainant was of that age at some time during
the period.

The Magistrates' Court at any time may order
that a charge-sheet be amended in any manner that
the court thinks necessary, unless the required
amendment cannot be made without injustice to
the accused.

If a charge-sheet is amended by order under this
section, the charge-sheet is to be treated as having
been filed in the amended form for the purposes of
the hearing and all proceedings connected with the
hearing.

An amendment of a charge-sheet that has the
effect of charging a new offence cannot be made
after the expiry of the period, if any, within which
a proceeding for the offence may be commenced.

If a limitation period applies to the offence
charged in the charge-sheet, the charge-sheet may
be amended after the expiry of the limitation
period if—

the charge-sheet before the amendment
sufficiently disclosed the nature of the
offence; and

the amendment does not amount to the
commencement of a proceeding for a new
offence; and

the amendment will not cause injustice to the
accused.

A charge-sheet is not invalid by reason only of a
failure to comply with Schedule 1.

A charge on a charge-sheet is not invalid by
reason only of—

omitting to state the time at which the
offence was committed unless time is an
essential element of the offence; or

incorrectly stating the time at which the
offence was committed; or

stating the offence to have been committed
on an impossible day or on a day that never
happened.

nodes.heading: Listing of matter for mention hearing or filing hearing in the Magistrates' Court

nodes.text:
If a charge-sheet contains a charge for a summary
offence, the proceeding must be listed for a
mention hearing.

Subject to subsection (3), if a charge-sheet
contains a charge for an indictable offence that
may be heard and determined summarily, the
proceeding may be listed for a mention hearing or
a filing hearing, having regard to any request for a
committal proceeding included on the charge-
sheet.

If a notice to appear is served under section 21
and a charge-sheet is filed in accordance with
section 22, the proceeding must be listed for a
mention hearing on the date specified in the notice
to appear.

Despite subsections (1) and (2), if a charge-sheet
contains a charge for an indictable offence that is
not an indictable offence that may be heard and
determined summarily, the proceeding must be
listed for a filing hearing.

A mention hearing is the first hearing for a charge that will be
heard and determined summarily.

A filing hearing is the first stage in a committal proceeding
under Chapter 4.

Section 28(1) sets out the indictable offences that may be
heard and determined summarily.

A criminal proceeding in the Magistrates' Court is
to be heard at the venue of the court that is nearest
to—
except where otherwise provided by this or any
other Act or by a nomination under subsection (2).

history.raw: Note to s. 11(1) amended by No. 33/2018 ss 38, 46.

nodes.text:
the place where the offence is alleged to
have been committed; or
the place of residence of the accused—

Part 2 of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 sets out the
special requirements for matters that may be heard in the
various Divisions of the Magistrates' Court: the Drug Court
Division, the Koori Court Division, the Specialist Family
Violence Court Division and the Neighbourhood Justice
Division.

The Chief Magistrate may from time to time, by
notice published in the Government Gazette,
nominate a venue of the Magistrates' Court as a
venue for the hearing of a specified criminal
proceeding or a specified class of criminal
proceeding.

A criminal proceeding in the Magistrates' Court
is not invalid only because it was conducted at a
venue of the court other than the venue referred to
in subsection (1) or nominated under
subsection (2).

history.raw: Pt 5.8 Div. 1 (Heading) amended by No. 38/2022 s. 78.

nodes.heading: Court may issue summons or warrant to arrest

nodes.text:
On the filing of a charge-sheet under section 6,
an application may be made to a registrar of the
Magistrates' Court for the issue of—
unless a notice to appear has been served on the
accused under Division 2.

history.raw: Note to s. 12(1) inserted by No. 1/2016 s. 22(2).

nodes.text:
a summons to answer to the charge directed
to the accused; or

a warrant to arrest in order to compel the
attendance of the accused—

An application under subsection (1)(b) must
be made by the informant personally but an
application under subsection (1)(a) may be made
by the informant or a person on behalf of the
informant.

An application under subsection (1) may be made
by the applicant in person, by post, by electronic
communication or otherwise in accordance with
the manner prescribed by the rules of court.

On an application under subsection (1), the
registrar must, if satisfied that the charge discloses
an offence known to law, issue—
a summons to answer to the charge; or
subject to subsection (5), a warrant to arrest.

A registrar of the Magistrates' Court must not
issue in the first instance a warrant to arrest unless
satisfied by sworn or affirmed evidence, whether
oral or by affidavit, that—

history.raw: S. 12(5) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.1).

nodes.text:
it is probable that the accused will not
answer a summons; or

the accused has absconded, is likely to
abscond or is avoiding service of a summons
that has been issued; or

a warrant is required or authorised by any
other Act or for other good cause.

If an accused fails to appear in answer to a summons,
sections 80 and 81 provide for the issue of a warrant to arrest
the accused.  Section 330 provides for the issue of a warrant
to arrest a person who has been remanded in custody or
granted bail to attend a hearing but fails to attend.
Section 29 of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 enables a

magistrate to exercise the powers of a registrar to issue a
summons or warrant.

nodes.heading: Summons or warrant to be accompanied by charge-sheet and notice when served
nodes.text:
A summons to answer to a charge issued under
section 12 or 14 or a warrant to arrest issued under
section 12, on service or execution on the accused,
must be accompanied by—
a copy of the charge-sheet; and

in the case of a charge for an offence against
a child who was 12 or 13 years of age at the
time of the alleged commission of the
offence, a copy of the record of reasons for
the charge; and

a notice, in the form prescribed by the rules
of court, containing—

if the charge is for an indictable offence
that may not be heard and determined
summarily or the charge-sheet contains
a request for a committal proceeding, a
summary of Part 4.4; and

if the charge is for any other indictable
offence or a summary offence, a
summary of Division 2 of Part 3.2; and

history.raw: S. 13(b)(ii) renumbered as s. 13(b)(iii) by No. 68/2009 s. 4(c).

nodes.text:
advice that the accused should seek
legal advice and that the accused has
the right, if eligible, to legal aid under
the Legal Aid Act 1978; and

history.raw: S. 13(b)(iii) renumbered as s. 13(b)(iv) by No. 68/2009 s. 4(d).

nodes.text:
details of how to contact Victoria Legal
Aid.

nodes.heading: Police or public official may issue summons

nodes.text:
Without limiting the power of a registrar of the
Magistrates' Court or the Court in any way—
may, after signing a charge-sheet containing a
charge, issue a summons to answer to the charge.

history.raw: Note to s. 14(1) inserted by No. 1/2016 s. 22(2).

nodes.text: a police officer; or

history.raw: S. 14(1)(a) substituted by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.2(a)).

nodes.text:
a public official acting in the performance
of his or her duty (whether the power to
commence the proceeding is conferred on
him or her by or under an Act or at common
law)—

If a police officer or a public official issues a
summons under subsection (1), he or she must file
the charge-sheet and summons in the Magistrates'
Court within 7 days after signing the charge-sheet.

If it appears to the Magistrates' Court that
subsection (2) has not been complied with in
relation to a proceeding, the court may strike out
the charge.

history.raw: Note to s. 14(3) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(d).

nodes.text:
Section 401(3) allows the court to award costs if a charge is
struck out.

A summons to answer to a charge must direct the
accused to appear at the venue of the Magistrates'
Court referred to in section 11 on a specified date
and at a specified time to answer the charge.

A summons to answer to a charge for an
indictable offence that is to be served on a
corporate accused must state that, if the accused
does not appear in answer to the summons, the
Magistrates' Court may proceed—

in the case of an indictable offence that may
be heard and determined summarily, to hear
and determine the charge in the absence of
the accused in accordance with Division 10
of Part 3.3; or

in any case, to conduct a committal
proceeding in the absence of the accused in
accordance with Chapter 4.

See sections 80, 81 and 82 for consequences of failing to
appear in answer to a summons.

Section 28(1) sets out the indictable offences that may be
heard and determined summarily.

nodes.heading: Personal service of summons
nodes.text:
Except where otherwise expressly enacted, every
summons to answer to a charge must be served
personally on the accused in accordance with
section 391—

history.raw: Note to s. 16 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(f).

nodes.text:
subject to paragraph (b), at least 14 days
before the return date;

in the case of a charge for an indictable
offence in respect of which a registrar of the
Magistrates' Court has fixed a date for a
filing hearing, at least 7 days before that date
or any other time before that date that is
prescribed by the rules of court.

See section 399(4) for filing in court of affidavit or declaration of
service.

nodes.heading: Summons for summary offence may be served by ordinary service

nodes.text:
A summons to answer to a charge for a summary
offence (other than a traffic camera offence) must
be served personally on the accused in accordance
with section 391 unless the informant is satisfied
that ordinary service is appropriate in all the
circumstances.

history.raw: Note to s. 17(1) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(h).

nodes.text: Section 394 provides for ordinary service.

In considering whether to effect service of a
summons by ordinary service, an informant must
consider whether it is an appropriate method of
service in all the circumstances as known by the
informant including—
the nature and gravity of the alleged offence;

the period of time that has elapsed since the
accused's address for service was
ascertained.

If a summons is served in accordance with
section 394(1)(a), evidence of service must
state—

how the informant ascertained the address to
which the summons was posted; and
the time and place of posting; and

whether the informant considered the matters
referred to in subsection (2) before
determining to effect service by post.

nodes.heading: Service of summons for traffic camera offence

nodes.text:
A summons to answer to a charge for a traffic
camera offence may be served personally on the
accused in accordance with section 391 or by
ordinary service in accordance with section 394.

If a summons is served in accordance with
section 394(1)(a) or (ab), evidence of service must
state—

how the informant ascertained the address to
which the summons was posted; and
the time and place of posting.

nodes.heading: Informant must nominate address etc. for service of documents

nodes.text:
An informant must nominate in writing a business
address, email address, if any, and fax number for
service on the informant of documents in relation
to a charge.

A nomination under subsection (1) may be
included on a charge-sheet or any other document
served with a charge-sheet.

nodes.heading: Extension of return date if summons not served

nodes.text:
If the informant has not served a summons to
answer to a charge, the appropriate registrar may
extend a return date specified in the summons
without cause on one occasion on the application
of the informant—
before the return date; or
within 28 days after the return date.

The appropriate registrar may extend a return date
on a subsequent occasion on the application of the
informant—
if the registrar is satisfied by sworn or affirmed
evidence, whether oral or by affidavit, that
reasonable efforts have been made to serve the
summons.

history.raw: S. 19(2) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.1).

nodes.text: before the current return date; or
within 28 days after the current return date—

See also section 331 as to the court's general power of
adjournment.

nodes.heading: Adjournment of proceeding on application of accused
nodes.text:
On the application of the accused, the appropriate
registrar may—

if the accused is on bail, on the return date
or on the date to which the proceeding is
adjourned, adjourn the proceeding to a later
date and extend bail but not vary the
conditions of bail or revoke bail.

See also section 331 as to the court's general power of
adjournment.

nodes.heading: Police or public official may serve notice to appear

nodes.text:
A police officer or a public official acting in the
performance of his or her duties may serve on a
person a notice to appear if the police officer or
public official reasonably suspects that the person
has committed—

history.raw: S. 21(1) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.3).

nodes.text: a summary offence; or

an indictable offence that may be heard and
determined summarily.
A notice to appear must—

state the name of the person serving the
notice; and

state a telephone number and email address
at which the person serving the notice may
be contacted and the business address of the
person and may state similar details for a
person authorised to act in relation to the
notice on behalf of the person serving the
notice; and

state the full name and address of the person
served with the notice; and

state in general terms the circumstances of
the suspected offence; and

direct the person served with the notice to
appear at a venue of the Magistrates' Court
on a date (at least 28 days after the date of
service of the notice) and at a time specified
in the notice to answer any charge in respect
of the suspected offence; and
include a summary of this Division; and
be signed by the person serving the notice.
A notice to appear must be served by—
giving it to the person to be served; or

if the person does not accept it, by putting it
down in the person's presence and telling the
person the nature of the document.

nodes.heading: Notice to appear lapses unless charge-sheet filed within 14 days

nodes.text:
If a police officer or a public official serves a
notice to appear on a person, the notice lapses on
the expiry of 14 days after service unless, within
that period, the police officer or public official
files in the Magistrates' Court—

a charge-sheet containing a charge against
the person for the suspected offence stated in
the notice to appear or a related offence; and
a copy of the notice to appear; and
evidence of service.

Failure to file a charge-sheet in accordance with
subsection (1) does not affect the filing of a
charge-sheet at any later time.

nodes.heading: Notice to be given on lapsing

nodes.text:
Within 7 days after the lapsing of a notice to
appear, the police officer or public official who
served the notice must ensure that—

history.raw: S. 23(1) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.5).

nodes.text:
written notice is given to the person on
whom the notice to appear was served that—
a charge-sheet has not been filed; and

the person is not required to appear at
the Magistrates' Court on the date and
at the time specified in the notice to
appear; and

the Magistrates' Court is notified that the
notice to appear has lapsed.

A notice under subsection (1) is given by sending
it by prepaid ordinary post addressed to the person
at the last known address of the person.

nodes.heading: Preliminary brief to be served if charge-sheet filed
nodes.text:
If a charge-sheet is filed in accordance with
section 22(1), the informant must—

serve a preliminary brief on the accused
within 21 days after the day on which the
charge-sheet is filed; and

on the return date have available a copy of
the preliminary brief for provision to the
accused or the legal practitioner representing
the accused, on request.
Section 36 sets out how a preliminary brief must be served.

Section 37 sets out the contents of a preliminary brief,
including a copy of the charge-sheet.

nodes.heading: Non-appearance of accused served with notice to appear

nodes.text:
If a charge-sheet containing a charge for a
summary offence is filed against an accused in
accordance with section 22(1) and the accused
does not appear in answer to the notice to appear,
the Magistrates' Court may—
issue a warrant to arrest the accused; or

proceed to hear and determine the charge in
the absence of the accused in accordance
with Division 10 of Part 3.3; or

adjourn the proceeding on any terms that it
considers appropriate.

If a charge-sheet containing a charge for an
indictable offence that may be heard and
determined summarily is filed against an accused
in accordance with section 22(1) and the accused
does not appear in answer to the notice to appear,
the Magistrates' Court may  issue a warrant to
arrest the accused.

nodes.heading: Notice to appear does not commence proceeding
nodes.text:
Service of a notice to appear does not commence a
criminal proceeding.

Chapter 8 contains general provisions that apply to all criminal
proceedings.

nodes.heading: When a summary hearing may be held
Summary offences
nodes.text:
A charge for a summary offence is to be heard
and determined summarily in accordance with this
Chapter or, if the case requires, Division 1 of
Part 5.8.

history.raw: Note to s. 27 amended by No. 47/2014 s. 257.

nodes.text:
The procedure set out in the Fines Reform Act 2014 may be used
instead of commencing a proceeding for certain offences. See
section 99 of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989.

nodes.heading: Indictable offences that may be heard and determined summarily

nodes.text:
A charge for any of the following indictable
offences may be heard and determined summarily
by the Magistrates' Court, if section 29 is
satisfied—
an offence referred to in Schedule 2;

an indictable offence under an Act or
subordinate instrument or an offence at
common law if the offence is described by
an Act or subordinate instrument as being—
a level 5 offence or level 6 offence; or

punishable by level 5 or level 6
imprisonment or fine or both; or

punishable by a term of imprisonment
not exceeding 10 years or a fine not
exceeding 1200 penalty units or both—
unless the contrary intention appears in this
or any other Act or in any subordinate
instrument.

A level 5 offence is punishable by 10 years imprisonment
maximum and a level 6 offence is punishable by 5 years
imprisonment maximum: section 109 of the Sentencing
Act 1991.

If an indictable offence is described as being
punishable in more than one way or in one of 2 or
more ways, all of those ways must be referred to
in subsection (1) for subsection (1) to apply.

If an indictable offence referred to in Schedule 2
is qualified by reference to a specified amount or
value or a specified kind of property, that
qualification is not affected by subsection (1)(b)
or (2).

nodes.heading: When an indictable offence may be heard and determined summarily

nodes.text:
The Magistrates' Court may hear and determine
summarily a charge for an offence to which
section 28(1) applies if—

the court considers that the charge is
appropriate to be determined summarily,
having regard to the matters in
subsection (2); and
the accused consents to a summary hearing.

Section 82 provides for a summary hearing
without consent in the case of a corporate
accused which fails to appear in answer to a
summons.

Section 168(3) provides that a charge transferred
by order under that section must be heard and
determined summarily.

For the purposes of subsection (1)(a), the
Magistrates' Court must have regard to—
the seriousness of the offence including—
the nature of the offence; and

the manner in which the offence is
alleged to have been committed, the
apparent degree of organisation and the
presence of aggravating circumstances;
and

whether the offence forms part of a
series of offences being alleged against
the accused; and

the complexity of the proceeding for
determining the charge; and

the adequacy of sentences available to the
court, having regard to the criminal record of
the accused; and

whether a co-accused is charged with the
same offence; and

any other matter that the court considers
relevant.

A legal practitioner appearing for an accused may,
on behalf of the accused, consent to a summary
hearing of a charge for an indictable offence.

Nothing in subsection (2) applies to a proceeding
in the Children's Court.

If a body corporate and a natural person are jointly
charged with an indictable offence which may be
heard and determined summarily, the Magistrates'
Court must not hear and determine the charge
summarily against either of the accused unless—

each of them consents to a summary hearing;
or

if the body corporate fails to appear in the
proceeding, the natural person consents to a
summary hearing and the court proceeds
under section 82 to hear and determine the
charge in the absence of the body corporate.

nodes.heading: Procedure for indictable offences that may be heard and determined summarily

nodes.text:
The informant or the accused may apply for a
summary hearing under section 29(1).

Without any application under subsection (1), the
Magistrates' Court may offer a summary hearing
under section 29(1).

An application for, or an offer of, a summary
hearing may be made at any time before the
Magistrates' Court determines whether to commit
the accused for trial.

Section 6(4) provides that an informant may include a
request for a committal proceeding in a charge-sheet
containing a charge for an indictable offence that may be
heard and determined summarily.

If an application for a summary hearing is
made before the hearing of any evidence, the
Magistrates' Court may seek from the prosecutor
or, if the informant is appearing in person, the
informant and he or she must give—
for the purpose of enabling the court to determine
whether to grant a summary hearing.

an outline of the evidence which will be
presented for the prosecution; and

any other information which the court
considers relevant—

Any statement made by the prosecutor or
informant under subsection (4) is not admissible
in evidence in any subsequent proceeding in
respect of the charge.

If the Magistrates' Court grants a summary
hearing, the hearing and determination of the
charge must be conducted in accordance with
Part 3.3.

Sections 112A to 113D of the Sentencing Act 1991 provide
for maximum penalties in the Magistrates' Court.

Subject to subsection (8), if—
the court may, with the consent of the accused,
admit as evidence in the summary hearing—
given or tendered during the committal hearing.
a committal hearing commences; and

the Magistrates' Court subsequently grants a
summary hearing—
the oral evidence of any witness; and
the statement of any witness; and
any document or exhibit—
If evidence is admitted under subsection (7)—

the Magistrates' Court must, at the request of
the informant or the accused, call or recall
(as the case requires) any witness for
examination or cross-examination; and

the hearing must otherwise be conducted in
the same manner as a proceeding for a
summary offence.

nodes.heading: Court may change place of hearing
nodes.text:
If the Magistrates' Court considers that—
the court may order that the hearing be held at
another place or venue of the court that the court
considers appropriate.

a fair hearing in a criminal proceeding
cannot otherwise be had; or

for any other reason it is appropriate to do
so—

nodes.heading: Accused entitled to copy of charge-sheet and particulars

nodes.text:
An accused is entitled to receive free of charge a
copy of the charge-sheet from the informant or the
appropriate registrar.

An accused is entitled to receive from the
informant reasonable particulars of the charge.

nodes.heading: Unrepresented accused who requires legal advice
nodes.text:
If—
the court must—

an accused is charged with an offence
punishable by imprisonment; and

the accused is unrepresented on the return
date—

ask the accused whether the accused has
sought legal advice; and

if satisfied that the accused has not had a
reasonable opportunity to obtain legal
advice, grant an adjournment if so requested
by the accused; and

inform the accused that the accused has the
right, if eligible, to legal aid under the Legal
Aid Act 1978.

If—
the court must direct that the property or part of it
be returned to the accused or to any other person
that the accused directs.

property has been taken from an accused;
and

the Magistrates' Court considers that the
property or part of it can be returned
consistently with the interests of justice and
with the safe custody of the accused—

If property has been taken from a person other
than the accused, the Magistrates' Court, on
application by the person, may direct that the
property be returned to the person at any time, and
subject to any condition, that the court considers
appropriate.

nodes.heading: When preliminary brief is to be served

nodes.text:
If required to do so by section 24, the informant
must serve a preliminary brief on the accused.

At any time after the commencement of a
proceeding, the accused, by written notice to the
informant, may request that a preliminary brief be
served.

If the accused gives notice under subsection (2),
the informant must serve on the accused a
preliminary brief within 14 days after receipt of
the notice.

Nothing in this section prevents the informant
from serving a preliminary brief on the accused at
any other time.

nodes.heading: How preliminary brief must be served

nodes.text:
A preliminary brief must be served personally on
the accused in accordance with section 391 unless
the informant is satisfied that ordinary service is
appropriate in all the circumstances.

history.raw: Note to s. 36(1) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(k).

nodes.text: Section 394 provides for ordinary service.

In considering whether to effect service of a
preliminary brief by ordinary service, the
informant must consider whether it is an
appropriate method of service in all the
circumstances as known by the informant
including—
the nature and gravity of the alleged offence;

the manner of service of the summons to
answer to the charge.
A preliminary brief must include—

a copy of the charge-sheet in respect of the
alleged offence; and

if applicable, a copy of the record of reasons;
and

a notice in the form prescribed by the rules
of court—

explaining this section and section 84;
and

advising that the accused has the right,
if eligible, to legal aid under the Legal
Aid Act 1978; and

providing details of how to contact
Victoria Legal Aid; and

a statement made by the informant
personally that complies with subsection (2)
and section 38; and

any evidentiary certificate issued under any
Act that is likely to be relevant to the alleged
offence and is available at the time the
preliminary brief is served; and

a copy of the criminal record of the accused
that is available at the time the preliminary
brief is served or a statement that the accused
has no previous convictions or infringement
convictions known at that time; and

if the informant refuses to disclose any
information, document or thing that is
required to be included in the preliminary
brief, a written notice that the informant
refuses disclosure under section 45,
identifying the ground for refusing
disclosure; and

a list of any other orders that are or will be
sought, as known at the time of preparation
of the preliminary brief.

A statement by the informant in a preliminary
brief must be a complete and accurate statement
of the material available to the prosecution at the
time the statement is sworn or affirmed, signed or
attested and must include—

history.raw: S. 37(2) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.1).

nodes.text:
a statement of the alleged facts on which the
charge is based, including reference to the
material available to the prosecution to
support the alleged facts; and

a description of the background to and
consequences of the alleged offence, if
known; and

a summary of any statements made by the
accused concerning the alleged offence,
including any confession or admission; and

a list of the names of all persons who, at the
time the statement is signed, may be called
by the prosecution as witnesses at the
hearing of the charge, indicating whether
those persons have made statements; and

a list of any things the prosecution may
tender as exhibits, indicating whether they
are in the possession of the prosecution at the
time the statement is signed.

A preliminary brief may include any other
information, document or thing that is relevant to
the alleged offence and may assist the accused in
understanding the evidence against the accused
that is available to the prosecution.

Statements of key witnesses may be included in the
preliminary brief.

If the Magistrates' Court hears and determines a charge in the
absence of the accused, section 84 provides that certain
documents in a preliminary brief served on the accused at
least 14 days before the hearing date are admissible in
evidence.

See section 86 as to proof of criminal record in the absence of
the accused.

nodes.heading: Requirements for informant's statement in preliminary brief
nodes.text:
A statement by the informant in a preliminary
brief must be—

history.raw: Note to s. 38(2) repealed by No. 68/2009 s. 9(c).
Note to s. 38 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 9(d).

nodes.text: in the form of an affidavit; or

signed by the informant and contain an
acknowledgment signed in the presence of a
person referred to in Schedule 3 that the
statement is true and correct and is made in
the belief that a person making a false
statement in the circumstances is liable to the
penalties of perjury; or

in a form, and attested to in a manner,
prescribed by the rules of court.
Section 414 provides for acknowledgment of false statements.

nodes.heading: When full brief must be served

nodes.text:
The accused, by written notice to the informant,
may request that a full brief be served.
A request under subsection (1) may be made—

if a preliminary brief is served within
21 days after the day on which the charge-
sheet is filed, at any time after a summary
case conference is held; or

in any other case, at any time after the
criminal proceeding has commenced.

If the accused gives a notice under subsection (1),
the informant must serve a full brief on the
accused at least 14 days before—
the contest mention hearing; or

if a contest mention hearing is not held, the
summary hearing.

The Magistrates' Court, by order, may vary the
date for service of a full brief to a specified date
that is earlier or later than the date for service
required by subsection (2).

Nothing in this section prevents agreement
between the informant and the accused to more
limited disclosure than is required in a full brief.

nodes.heading: How full brief must be served

nodes.text:
A full brief must be served personally on the
accused in accordance with section 391 unless the
informant is satisfied that ordinary service is
appropriate in all the circumstances.

history.raw: Note to s. 40(1) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(m).

nodes.text: Section 394 provides for ordinary service.

In considering whether to effect service of a full
brief by ordinary service, the informant must
consider whether it is an appropriate method of
service in all the circumstances as known by the
informant including—
the nature and gravity of the alleged offence;

the manner of service of the summons to
answer to the charge.

history.raw: Notes to s. 41 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(n).

nodes.text:
Unless earlier disclosed to the accused, whether in
a preliminary brief, at a summary case conference
or otherwise, a full brief must contain—

a notice in the form prescribed by the rules
of court—

explaining this section and section 83;
and

advising that the accused has the right,
if eligible, to legal aid under the Legal
Aid Act 1978; and

providing details of how to contact
Victoria Legal Aid; and

a copy of the charge-sheet relating to the
alleged offence; and

if applicable, a copy of the record of reasons;
and

a copy of the criminal record of the accused
or a statement that the accused has no
previous convictions or infringement
convictions; and

any information, document or thing on which
the prosecution intends to rely at the hearing
of the charge including—

a copy of any statement relevant to
the charge signed by the accused, or a
record of interview of the accused, that
is in the possession of the informant;
and

a copy, or a transcript, of any
audio-recording or audiovisual
recording required to be made under
Subdivision (30A) of Division 1 of
Part III of the Crimes Act 1958; and

a copy or statement of any other
evidentiary material that is in the
possession of the informant relating to
a confession or admission made by the
accused relevant to the charge; and

a list of the persons the prosecution
intends to call as witnesses at the
hearing, together with a copy of each
of the statements made by those
persons; and
See section 47 for requirements for statements.

a legible copy of any document which
the prosecution intends to produce as
evidence; and

a list of any things the prosecution
intends to tender as exhibits; and

a clear photograph, or a clear copy of
such a photograph, of any proposed
exhibit that cannot be described in
detail in the list; and

a description of any forensic procedure,
examination or test that has not yet
been completed and on which the
prosecution intends to rely as tending to
establish the guilt of the accused; and

any evidentiary certificate issued under
any Act that is likely to be relevant to
the alleged offence; and

any other information, document or thing in
the possession of the prosecution that is
relevant to the alleged offence including—

a list of the persons (including experts)
who have made statements or given
information relevant to the alleged
offence but who the prosecution does
not intend to call as witnesses at the
hearing; and

a copy of every statement referred to in
subparagraph (i) made by each of those
persons or, if the person has not made a
statement, a written summary of the
substance of any evidence likely to be
given by that person or a list of those
statements or written summaries; and

a copy of every document relevant to
the alleged offence that the prosecution
does not intend to tender as an exhibit
at the hearing or a list of those
documents; and

a list containing descriptions of any
things relevant to the alleged offence
that the prosecution does not intend to
tender as exhibits at the hearing; and

a clear photograph, or a clear copy of
such a photograph, of any thing
relevant to the alleged offence that
cannot be described in detail in the list;
and

a copy of—
carried out on behalf of the prosecution
and relevant to the alleged offence but
on which the prosecution does not
intend to rely; and

records of any medical
examination of the accused; and

reports of any forensic procedure
or forensic examination conducted
on the accused; and
the results of any tests—

a copy of any other information,
document or thing required by the rules
of court to be included in a full brief;
and

subject to section 32C of the Evidence
(Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1958,
a copy of any information, document or
thing that is relevant to the credibility
of a witness for the prosecution; and

The witness' criminal history (including
pending charges), or the giving of a letter of
assistance to the witness, the reduction of
criminal charges against the witness, other
favourable treatment in a criminal proceeding,
or any payment or reward provided, as a result
of the witness' cooperation with police.

if the informant refuses to disclose any
information, document or thing that is
required to be included in the full brief, a
written notice that the informant refuses
disclosure under section 45, identifying the
ground for refusing disclosure.

Section 48 applies to information and other
material supplied in a full brief.

For the purposes of subsection (1)(e), relevant
includes, in relation to information, documents
and things, any information, document or thing
that might reasonably be expected to—
undermine the case for the prosecution; or
assist the case for the accused.

See section 416 as to the prosecution's general obligation of
disclosure.

Section 39(4) enables an informant and an accused to agree to
the provision of less material in the full brief than is required
by section 41.

If the Magistrates' Court hears and determines a charge in the
absence of the accused, section 83 provides that certain
documents in a full brief served on the accused are admissible
in evidence.

See section 86 as to proof of criminal record in the absence of
the accused.

Subject to any order of a court, in a proceeding in
which a full brief is served, the relevant officer
must complete a disclosure certificate in the form
prescribed by the regulations describing—

any relevant information, document or thing
not contained in the full brief because it is
the subject of—

a claim of privilege or public interest
immunity; or
immunity conferred by statute; or

a prohibition or restriction provided by
statute that has the effect of precluding
disclosure to the prosecution or the
defence; and

the nature of the privilege, immunity,
prohibition or restriction to which that
information, document or thing is subject;
and

any other matter prescribed by the
regulations.
The informant must—

file a copy of the disclosure certificate with
the registrar within 7 days after service of the
full brief on the accused; and

if the DPP is conducting the proceeding,
forward a copy of the disclosure certificate to
the DPP within 7 days after service of the
full brief on the accused; and

serve a copy of the disclosure certificate on
the accused at the same time as the full brief
is served on the accused.

Nothing in this section limits or otherwise
affects—

the power of the court to hear and determine
an application with respect to the disclosure
of information, documents or things; or

the power of the court to make any order or
other decision that it has power to make with
respect to the disclosure of information,
documents or things; or

the operation of a provision made by or
under any other Act, including an Act of the
Commonwealth, that prohibits or restricts, or
that authorises a court or tribunal to prohibit
or restrict, the disclosure of information for
or in connection with any proceeding.
In this section, relevant officer means—
the informant; or

if the informant did not investigate the
offence that is the subject of the proceeding,
the law enforcement officer who prepared
the full brief.

See section 416 as to the prosecution's general obligation of
disclosure.

history.raw: Note to s. 42 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(o).

nodes.text:
This section applies to any information, document
or thing that—

comes into the informant's possession or
comes to the informant's notice after the
service of a preliminary brief or a full brief,
as the case may be; and

would have been required to be listed, or a
copy of which would have been required to
be served, in the preliminary brief or the full
brief.

The informant must serve on the accused a copy
of the document or list as soon as practicable after
the information, document or thing comes into the
informant's possession or comes to the informant's
notice.

If the informant refuses to disclose any
information, document or thing that is required to
be disclosed under this section, the informant
must serve on the accused as soon as practicable a
written notice that the informant refuses
disclosure under section 45, identifying the
ground for refusing disclosure.

See section 416 as to the prosecution's general obligation of
disclosure.

nodes.heading: Accused may make request for material etc. not provided

nodes.text:
The accused may give to the informant a written
request for—
a copy of any things listed in a full brief;

a copy of any information, document or
thing specified by the accused that is
required by or under this Act to be included
in a preliminary brief or a full brief, as the
case may be, and was not so included;

particulars of previous convictions of any
witness who the prosecution intends to call at
the hearing.

Subject to subsection (3), a request under
subsection (1) may be made at any time after
service of the preliminary brief or the full brief,
whichever first occurs.

Unless the Magistrates' Court otherwise orders, a
request under subsection (1) must be made at least
7 days before—
the contest mention hearing; or

if a contest mention hearing is not held, the
summary hearing.

nodes.heading: Inspection of exhibits that include child abuse material where accused is legally represented

nodes.text: This section applies if—

a request under section 43(1)(c) relates to an
exhibit, or a part of an exhibit, that is child
abuse material; and

history.raw: S. 43A(1)(a) amended by No. 47/2016 s. 37(3). Example to s. 43A(2) amended by No. 47/2016 s. 37(4).

nodes.text: the accused is legally represented.

The accused may request inspection of the exhibit,
or the part of the exhibit, by the accused's legal
practitioner (but not the accused personally).

The informant may agree with the accused's legal
practitioner on a time and place for the accused's legal
practitioner to inspect exhibits that include child abuse
material. The legal practitioner may not show such an
exhibit to the accused but may discuss its content with the
accused in order to obtain instructions.

nodes.heading: Informant must comply with request or state grounds of refusal

nodes.text:
Within 7 days after the informant receives a
request under section 43, the informant must
comply with the request or serve on the accused a
written notice that the informant refuses to comply
with the request, identifying the grounds for
refusing disclosure.

The Magistrates' Court may vary a time limit
referred to in this section.

nodes.heading: Grounds on which informant may refuse disclosure

history.raw: Notes to s. 45 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(p).

nodes.text:
The informant may refuse to disclose any
information, document or thing that is required by
this Division to be disclosed to the accused if the
informant considers that disclosure would, or
would be reasonably likely to—

prejudice the investigation of a contravention
or possible contravention of the law or
prejudice the enforcement or proper
administration of the law in a particular
instance; or

prejudice the fair hearing of the charge
against a person or the impartial adjudication
of a particular case; or

disclose, or enable a person to ascertain, the
identity of a confidential source of
information in relation to the enforcement or
administration of the law; or

disclose methods or procedures for
preventing, detecting, investigating or
dealing with matters arising out of
contraventions or evasions of the law the
disclosure of which would, or would be
reasonably likely to, prejudice the
effectiveness of those methods or
procedures; or

endanger the lives or physical safety of
persons engaged in, or in connection with,
law enforcement or persons who have
provided confidential information in relation
to the enforcement or administration of the
law; or

endanger the life or physical safety of a
person referred to in section 43(1)(a) or of a
family member, as defined in the Family
Violence Protection Act 2008, of such a
person; or

result in the disclosure of child abuse
material to the accused personally.

history.raw: S. 45(1)(g) inserted by No. 42/2015 s. 15(1)(b), amended by No. 47/2016 s. 37(5).

nodes.text:
The informant may not refuse, on the ground
referred to in subsection (1)(g), a request under
section 43(1)(c) for inspection of exhibits by the
accused's legal practitioner (but not the accused
personally).

The informant may refuse to disclose any
information, document or thing that is requested
under section 43(1)(d) on any ground on which
the informant would be entitled to refuse to
produce the information, document or thing under
a witness summons.

The informant may refuse to disclose the
particulars of any previous conviction of any
witness who the informant intends to call at the
hearing if the previous conviction is, because of
its character, irrelevant to the proceeding but
the informant must advise the accused of the
existence of any undisclosed previous convictions.
See section 14 of the Victims' Charter Act 2006 as to
victims' privacy.

See section 416 as to the prosecution's general obligation of
disclosure.

nodes.heading: Accused may apply for order requiring disclosure

nodes.text:
The accused may apply to the Magistrates' Court
for an order under subsection (2) requiring
disclosure if—

the informant has served on the accused
under section 45 a statement of grounds for
refusing disclosure; or

the informant has failed to give disclosure in
accordance with this Division.

On application under subsection (1), the
Magistrates' Court may order that the informant
disclose to the accused any information, document
or thing in accordance with a request under
section 43 or a requirement of this Division.

Without limiting subsection (2), if an application
under subsection (1) relates to an informant's
refusal to disclose any information, document or
thing on the ground referred to in section 45(1)(g),
the Magistrates' Court, having regard to whether
the accused is legally represented, may order, on
any conditions specified by it, that the disclosure
be made to—

the accused's legal practitioner (but not the
accused personally); or
the accused personally.

history.raw: Note to s. 47(4) repealed by No. 68/2009 s. 9(f).
Note to s. 47 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 9(g).

nodes.text:
Subject to subsection (3), a statement referred to
in section 41 which the informant intends to
tender at the hearing of the charge if the accused
does not appear must be—
in the form of an affidavit; or

signed by the person making the statement
and contain an acknowledgment signed in
the presence of a person referred to in
Schedule 3 that the statement is true and
correct and is made in the belief that a
person making a false statement in the
circumstances is liable to the penalties of
perjury; or

in a form, and attested to in a manner,
prescribed by the rules of court.

If a person under the age of 18 years makes a
statement which the informant intends to tender as
mentioned in subsection (1), the statement must
include the person's age.

If a person who cannot read makes a statement
which the informant intends to tender as
mentioned in subsection (1)—

the statement must be read to the person
before he or she signs it; and

the acknowledgment must state that the
statement was read to the person before he or
she signed it.
Section 414 provides for acknowledgment of false statements.

nodes.heading: Disclosure of address or telephone number of witness

nodes.text:
The informant must not disclose the address or
telephone number (including a private, business
or official address or telephone number) of any
person in any information, document or thing
provided to the accused under this Division
unless—
the informant believes that—

the information, document or thing
does not identify the address or
telephone number as that of any
particular person; or

the address or telephone number is
relevant to the offence charged and
disclosure is not likely to present a
reasonably ascertainable risk to the
welfare or physical safety of any
person; or

the Magistrates' Court permits the disclosure
in accordance with subsection (3) on
application made by the informant or the
accused.

For the purposes of subsection (1), the informant
may delete, or render illegible, an address or
telephone number included in the information,
document or thing before service on the accused.

The Magistrates' Court may grant an application
made under subsection (1)(b) if the court is
satisfied that—

the address or telephone number is relevant
to the offence charged; and
one of the following applies—

disclosure is not likely to present a
reasonably ascertainable risk to the
welfare or physical safety of any
person; or

having regard to the matters referred to
in subsection (4), the interests of justice
outweigh any risk referred to in
subparagraph (i).

For the purposes of subsection (3)(b)(ii), the
Magistrates' Court must have regard to—
the right to privacy of the witness; and

the right of the accused to prepare properly
for the hearing.

See section 14 of the Victims' Charter Act 2006 as to victims'
privacy.

nodes.heading: Informant may place material on database

history.raw: Note to s. 49 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 9(i).

nodes.text: This section applies if—

the informant is a police officer or an officer
of a prescribed agency; and

history.raw: S. 49(1)(a) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.5).

nodes.text:
the accused's legal practitioner is authorised
by the Secretary to the Department of Justice
to access electronically the information,
documents and things referred to in
section 43; and

it is practicable to transmit electronically the
information, documents and things that are
required to be disclosed.

Subject to this Division, the informant must place
on the prescribed database a copy of—
the preliminary brief, if any; and
the full brief; and

all additional information, documents and
things, if any, requested by the accused
under section 43; and

all additional information, documents and
things required to be disclosed under
section 42.

Placement of copies of material on the prescribed
database under subsection (2) is deemed to be
service for the purposes of this Division.

Time limits provided in this Division for service of a
preliminary brief, a full brief or particular information,
documents or things still apply.

A statement by the informant in a copy of a
preliminary brief placed on the prescribed
database need not be sworn, affirmed or attested
as required by section 38 if—

history.raw: S. 49(4) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.2).

nodes.text:
the database technology does not permit
placement of the copy in that form; and

a physical copy of the preliminary brief
complies with section 38.

An informant who places an unsworn, unaffirmed
or unattested preliminary brief on the prescribed
database must retain the physical copy of the
preliminary brief that is sworn, affirmed or
attested for a period of 12 months after the
determination of the charge.

history.raw: S. 49(5) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.3).
Note to s. 49(5) repealed by No. 68/2009 s. 9(h).

nodes.text: Section 414 provides for acknowledgment of false statements.

nodes.heading: Preliminary disclosure of case of accused

nodes.text:
If the accused intends to call a person as an
expert witness at the hearing of the charge,
the accused must serve on the informant in
accordance with section 392 and file in court a
copy of the statement of the expert witness in
accordance with subsection (2)—

at least 7 days before the day on which the
contest mention hearing is to be held; or

if there is no contest mention hearing, at least
7 days before the summary hearing; or

if the statement is not then in existence, as
soon as possible after it comes into
existence.
The statement must—

contain the name and business address of the
witness; and

describe the qualifications of the witness to
give evidence as an expert; and

set out the substance of the evidence it is
proposed to adduce from the witness as an
expert, including the opinion of the witness
and the acts, facts, matters and circumstances
on which the opinion is formed.

Section 177 of the Evidence Act 2008 provides for certificates of
expert evidence.

This section applies to an accused on a summary
hearing, if the accused is represented by a legal
practitioner.

An accused must not, without leave of the court—
in support of an alibi unless the accused has given
notice of alibi within the period referred to in
subsection (3).
give evidence personally; or
adduce evidence from another witness—

A notice of alibi is given by serving the notice on
the prosecutor or the informant—

at least 7 days before the day on which the
contest mention hearing is to be held; or

if there is no contest mention hearing, at least
7 days before the summary hearing; or

if the notice is not then in existence, as soon
as possible after it comes into existence.

A notice of alibi must be served in accordance
with section 392.
A notice of alibi must contain—

particulars as to time and place of the alibi;
and

the name and last known address of any
witness to the alibi; and

if the name and address of a witness are not
known, any information which might be of
material assistance in finding the witness.

If the name and address of a witness are not
included in a notice of alibi, the accused must not
call that person to give evidence in support of the
alibi unless the court is satisfied that the accused
took reasonable steps to ensure that the name and
address would be ascertained.

If the accused is notified by the informant that a
witness named or referred to in a notice of alibi
has not been traced, the accused must give written
notice to the informant, without delay, of any
further information which might be of material
assistance in finding the witness.

The court must not refuse leave under
subsection (2) if it appears to the court that the
accused was not informed of the requirements of
this section.

If—
the court must grant an adjournment for a period
that appears to the court to be necessary to enable
investigation of the alibi unless it appears that to
do so would prejudice the proper presentation of
the case of the accused.

an accused gives notice of alibi under this
section; and
the prosecutor requests an adjournment—

nodes.heading: Offence to communicate with alibi witness

nodes.text:
If a person (other than a person referred to in
subsection (2)) has been named or referred to as a
proposed witness in a notice of alibi given under
section 51—
must not communicate with that person directly or
indirectly with respect to the charge or any related
matter before the conclusion of the proceeding,
including any rehearing, without the consent and
presence during the communication of—
Penalty: Level 8 imprisonment (1 year
maximum)
a person acting for the prosecution; or
a police officer—

history.raw: S. 52(1)(b) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.5).

nodes.text:
the legal practitioner representing the
accused; or
if not legally represented, the accused.

Subsection (1) does not apply to a person who the
accused has been notified may be called as a
witness for the prosecution at the summary
hearing.

nodes.heading: Mention hearing, summary case conference and contest mention hearing
Mention hearing
nodes.text:
At a mention hearing, the Magistrates' Court
may—

proceed immediately to hear and determine
the charge;
fix a date for a contest mention hearing;

fix a date for a summary hearing of the
charge;

make any other order or give any direction
that the court considers appropriate.

nodes.heading: Documents to be provided by police at first mention hearing

nodes.text:
This section applies if the informant is a police
officer.

history.raw: S. 53A(1) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.5).

nodes.text:
At the first mention hearing, the informant must
have the following documents available for
provision to the accused or the legal practitioner
representing the accused—
a copy of the preliminary brief (if prepared);
a copy of the full brief (if prepared);

if neither a preliminary brief nor a full brief
has been prepared—

a copy of the charge-sheet in respect of
the alleged offence; and

if applicable, a copy of the record of
reasons; and

a statement of the alleged facts on
which the charge is based; and
either—

a copy of the criminal record of
the accused that is available at the
time of the first mention hearing;
or

a statement that the accused has
no previous convictions or
infringement convictions known
at that time.

This section does not apply to a proceeding for a
traffic camera offence.

A summary case conference is a conference
between the prosecution and the accused for the
purpose of managing the progression of the case
including—

identifying and providing to the accused any
information, document or thing in the
possession of the prosecution that may assist
the accused to understand the evidence
available to the prosecution; and
identifying any issues in dispute; and

The presumption against criminal responsibility arises
for an offence allegedly committed by a child when
the person was 12 or 13 years of age.

identifying the steps required to advance the
case; and

any other purpose prescribed by the rules of
court.

If a preliminary brief is served within 21 days
after the day on which the charge-sheet is filed, a
summary case conference must be conducted
before—

the charge is set down for a contest mention
hearing or a summary hearing; or

a request for a full brief is made under
section 39(1).

The Magistrates' Court may direct the parties to
attend a summary case conference.

Nothing in this section prevents a summary case
conference from being conducted at any other
time, if the parties agree.

If an accused is not legally represented, the
Magistrates' Court may dispense with the
requirement under subsection (2) to conduct a
summary case conference.

A summary case conference must be conducted in
accordance with the rules of court.

Evidence of—
is not admissible in any proceeding before any
court or tribunal or in any inquiry in which
evidence is or may be given before any court or
person acting judicially,
unless—

anything said or done in the course of a
summary case conference; or

any document prepared solely for the
purposes of a summary case conference—

all parties to the summary case conference
agree to the giving of the evidence; or

the proceeding is a criminal proceeding for
an offence alleged to have been committed
during, or in connection with, the summary
case conference.
This section applies to a proceeding for—
a summary offence; or

an indictable offence that may be heard and
determined summarily.

The Magistrates' Court may, between the return
date and the day on which the charge is heard,
from time to time conduct a contest mention
hearing.

At a contest mention hearing, the Magistrates'
Court may—

require the parties to advise as to the
estimated number and the availability of
witnesses (other than the accused) for the
hearing of the charge and whether any
witnesses are from interstate or overseas;

require the accused to advise whether the
accused is legally represented and has
funding for continued legal representation up
to and including the hearing of the charge;

require the parties to advise whether there
are any particular requirements of, or
facilities needed for, witnesses and
interpreters;

order a party to make, file in court or serve
(as the case requires) any written or oral
material required by the court for the
purposes of the proceeding;

if the court considers that it is in the interests
of justice to do so, dispense with or vary any
requirement imposed on a party by or under
this Part;

require or request a party to do anything else
for the case management of the proceeding.

The accused must attend all contest mention
hearings.

history.raw: Note 1 to s. 55(4) amended by No. 38/2016 s. 9(2).

nodes.text: Section 3 defines attend.
See section 334 in relation to a corporate accused.

Section 330 gives the court power to excuse an accused
from attending a hearing.

nodes.heading: Joint or separate hearing of charges
Multiple charges on single charge-sheet or multiple accused named on single charge-sheet

nodes.text:
If a charge-sheet contains more than one charge,
the charges must be heard together unless an order
is made under section 58.

If a charge-sheet names more than one accused,
whether in the same charge or separate charges,
the charge or charges against all accused must be
heard together unless an order is made under
section 58.

A separate charge-sheet must be filed against each
accused.

nodes.heading: Joint hearing of charges on separate charge-sheets
nodes.text:
On the application of the prosecutor or the
accused, the Magistrates' Court may order that any
number of charges in separate charge-sheets be
heard together.

If a charge-sheet contains more than one charge,
the Magistrates' Court may order that any one or
more of the charges be heard separately.

If a charge-sheet names more than one accused,
the Magistrates' Court may order that charges
against a specified accused be heard separately.

The Magistrates' Court may make an order under
subsection (1) or (2) if the court considers that—

the case of an accused may be prejudiced
because the accused is charged with more
than one offence in the same charge-sheet; or

a hearing with co-accused would prejudice
the fair hearing of the charge against the
accused; or

for any other reason it is appropriate to do
so.

The Magistrates' Court may make an order under
subsection (1) or (2) before or during the hearing.

If the Magistrates' Court makes an order under
subsection (1) or (2), the prosecutor may elect
which charge is to be heard first.

The procedure on the separate hearing of a charge
is the same in all respects as if the charge had
been set out in a separate charge-sheet.

If the Magistrates' Court makes an order for a
separate hearing under subsection (1) or (2), the
court may make any order for or in relation to the
bail of the accused that the court considers
appropriate.
This section does not apply to—

an offence punishable by a minimum or
fixed sentence or penalty, including
cancellation or suspension of a licence or
permit to drive a motor vehicle and
disqualification under the Road Safety
Act 1986 or the Sentencing Act 1991 from
obtaining such a licence or permit or from
driving a motor vehicle on a road in Victoria
but not including the incurring of demerit
points under the Road Safety Act 1986 or
regulations made under that Act; or

an offence against section 49(1) of the Road
Safety Act 1986 not referred to in
paragraph (a).

If, at any time before taking a formal plea from an
accused in a criminal proceeding for a summary
offence or an indictable offence that may be heard
and determined summarily—
the Magistrates' Court may adjourn the proceeding
for a period not exceeding 12 months to enable the
accused to participate in and complete the
diversion program.

the accused acknowledges to the Magistrates'
Court responsibility for the offence; and

it appears appropriate to the Magistrates'
Court, which may inform itself in any way it
considers appropriate, that the accused
should participate in a diversion program;
and

both the prosecution and the accused consent
to the Magistrates' Court adjourning the
proceeding for this purpose—

An accused's acknowledgment to the Magistrates'
Court of responsibility for an offence is
inadmissible as evidence in a proceeding for that
offence and does not constitute a plea.

If an accused completes a diversion program to
the satisfaction of the Magistrates' Court—
no plea to the charge is to be taken; and

the Magistrates' Court must discharge the
accused without any finding of guilt; and

the fact of participation in the diversion
program is not to be treated as a finding of
guilt except for the purposes of—

Division 1 of Part 3 and Part 10 of the
Confiscation Act 1997; and

section 9 of the Control of Weapons
Act 1990; and

section 151 of the Firearms Act 1996;
and
Part 4 of the Sentencing Act 1991; and

the fact of participation in the diversion
program and the discharge of the accused
is a defence to a later charge for the same
offence or a similar offence arising out of
the same circumstances.

If an accused does not complete a diversion
program to the satisfaction of the Magistrates'
Court and the accused is subsequently found
guilty of the charge, the Magistrates' Court must
take into account the extent to which the accused
complied with the diversion program when
sentencing the accused.

Nothing in this section affects the requirement to
observe the rules of natural justice.

This section does not affect the incurring of
demerit points under the Road Safety Act 1986 or
regulations made under that Act.

history.raw: S. 60 amended by No. 49/2012 s. 4 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text:
At any time during a proceeding for a summary
offence or an indictable offence that may be heard
and determined summarily, the Magistrates' Court
may indicate that, if the accused pleads guilty to
the charge for the offence at that time, the court
would be likely to impose on the accused—

a sentence of imprisonment that commences
immediately; or
a sentence of a specified type.

Section 126 of the Magistrates' Court Act 1989 enables
the court to close a proceeding to the public.

Without limiting its discretion under
subsection (1), the Magistrates' Court may
decide not to give a sentence indication under
subsection (1) if the Magistrates' Court considers
there is insufficient information before it of the
impact of the offence on any victim of the
offence.

Under section 5(2)(daa) of the Sentencing Act 1991, in
sentencing an offender a court must have regard to the
impact of the offence on any victim of the offence.

If—
the court, when sentencing the accused for the
offence, must not impose a more severe type of
sentence than the type of sentence indicated.

the Magistrates' Court gives a sentence
indication under section 60; and

the accused pleads guilty to the charge for
the offence at the first available
opportunity—

If—
the court that hears and determines the charge
must be constituted by a different magistrate,
unless all the parties otherwise agree.

the Magistrates' Court gives a sentence
indication under section 60; and

the accused does not plead guilty to the
charge for the offence at the first available
opportunity—

A sentence indication does not bind the
Magistrates' Court on any hearing before the court
constituted by a different magistrate.

A decision to give or not to give a sentence
indication is final and conclusive.

An application for a sentence indication and the
determination of the application are not
admissible in evidence against the accused in any
proceeding.

This section does not affect any right to appeal
against sentence.

nodes.heading: Charge to be read or explained to accused before plea

nodes.text:
Subject to subsection (2), the Magistrates' Court
must ensure that any charge, as set out in the
charge-sheet, is read to the accused or its
substance is explained to the accused before the
accused is asked to plead to the charge.

It is not necessary that a charge be read, or its
substance explained, to an accused who is
represented by a legal practitioner if the
Magistrates' Court considers it appropriate not to
do so.

nodes.heading: Legal practitioner may enter plea on behalf of accused
nodes.text:
A legal practitioner appearing for an accused may,
on behalf of the accused, enter a plea.

If, when an accused is asked to plead to a charge,
the accused will not answer directly to the charge,
the Magistrates' Court may order that a plea of not
guilty be entered on behalf of the accused.

A plea of not guilty entered under subsection (1)
has the same effect as if the accused in fact had
pleaded not guilty.

See the Crimes (Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be Tried)
Act 1997 when an accused is or may be unfit to stand trial.

nodes.heading: Pleading to course of conduct charge

nodes.text:
In this section course of conduct charge has the
same meaning as in clause 4A of Schedule 1.

This section applies if an accused, on being asked
to plead to a course of conduct charge, informs the
court that they—

would plead guilty to the charge if it related
only to a specified period falling within the
period to which the charge set out in the
charge-sheet relates; and

would plead not guilty to the charge insofar
as it relates to any other period within the
period to which the charge set out in the
charge-sheet relates.

If an accused informs the court in accordance
with subsection (2) and the court is satisfied
that, having regard to that information, it is not
appropriate for the accused to be asked to plead to
the charge, the court may adjourn the proceeding
to allow a fresh charge-sheet to be filed relating
only to the specified period referred to in
subsection (2)(a).
If a fresh charge-sheet as described in subsection

is filed and the accused does not plead guilty
to the charge as set out in that charge-sheet, a
further fresh charge-sheet may be filed that sets
out the original charge or an amended version of
that charge.

If the accused does not plead to that charge, the
Magistrates' Court may order that a plea of not
