any other recording a transcript of which has
been served in the hand-up brief, other than a
recording that is inadmissible under
section 134(2).

The Magistrates' Court may rule as inadmissible
the whole or any part of—
a statement; or

any exhibit or document referred to in a
statement; or
the contents of a recording.

A recording, a transcript of which has been served
in the hand-up brief, is only admissible if it is
proved that the accused and his or her legal
practitioner were given a reasonable opportunity
to listen to and, in the case of an audiovisual
recording, view the recording.

nodes.heading: Procedure if accused makes admission of relevant fact or matter

nodes.text:
If under section 184 of the Evidence Act 2008 an
accused makes, during a committal proceeding, an
admission of any fact or matter that is relevant in
the proceeding, the Magistrates' Court must cause
the admission to be included in the record of the
proceeding.

An admission made by an accused during a
committal proceeding may be used in evidence at
the subsequent trial.

nodes.heading: Determination of committal proceeding where hand-up brief used
nodes.text:
If a hand-up brief is served and the accused has
not elected to stand trial under section 143, the
Magistrates' Court must commit the accused for
trial in accordance with section 144—

history.raw: S. 141 amended by Nos 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.1), 48/2018 s. 27, substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 7.

nodes.text:
if there is to be no cross-examination of
witnesses, at the end of the committal
mention hearing; or

if there is to be cross-examination of
witnesses, at the end of the committal
hearing.

nodes.heading: Determination of committal proceeding where plea brief used

nodes.text:
If a plea brief is served, the Magistrates' Court, at
the committal mention hearing, must—

ask how the accused pleads to the charge to
which the committal proceeding relates; and

if the accused pleads guilty, commit the
accused for trial in accordance with
section 144.

If the accused does not plead guilty to the charge
to which the committal proceeding relates, the
Magistrates' Court must direct the informant to
prepare and serve a hand-up brief.

nodes.heading: Determination of committal proceeding where accused elects to stand trial

nodes.text:
Any time after the service on an accused of a
hand-up brief, the accused may elect to stand trial.
An election is made by—

filing with the registrar a notice in the form
prescribed by the rules of court and signed
by the accused; and

serving a copy of the notice on the informant
in accordance with section 392.

As soon as practicable after a notice is filed with
the registrar under this section, the Magistrates'
Court must—

if the accused is in custody, direct that the
accused be brought before the court; or

if the accused is not in custody, direct that a
summons to attend or warrant to arrest be
issued.

On the attendance of the accused before the
Magistrates' Court, if the court considers that the
accused understands the nature and consequence
of the election, the court must commit the accused
for trial in accordance with section 144.

nodes.heading: Procedure before and on committing accused for trial

nodes.text:
Before committing an accused for trial, the
Magistrates' Court must, in the manner prescribed
by the rules of court, if any—

ask the accused whether the accused pleads
guilty or not guilty to the charge; and

inform the accused that the sentencing court
may take into account a plea of guilty and
the stage in the proceeding at which the plea
or an intention to plead guilty is indicated.

On committing an accused for trial, the
Magistrates' Court must—

if the accused was not represented by a legal
practitioner in the committal proceeding—

explain to the accused the importance
of obtaining legal representation for the
trial; and

advise that the accused has the right, if
eligible, to legal aid under the Legal
Aid Act 1978; and

warn the accused that, if the accused
wishes to be legally aided, it is the
accused's responsibility to make
application to Victoria Legal Aid as
soon as possible; and

explain to the accused, in a manner likely to
be understood by the accused—

the provisions of section 190
(alibi evidence), if relevant; and

the provisions of sections 342, 344
and 346, if relevant; and

any other information required to be
given by the rules of court; and

if the accused is a natural person, remand the
accused in custody, or grant bail, until trial
or a date before trial fixed by the court; and

history.raw: Note to s. 144(2)(c) substituted as Notes by No. 26/2017 s. 22.

nodes.text: Section 13 of the Bail Act 1977 prevents the

Magistrates' Court granting bail to a person
committed for trial on a charge of treason.

See section 333 where the accused is undergoing
a sentence of detention in a youth justice centre.

in the case of a corporate accused, order the
accused to appear, by a representative or a
legal practitioner, on the day on which the
trial of the accused is listed to commence or
on any other day specified by the court.

See section 252 (offence for corporate accused to fail
to appear on day trial listed to commence etc.).

nodes.heading: Transfer of summary offences that are related offences on or after committal

nodes.text:
Subject to subsection (3), on committal for trial
of an accused charged with an indictable offence,
the Magistrates' Court must order that all
proceedings in respect of charges against the
accused for summary offences that are related
offences are transferred to the court to which the
accused has been committed for trial.

If—
the Magistrates' Court must, subject to
subsection (3), order that the proceeding for the
summary offence is transferred to the court in
which the accused is to be tried.

an accused charged with an indictable
offence is committed for trial; and

before trial of the indictable offence, the
accused is charged with a summary offence
that is a related offence—

If the informant to a charge for a summary
offence that is a related offence or, if the DPP is
prosecuting the charge, the DPP and the accused
agree, the Magistrates' Court may order that the
proceeding for that charge is not transferred under
this section.
See the definition of related offences in section 3.

Section 242 enables the Supreme Court or the County Court
to hear and determine a charge for a related summary offence.

nodes.heading: Documents to be forwarded to DPP
nodes.text:
After committal the Magistrates' Court must
ensure there are forwarded to the DPP—
the depositions; and

all exhibits which have remained in the
custody of the Magistrates' Court; and

all recordings referred to in section 139
admitted in evidence in the committal
proceeding; and

copies of all process filed in the Magistrates'
Court in the proceeding; and

copies of all bail undertakings in the
proceeding.

nodes.heading: Accused entitled to copies of depositions and exhibits
nodes.text:
An accused committed for trial is entitled as soon
as possible after being committed—
to receive free of charge from the DPP—
a copy of the depositions; and

a transcript of any recording admitted
in evidence, if a transcript has not
previously been supplied to the
accused; and
to examine any exhibits.

nodes.heading: Absent corporate accused to be notified of committal
nodes.text:
If a corporate accused does not appear at its
committal proceeding and is committed for trial
in its absence, the DPP or, if the DPP did not
conduct the committal proceeding, the informant
must serve on the accused in accordance with
section 393 within 14 days after the committal a
notice stating—

that the Magistrates' Court has ordered the
accused to appear, by a representative or a
legal practitioner, on the day on which the
trial of the accused is listed to commence or
on any other day specified by the court and
that it is an offence not to comply with that
order; and

the date and time specified in the order at
which the accused must appear, by a
representative or a legal practitioner; and

that if the accused does not appear on the
date and time specified in the order the court
may, in its absence, proceed to hear and
determine the charge.

nodes.heading: Special mention hearing
nodes.text:
At a special mention hearing, the Magistrates'
Court may—

change the date fixed by the court for any
hearing in a committal proceeding;

if the court considers it appropriate to do
so, immediately conduct a committal
mention hearing and determine a committal
proceeding in accordance with section 141,
142 or 143.

If a corporate accused does not appear in answer
to a summons to answer to a charge for an
indictable offence, the Magistrates' Court may
conduct a committal proceeding in the absence of
the accused if—

the court is satisfied that the charge and the
date of the committal mention hearing in
relation to it have been brought to the notice
of the accused; and

the court considers that it is appropriate to do
so.

If the Magistrates' Court conducts a committal
proceeding in the absence of a corporate accused,
the court may dispense with or vary any
requirement imposed by or under this Chapter.

nodes.heading: Nothing in Chapter affects certain powers of DPP
nodes.text:
Nothing in this Chapter affects the power of the
DPP—

to file an indictment against a person for
an offence if, on a committal proceeding
conducted in relation to a charge for that
offence, the Magistrates' Court ordered the
person to be discharged on the charge; or

to discontinue a prosecution under
section 177, or not to take within the
period prescribed by section 163 any step
mentioned in that section, in relation to a
charge on which a person was committed for
trial.

nodes.heading: DPP may give directions for release of property tendered in evidence

nodes.text:
If property is tendered in evidence during a
committal proceeding and an accused is
committed for trial for an offence with respect
to the property, a person may apply in writing to
the DPP for the release of the property.

On receipt of an application under subsection (1),
the DPP may give directions in writing that the
property be released to the applicant.

The release of property under subsection (2) may
be subject to a condition that the property released
must be produced at the trial and to any other
conditions that the DPP considers appropriate.

The DPP may require a person to whom
property is released under this section to give an
undertaking to comply with the conditions to
which the release is subject.

A person must not fail, without reasonable cause,
to comply with an undertaking given by the
person under subsection (4).
Penalty: Level 10 fine (10 penalty units
maximum).

Directions given under subsection (2) do not
affect the legal title to the property or any legal
right to possession of the property.

The DPP is not liable for or with respect to any
direction given by the DPP under subsection (2).

Chapter 8 contains general provisions that apply to all criminal
proceedings.

nodes.heading: Application of Chapter
nodes.text: This Chapter applies if—

an accused is committed for trial under
Chapter 4; or

a direct indictment is filed against an
accused.

nodes.heading: DPP or Crown Prosecutor may file an indictment

nodes.text:
Subject to the Public Prosecutions Act 1994, the
DPP or a Crown Prosecutor in the name of the
DPP may file an indictment.

An indictment may be filed at any time, except
where otherwise provided by or under this or any
other Act.

Section 163 provides time limits for the filing of certain
indictments.
An indictment must—
be in writing; and

be signed by the DPP or a Crown Prosecutor
in the name of the DPP; and
comply with Schedule 1.

Section 253 abolishes the common law procedure of calling a
grand jury.

Section 172 permits the DPP to nominate an address for
service of documents.  That information may be included on
an indictment.

nodes.heading: Choice of Supreme Court or County Court for filing an indictment

nodes.text: An indictment may be filed in—
the Supreme Court; or

the County Court, if all of the indictable
offences alleged in the indictment are within
the jurisdiction of that court.

See section 36A of the County Court Act 1958 for
the criminal jurisdiction of the County Court.

In determining whether to file an indictment in the
Supreme Court or in the County Court, the DPP or
a Crown Prosecutor must have regard to—
the complexity of the case; and
the seriousness of the alleged offence; and

any particular importance attaching to the
case; and

any other consideration that the DPP or
Crown Prosecutor considers relevant.

nodes.heading: Direct indictment commences criminal proceeding
nodes.text:
The filing of a direct indictment commences a
criminal proceeding.

history.raw: Notes to s. 161 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zf).

nodes.text:
See the definition of direct indictment in section 3.
This includes an indictment filed after the Magistrates' Court
declines to commit an accused for trial in respect of the
offence charged in the indictment or a related offence.
A criminal proceeding may also be commenced—
in accordance with section 6; or

by a direction under section 415 that a person be tried
for perjury.

nodes.heading: Filing of any other indictment does not commence criminal proceeding
nodes.text:
The filing of an indictment other than a direct
indictment does not commence a new criminal
proceeding against the accused.

nodes.heading: Time limits for filing certain indictments

nodes.text:
If a person is committed for trial in respect of an
offence other than a sexual offence, the DPP or a
Crown Prosecutor may file an indictment against
the person—

within 6 months after the date of committal;
or

if the period referred to in paragraph (a) or
any extension of that period is extended
under section 247, within the extended
period.

If a person is committed for trial in respect of a
sexual offence in which the complainant was a
child or a person with a cognitive impairment
when the criminal proceeding was commenced,
the DPP or a Crown Prosecutor may file an
indictment against the person—
within 14 days after the date of committal; or

if the period referred to in paragraph (a) or
any extension of that period is extended
under section 247, within the extended
period.

If a person is committed for trial in respect of a
sexual offence other than one referred to in
subsection (2), the DPP or a Crown Prosecutor
may file an indictment against the person—

at least 28 days before the day on which the
trial is listed to commence; or

if the period referred to in paragraph (a), or
any extension or abridgment of that period,
is extended or abridged under section 247,
within the extended or abridged period.

In this section—
fresh indictment means an indictment which
includes a charge for the same offence as an
offence charged in an indictment previously
filed in court against that accused or a related
offence.

Nothing in section 163 prevents the filing of a
fresh indictment.

The filing of a fresh indictment does not
commence a new criminal proceeding.

On the filing of a fresh indictment against an
accused, proceedings in relation to a charge for
the same offence or a related offence in an
indictment previously filed in court against that
accused are discontinued.
See the definition of related offences in section 3.

history.raw: Note to s. 165 inserted by No. 81/2011 s. 13.

nodes.text:
The court at any time may order that an
indictment be amended in any manner that the
court thinks necessary, unless the required
amendment cannot be made without injustice to
the accused.

If an indictment is amended by order under this
section, the indictment is to be treated as having
been filed in the amended form for the purposes of
the trial and all proceedings connected with the
trial.

Section 327Q provides a limitation on amendments in the case of
direct indictments under Chapter 7A.

An indictment is not invalid by reason only of a
failure to comply with Schedule 1.

A charge on an indictment is not invalid by reason
only of—

omitting to state the time at which the
offence was committed unless time is an
essential element of the offence; or

incorrectly stating the time at which the
offence was committed; or

stating the offence to have been committed
on an impossible day or on a day that never
happened.

nodes.heading: Supreme Court may order that accused be tried in County Court or Supreme Court

history.raw: Note to s. 167 inserted by No. 38/2022 s. 77.

nodes.text:
If—
the Supreme Court may order that the accused be
tried at a sitting of the County Court specified in
the order.

an indictment against an accused is filed in
the Supreme Court; and

the offence charged in the indictment may be
tried by the County Court—

If an indictment against an accused is filed in the
County Court, the Supreme Court may order that
the accused be tried at a sitting of the Supreme
Court specified in the order.

If an order is made under section 167(1) or (2), the Supreme Court
may also order that a proceeding for a summary offence be
transferred from the Supreme Court to the County Court under
section 241A(1) or from the County Court to the Supreme Court
under section 241A(2) (as the case requires).

nodes.heading: Court may transfer certain charges to Magistrates' Court or Children's Court

nodes.text:
At any time except during trial, the Supreme
Court or the County Court may order that a
proceeding for a charge for an indictable offence
that may be heard and determined summarily be
transferred to the Magistrates' Court or the
Children's Court (as the case requires) if—
the accused consents to the transfer; and

the court considers that the charge is
appropriate to be determined summarily,
having regard to—

in the case of the Magistrates' Court,
the matters in section 29(2); or

in the case of the Children's Court,
whether the Children's Court is required
to hear and determine the charge
summarily by section 356(3) of the
Children, Youth and Families
Act 2005.

See section 28 for indictable offences that may be heard and
determined summarily.

Subject to section 168A, the court must not
transfer a charge that the Magistrates' Court or the
Children's Court has refused to hear and determine
summarily unless there has been a significant
change in the charges against the accused or in the
prosecution case against the accused.

If an order is made under this section, the
transferred charge must be heard and determined
summarily.

If an order is made under this section, the
transferring court may—

order that the accused appear before the
Magistrates' Court or the Children's Court
(as the case requires) on a specified date; or

if the accused is a natural person, remand the
accused in custody, or grant bail, to appear
before the Magistrates' Court or the
Children's Court (as the case requires) on a
specified date; or

in the case of a corporate accused, order the
accused to appear, by a representative or a
legal practitioner, before the Magistrates'
Court on a specified date.

Despite section 168(2), the court may, under
section 168(1), transfer a charge in respect of an
accused who is a child to the Children's Court if—

the charge is one that the Children's Court
has determined, under section 356(6),

or (7C) of the Children, Youth
and Families Act 2005, not to hear and
determine summarily; and

the court is satisfied that the sentencing
options available to the Children's Court
under the Children, Youth and Families
Act 2005 are adequate to respond to the
child's offending; and

the court is satisfied that any of the following
applies—

there is a substantial and compelling
reason why the charge should be heard
and determined summarily.

In determining whether there is a substantial and
compelling reason why the charge should be heard
and determined summarily, the court must have
regard to the intention of Parliament that the
following charges should not normally be heard
and determined summarily—

a charge for an offence referred to in
paragraph (f) of the definition of Category A
serious youth offence in section 3
committed by a child aged 16 years or over;

history.raw: S. 168A(1)(a) amended by No. 16/2020 s. 18, repealed by No. 54/2025 s. 24(2).

nodes.text:
These offences are terrorism and foreign incursion
offences.

a charge for a designated offence (within the
meaning of section 516 of the Children,
Youth and Families Act 2005) committed
by a child aged 14 years;

a charge for an offence against section 79 of
the Crimes Act 1958 (carjacking) committed
by a child who was 14 years of age or over.

Despite section 168(2), the court may, under
section 168(1), transfer a charge to the Children's
Court if the charge is for an offence referred to in
paragraph (b) or (c) of the definition of
Category B serious youth offence in section 3
committed when the child was aged 16 years or
over, after considering whether section 356(3)
of the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005
has the effect that the offence should not be heard
and determined summarily.

history.raw: Note to s. 168A(3) inserted by No. 54/2025 s. 24(7).

nodes.text:
The offences referred to in paragraphs (b) and (c) of the
definition of Category B serious youth offence in section 3
are rape and rape by compelling sexual penetration.

Despite section 168(2), the court may, under
section 168(1), transfer to the Children's Court a
charge that the Children's Court has determined,
under section 356(8A) of the Children, Youth
and Families Act 2005, not to hear and determine
summarily if the court is satisfied that there is a
substantial and compelling reason why the charge
should be heard and determined summarily.

nodes.heading: Place of hearing of criminal trial

nodes.text:
A criminal trial in the Supreme Court or the
County Court is to be held in the court sitting at
the place that is nearest to the place where the
offence is alleged to have been committed, unless
an order is made under section 192.

A criminal trial is not invalid only because it was
conducted at a place other than the place referred
to in subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Multiple charges or multiple accused on single indictment

nodes.text:
If an indictment contains more than one charge,
the charges must be heard together unless an order
is made under section 193 or 195.

If an indictment names more than one accused,
whether in the same charge or separate charges,
the charge or charges against all accused must be
tried together unless an order is made under
section 193.

The DPP must, as soon as practicable after an
indictment is filed, serve on the accused—
a copy of the indictment; and

if the DPP does not have notice that the
accused is represented by a legal practitioner,
a notice in the form prescribed by the rules
of court—

advising that legal representation
should be sought and that the accused
has the right, if eligible, to legal aid
under the Legal Aid Act 1978; and

providing details of how to contact
Victoria Legal Aid.

If a direct indictment is filed, the copy indictment
referred to in subsection (1)(a) must be served
personally on the accused in accordance with
section 391.

nodes.heading: DPP may nominate address etc. for service of documents

nodes.text:
The DPP may nominate in writing a business
address, email address or fax number for service
on the DPP of documents in relation to a charge.

A nomination under subsection (1) may be
included on an indictment or any other document
served on the accused.

nodes.heading: Extra notice for corporate accused
nodes.text:
If a corporate accused—
the DPP must serve with the copy indictment a
notice stating—

is to be served with a copy of an indictment
under section 171(1); and

has not been served with a notice in relation
to that offence under section 148—

the date and time specified in the order under
section 144(2)(d) at which the accused must
appear, by a representative or a legal
practitioner; and

that if the accused does not appear on the
date and time specified in the order, the court
may, in its absence—
proceed with the trial; and

if applicable, proceed to hear and
determine a summary offence under
Division 1 of Part 5.8.

nodes.heading: Compelling attendance when direct indictment filed

history.raw: Note to s. 174 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zh).

nodes.text:
On the filing in court of a direct indictment
against an accused, the DPP may apply to the
court for the issue of a summons or a warrant to
arrest in order to compel the attendance of the
accused.

On an application under subsection (1), the court,
if satisfied that the charge discloses an offence
known to law, must issue—

a summons requiring the accused to attend at
the court on a specified date and at a
specified time to answer to the indictment; or
subject to subsection (3), a warrant to arrest.

The court must not issue in the first instance a
warrant to arrest unless satisfied by sworn or
affirmed evidence, whether oral or by affidavit,
that—

history.raw: S. 174(3) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.1).

nodes.text:
it is probable that the accused will not
answer a summons; or

the accused has absconded, is likely to
abscond or is avoiding service of a summons
that has been issued; or

a warrant is required or authorised by any
other Act or for other good cause.

If the accused fails to attend before the court on
the date and at the time specified in the summons,
the court, on the application of the DPP, may issue
a warrant to arrest the accused.

Section 411 provides that an arrested person must, if practicable,
be brought before the court which issued the warrant.

The DPP must serve a summons issued under
section 174 by personal service on the accused in
accordance with section 391 at least 14 days
before the date specified in the summons.

A summons served on the accused must be
accompanied by—
a copy of the indictment; and

if applicable, a notice required by
section 171(1); and

in the case of a corporate accused, a notice
stating that, if the accused does not appear in
answer to the summons, the court may, in its
absence—
proceed with the trial; and

if applicable, proceed to hear and
determine a summary offence under
Division 1 of Part 5.8.

nodes.heading: Warrant to be accompanied by indictment and notice
nodes.text:
On execution of a warrant issued under
section 174, the warrant must be accompanied by
a copy of the indictment and, if applicable, a
notice required by section 171(1).

nodes.heading: DPP may discontinue a prosecution without adjudication

nodes.text:
The DPP may discontinue a prosecution for an
offence against an accused by—

announcing the discontinuance in court
(including by audio link or audio visual
link); or

filing in court written notice of the
discontinuance, signed by the DPP.
A prosecution may be discontinued—
at any time except during trial;

whether or not an indictment against the
accused has been filed.

If an indictment has not been filed against the
accused, the written notice referred to in
subsection (1)(b) must be filed in the court to
which the accused has been committed for trial.

If a discontinuance of prosecution is announced in
court, written notice of the discontinuance, signed
by the DPP, must be filed in court as soon as
practicable after the announcement.

The DPP must serve a copy of a written notice of
discontinuance that has been filed in court under
subsection (1)(b) or (4) on—
the accused; or
if the accused is dead, on—

the legal practitioner who last
represented the accused, if that legal
practitioner can reasonably be
identified; or

the next of kin of the accused, if that
person can reasonably be identified.

A discontinuance of prosecution does not amount
to an acquittal.

An accused may be indicted on a charge in respect
of which an earlier prosecution has been
discontinued.

nodes.heading: Release from custody on discontinuance of prosecution

nodes.text:
If—
the DPP must immediately notify the person who
has legal custody of the person that the
prosecution has been discontinued.

a prosecution for a charge against a person is
discontinued under section 177; and

the person is in custody in relation to that
charge, irrespective of whether the person is
in custody for any other reason—

On notification being given under subsection (1),
the person in custody is to be released, if the
person is not in custody for any other reason.

See Part 1A of the Corrections Act 1986 and section 483 of the
Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 as to who has legal
custody.

nodes.heading: Directions hearing
nodes.text:
At any time except during trial, the court may
conduct one or more directions hearings.
Section 210 sets out when a trial commences.

nodes.heading: Accused may be arraigned at a directions hearing

nodes.text:
The accused may be arraigned at a directions
hearing, if an indictment has been filed against the
accused.
Section 215 sets out how and when arraignment occurs.

Arraignment at a directions hearing does not
commence a trial: see section 210.

Despite subsection (1), if the accused pleads not
guilty to one or more charges in the indictment
and indicates an intention to plead not guilty to
one or more remaining charges, it is not necessary
for those remaining charges to be read to the
accused and the accused must be taken to have
pleaded not guilty to those charges.

nodes.heading: Powers of court at directions hearing

nodes.text:
At a directions hearing, the court may make or
vary any direction or order, or require a party to
do anything that the court considers necessary, for
the fair and efficient conduct of the proceeding.
Without limiting subsection (1), the court may—

require the accused to advise whether the
accused is legally represented and has
funding for continued legal representation up
to and including the trial;

without being limited by section 200, require
the parties to notify the court of any pre-trial
issues that the parties intend to raise or any
orders under section 199(1) or 206A that the
parties intend to seek;

without being limited by section 200, set a
timetable for the hearing of pre-trial issues or
applications for orders under Division 3, 4
or 5;

in the case of a trial for a sexual offence, a
family violence offence or an offence against
section 21A(1) of the Crimes Act 1958
(stalking) in which the complainant was a
child or a person with a cognitive
impairment when the criminal proceeding
was commenced—

history.raw: S. 181(2)(d) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 19, substituted by No. 48/2012 s. 13, amended by Nos 5/2025 s. 16, 1/2026 s. 71.

nodes.text:
require the prosecutor to advise as to
the availability of the complainant, and
the accused to advise as to his or her
own availability for the special hearing
to be held under Division 6 of Part 8.2;
and

give a direction under section 370(1A)
that the special hearing is to be held
before the trial or during the trial; and

if the special hearing is to be held
during the trial, specify the date on
which the special hearing is to
commence;

See section 5 as to the commencement of a criminal
proceeding.

require the parties to provide an estimate of
the length of the trial;

require the parties to advise as to the
estimated number and the availability of
witnesses (other than the accused) and any
relevant requirements of witnesses and
interpreters;

order a party to make, file in court or serve
(as the case requires) any written or oral
material required by the court for the
purposes of the proceeding;

order the prosecution to file in court and
serve on the accused a copy of any material
on which the prosecution intends to rely at
the trial;

determine an application for a sentence
indication.

At a directions hearing, the court may make any
order or other decision that can be made or
decided before trial by or under this or any other
Act.

history.raw: Note to s. 181(3) amended by No. 32/2024 s. 820(2).

nodes.text:
Sections 199(1) and 206A indicate the issues that may be
decided before trial under this Act.

In this section course of conduct charge has the
same meaning as in clause 4A of Schedule 1.

This section applies if the charge on an indictment
is a course of conduct charge and the accused—

would plead guilty to the charge if it related
only to a specified period falling within the
period to which the charge relates; and

would plead not guilty to the charge insofar
as it relates to any other period within the
period to which the charge relates.

The accused must, at a directions hearing or
otherwise, advise the court of the matters referred
to in subsection (2) as soon as possible after
deciding how to plead to the charge on the
indictment.

If an accused advises the court in accordance
with subsection (3) and the court is satisfied that,
having regard to that advice, it is not appropriate
for the accused to be arraigned, the accused must
not be arraigned at a directions hearing pending
the filing of a fresh indictment or the making of a
decision to proceed with the indictment as already
filed.

If a fresh indictment is filed against the accused
containing a charge relating only to the specified
period referred to in subsection (2)(a) and the
accused does not plead guilty to the charge on that
indictment, a further fresh indictment may be filed
containing the original charge or an amended
version of that charge.

The accused may be arraigned on that further
fresh indictment unless the court considers that it
is not in the interests of justice to do so.

nodes.heading: Summary of prosecution opening and notice of pre-trial admissions

nodes.text:
Unless the court otherwise directs, at least 28 days
before the day on which the trial of the accused is
listed to commence, the DPP must serve on the
accused and file in court—
a summary of the prosecution opening; and
a notice of pre-trial admissions.

The summary of the prosecution opening must
outline—

the manner in which the prosecution will put
the case against the accused; and

the acts, facts, matters and circumstances
being relied on to support a finding of guilt.

The notice of pre-trial admissions must identify
the statements of the witnesses whose evidence,
in the opinion of the DPP, ought to be admitted
as evidence without further proof, including
evidence that is directed solely to formal matters
including—
continuity; or
a person's age; or

proving the accuracy of a plan, or that
photographs were taken in a certain manner
or at a certain time.

If an accused has not received, under section 147,
a copy of a statement identified in a notice of
pre-trial admissions, the notice must contain a
copy of the statement.

nodes.heading: Response of accused to summary of prosecution opening and notice of pre-trial admissions

nodes.text:
After being served with a copy of the documents
referred to in section 182, the accused must serve
on the prosecution in accordance with section 392
and file in court, at least 14 days before the day on
which the trial of the accused is listed to
commence—

a copy of the response of the accused to the
summary of the prosecution opening; and

a copy of the response of the accused to the
notice of pre-trial admissions.

The response of the accused to the summary of the
prosecution opening must identify the acts, facts,
matters and circumstances with which issue is
taken and the basis on which issue is taken.

The response of the accused to the notice of
pre-trial admissions must indicate what evidence,
as set out in the notice of pre-trial admissions, is
agreed to be admitted as evidence without further
proof and what evidence is in issue and, if issue is
taken, the basis on which issue is taken.

Despite subsections (2) and (3), the accused is not
required to state—
whether the accused will give evidence.

nodes.heading: Intention to depart at trial from document filed and served
nodes.text:
If a party intends to depart substantially at trial
from a matter set out in a document served and
filed by that party under this Division, the party—

must so inform the court and the other party
in advance of the trial; and

if the court so orders, must inform the court
and the other party of the details of the
proposed departure.

history.raw: Notes to s. 185 amended by No. 68/2009 ss 49(i), 51(zk).

nodes.text:
This section applies to any information, document
or thing that—
and would have been required to be listed, or a
copy of which would have been required to be
served, in the hand-up brief.

comes into the possession of the prosecution
after an accused is committed for trial; or

is in the possession of the prosecution
when, or comes into the possession of the
prosecution after, a direct indictment is filed
against an accused—
See section 110 for the contents of a hand-up brief.

Subject to subsection (4) and section 185A, the
prosecution must serve on the accused a copy of
the document or list as soon as practicable after—
as the case requires.

the information, document or thing comes
into the possession of the prosecution; or

the direct indictment is filed against the
accused—

If the information, document or thing cannot
reasonably be copied, the prosecution must advise
the accused of the existence of the information,
document or thing and make it available for
inspection at a time and place agreed between the
accused and the prosecution.

The prosecution need not provide any
information, document or thing under this section
if it has already been provided to the accused by
the prosecution.

Section 188 requires the prosecution to serve a notice if
additional evidence is to be given at trial.

See section 416 as to the prosecution's general obligation of
disclosure.

nodes.heading: Disclosure of evidence that is child abuse material

nodes.text:
The prosecution need not provide, or make
available for inspection, any information,
document or thing that is required by section 185
to be provided or made available for inspection if
the prosecutor believes that doing so will result in
the disclosure of child abuse material to the
accused personally.

The accused may apply to the court for an order
requiring the prosecution to provide, or make
available for inspection, any information,
document or thing not provided or made
available for inspection under subsection (1).

The court, having regard to whether the accused is
legally represented, may order, on any conditions
specified by it, that the information, document or
thing be provided to or made available for
inspection by—

the accused's legal practitioner (but not the
accused personally); or
the accused personally.

nodes.heading: Disclosure of address or telephone number of witness

nodes.text:
The prosecution must not disclose the address or
telephone number (including a private, business or
official address or telephone number) of any
person in any information, document or thing
provided to the accused under this Division
unless—
the prosecutor believes that—

the information, document or thing
does not identify the address or
telephone number as that of any
particular person; or

the address or telephone number is
relevant to the offence charged and
disclosure is not likely to present a
reasonably ascertainable risk to the
welfare or physical safety of any
person; or

the court permits the disclosure in
accordance with subsection (3) on
application made by the prosecutor or the
accused.

For the purposes of subsection (1), the prosecution
may delete, or render illegible, an address or
telephone number included in the information,
document or thing before service on the accused.

The court may grant an application made under
subsection (1)(b) if the court is satisfied that—

the address or telephone number is relevant
to the offence charged; and
one of the following applies—

disclosure is not likely to present a
reasonably ascertainable risk to the
welfare or physical safety of any
person; or

having regard to the matters referred to
in subsection (4), the interests of justice
outweigh any risk referred to in
subparagraph (i).

For the purposes of subsection (3)(b)(ii), the court
must have regard to—
the right to privacy of the witness; and

the right of the accused to prepare properly
for the trial.

See section 14 of the Victims' Charter Act 2006 as to victims'
privacy.

The accused may request the prosecutor to
provide particulars of previous convictions of any
witness who the prosecution intends to call at the
trial.

A request under subsection (1) does not require
the prosecutor to give to the accused particulars of
any previous conviction of any witness if the
previous conviction is, because of its character,
irrelevant to the proceeding but the prosecutor
must advise the accused of the existence of any
undisclosed previous convictions.
See section 14 of the Victims' Charter Act 2006 as to
victims' privacy.

At a directions hearing the court may hear and determine any
objection to disclosure of any information, document or
thing: section 181(2)(i).

In this section—
additional evidence means any evidence that is
not included in the depositions in the
proceeding.

If the DPP intends to call a witness at trial to give
additional evidence, the DPP must serve on the
accused and file in court—

a notice of intention to call additional
evidence; and

a copy of the statement of the proposed
witness containing the additional evidence or
an outline of the additional evidence that the
witness is expected to give.
See the definition of depositions in section 3.

Section 185 (Continuing obligation of disclosure) requires
the prosecution to serve a copy of a document as soon as
practicable after the document comes into the possession of
the prosecution.

If the accused intends to call a person as an expert
witness at the trial, the accused must serve on the
prosecution in accordance with section 392 and
file in court a copy of the statement of the expert
witness in accordance with subsection (2)—

at least 14 days before the day on which the
trial of the accused is listed to commence; or

if the statement is not then in existence, as
soon as possible after it comes into
existence.
The statement must—

contain the name and business address of the
witness;

describe the qualifications of the witness to
give evidence as an expert;

set out the substance of the evidence it is
proposed to adduce from the witness as an
expert, including the opinion of the witness
and the acts, facts, matters and circumstances
on which the opinion is formed.

Section 177 of the Evidence Act 2008 provides for certificates of
expert evidence.

An accused must not, without leave of the court—
in support of an alibi unless the accused has given
notice of alibi within the period referred to in
subsection (2).
give evidence personally; or
adduce evidence from another witness—

A notice of alibi must be given by serving the
notice on the DPP within 14 days after—

the day on which the accused was committed
for trial on the charge to which the alibi
relates; or

if paragraph (a) does not apply, the day on
which the accused received a copy of the
indictment.

A notice of alibi must be served in accordance
with section 392.
A notice of alibi must contain—

particulars as to time and place of the alibi;
and

the name and last known address of any
witness to the alibi; and

if the name and address of a witness are not
known, any information which might be of
material assistance in finding the witness.

If the name and address of a witness are not
included in a notice of alibi, the accused must not
call that person to give evidence in support of the
alibi unless the court is satisfied that the accused
took reasonable steps to ensure that the name and
address would be ascertained.

If the accused is notified by the DPP that a
witness named or referred to in a notice of alibi
has not been traced, the accused must give written
notice to the DPP, without delay, of any further
information which might be of material assistance
in finding the witness.

The court must not refuse leave under
subsection (1) if it appears to the court that the
accused was not informed of the requirements of
this section.

If—
the court must grant an adjournment for a period
that appears to the court to be necessary to enable
investigation of the alibi unless it appears that to
do so would prejudice the proper presentation of
the case of the accused.

an accused gives notice of alibi under this
section; and
the DPP requests an adjournment—

nodes.heading: Offence to communicate with alibi witness

nodes.text:
If a person (other than a person referred to in
subsection (2)) has been named or referred to as a
proposed witness in a notice of alibi given under
section 190—
must not communicate with that person directly or
indirectly with respect to the charge or any related
matter before the conclusion of the proceeding,
including any new trial or rehearing, without the
consent and presence during the communication
of—
Penalty: Level 8 imprisonment (1 year
maximum)
a person acting for the prosecution; or
a police officer—

history.raw: S. 191(1)(b) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.5).

nodes.text:
the legal practitioner representing the
accused; or
if not legally represented, the accused.

Subsection (1) does not apply to a person who the
accused has been notified may be called as a
witness for the prosecution at the trial.

nodes.heading: Power to change place of trial
nodes.text:
If a court considers that—
the court may order that the trial be held at any
other place that the court considers appropriate.

a fair trial in a criminal proceeding cannot
otherwise be had; or

for any other reason it is appropriate to do
so—

If an indictment contains more than one charge,
the court may order that any one or more of the
charges be tried separately.

If an indictment names more than one accused, the
court may order that charges against a specified
accused be tried separately.

The court may make an order under subsection (1)
or (2) if the court considers that—

the case of an accused may be prejudiced
because the accused is charged with more
than one offence in the same indictment; or

a trial with the co-accused would prejudice
the fair trial of the accused; or

for any other reason it is appropriate to do
so.

The court may make an order under subsection (1)
or (2) or under section 195 before trial or during a
trial.

If the court makes an order under subsection (1)
or (2) or under section 195, the prosecutor may
elect which charge is to be tried first.

If an order under subsection (1) or (2) or under
section 195 is made after a jury is empanelled, the
court may order that the jury be discharged from
giving a verdict on the indictment.

The procedure on the separate trial of a charge is
the same in all respects as if the charge had been
set out in a separate indictment.

If the court makes an order for a separate trial
under subsection (1) or (2) or under section 195,
the court may make any order for or in relation to
the bail of the accused that the court considers
appropriate.

In this section—
sexual offence includes an offence to which
clause 1 of Schedule 1 to the Sentencing
Act 1991 applies.

Despite section 193 and any rule of law to the
contrary (other than the Charter of Human Rights
and Responsibilities), if in accordance with this
Act 2 or more charges for sexual offences are
joined in the same indictment, it is presumed that
those charges are to be tried together.

The presumption created by subsection (2) is not
rebutted merely because evidence on one charge is
inadmissible on another charge.

nodes.heading: Order for separate trial—conspiracy
nodes.text:
Despite section 193, if an indictment contains a
charge of conspiracy to commit an offence and
another charge alleging the commission of that
offence, the court must order that the charge of
conspiracy be tried separately from the other
charge, unless the court considers that it would be
in the interests of justice to try those charges
together.

nodes.heading: Other powers of court not affected
nodes.text:
Any power of the court under section 165, 193
or 195 is in addition to any other power of the
court for the same or similar purposes.

nodes.heading: Order for legal representation for accused

nodes.text:
In this section—
private law practice has the same meaning as in
the Legal Aid Act 1978;
private legal practitioner has the same meaning as
in the Legal Aid Act 1978.

Subject to subsection (3) and despite any rule of
law to the contrary (other than the Charter of
Human Rights and Responsibilities), the fact that
an accused has been refused legal assistance in
respect of a trial is not a ground for an
adjournment or stay of the trial.

If a court is satisfied at any time that—
the court may order Victoria Legal Aid to provide
legal representation to the accused, on any
conditions specified by the court, and may adjourn
the trial until that legal representation has been
provided.

it will be unable to ensure that the accused
will receive a fair trial unless the accused is
legally represented in the trial; and

the accused is in need of legal representation
because the accused is unable to afford the
full cost of obtaining from a private law
practice or private legal practitioner legal
representation in the trial—

Despite anything in the Legal Aid Act 1978,
Victoria Legal Aid must provide legal
representation in accordance with an order under
subsection (3).

Despite anything to the contrary in
subsection (3)—

if the court is satisfied that, in relation to the
trial, the accused has engaged in vexatious or
unreasonable conduct that has contributed to
the accused's inability to afford the full cost
of obtaining from a private law practice or
private legal practitioner legal representation
in the trial, the court may refuse to make an
order under subsection (3);

the legal burden of proof for the purposes of
subsection (3)(b) that the accused is unable
to afford the full cost of obtaining legal
representation rests on the accused;

for the purposes of proving under
subsection (3)(b) that the accused is unable
to afford the full cost of obtaining legal
representation, regard must be had to
property—
as determined in accordance with section 9
or 10 of the Confiscation Act 1997;

that is subject to the effective control of
the accused (whether or not the accused
has an interest in it); or
in which the accused has an interest—

the conditions that may be specified by the
court under subsection (3) do not include
conditions relating to the identity, number or
remuneration of persons representing the
accused.

A court must give Victoria Legal Aid an
opportunity to appear and be heard before an
order is made under subsection (3).

Despite anything to the contrary in this or any
other Act, Victoria Legal Aid may appeal to the
Court of Appeal, if the Court of Appeal gives
leave to do so, from an order under subsection (3)
made by the Trial Division of the Supreme Court
constituted by a Judge.

nodes.heading: Pre-trial taking of evidence and cross-examination

history.raw: Pt 5.5 Div. 3A (Heading) inserted by No. 48/2018 s. 29.

nodes.heading: Order for taking evidence from a witness before trial

nodes.text:
At any time except during trial, a party to a
criminal proceeding may apply to the court for
an order under this section that the evidence
(including cross-examination and re-examination)
of a person be taken at a time and place fixed by
the court.

An application may be made under subsection (1)
only if—

it is reasonably anticipated that the person
will be unavailable to give evidence at the
trial of the accused; or

the parties agree that the evidence of the
person should be taken before the trial of the
accused; or

for any other reason the court considers that
it is appropriate that the evidence of the
person should be taken before the trial of the
accused.

An application under subsection (1) must state the
grounds on which an order is sought.

The court must not make an order referred to in
subsection (1) unless it is satisfied that it is in the
interests of justice that the evidence of the witness
be taken.

An order referred to in subsection (1) may include
a direction that the evidence of the person is to be
given or recorded in a specified manner in
accordance with the Evidence (Miscellaneous
Provisions) Act 1958.

history.raw: S. 198(5) amended by No. 69/2009 s. 54(Sch. Pt 2 item 18.1).
Note to s. 198(5) amended by No. 69/2009 s. 54(Sch. Pt 2 item 18.2).

nodes.text:
Part VI of the Evidence (Miscellaneous Provisions)
Act 1958 provides for the recording of evidence.

nodes.heading: Order for accused to cross-examine witness before trial in certain cases

nodes.text: This section applies to a criminal proceeding—
to which section 123 applies; or

in which an accused has been committed for
trial under section 127B, 127C or 127E.

At any time except during trial, an accused may
apply to the court for an order under this section
that the accused cross-examine a witness, other
than a complainant in a criminal proceeding to
which section 123 applies, at a time and place
fixed by the court.
An application under subsection (2) must state—

each issue for which leave to cross-examine
is sought; and

how cross-examination of the witness on the
issue is directly and substantially relevant to
that issue; and

the reasons why, in the interests of justice,
the witness should be cross-examined on that
issue; and

why the accused is of the view that the
reasons referred to in paragraph (c) are
substantial reasons.

The court must not make the order sought in the
application unless the court is satisfied that—

the accused has identified an issue to which
the proposed questioning relates; and

cross-examination of the witness on the issue
is directly and substantially relevant to that
issue; and

there are substantial reasons why, in the
interests of justice, the witness should be
cross-examined on that issue.

In determining whether there are substantial
reasons why, in the interests of justice, the witness
should be cross-examined on that issue, the
court—

must have regard to the need to ensure the
matters set out in section 124(4); and

may have regard to whether the prosecution
consents to or opposes the order being made.

In addition, if the witness is a specified witness
(within the meaning of section 124(5A)), the court
must have regard to the matters set out in section
124(5).

If the court makes the order sought in the
application, the court must identify each issue on
which the witness may be cross-examined.

nodes.heading: Order for accused to conduct limited preparatory cross-examination

nodes.text:
An accused may apply to the court for an order
under this section that the accused cross-examine
a witness at a time and place fixed by the court.
An application under subsection (1) must state—

the issue to which the proposed questioning
relates; and
the purpose of the proposed questioning.

The court must not make the order sought in the
application unless the court is satisfied that it is
necessary to do so in order to avoid a serious risk
that the trial would be unfair.

In determining whether it is necessary to make the
order sought in the application in order to avoid a
serious risk that the trial would be unfair, the court
must have regard to—

the purposes of a committal proceeding as
set out in section 97; and

the limitations that apply in relation to cross-
examination of a witness at a committal
hearing.

If the court makes the order sought in the
application, the prosecution may re-examine a
witness who is cross-examined in accordance with
the order.
This section applies—
before trial; and
during trial.
During trial—

an application for an order under this section
must be heard in the absence of the jury; and

any cross-examination or re-examination in
accordance with an order under this section,
must be conducted in the absence of the jury.

nodes.heading: Abolition of Basha procedure
nodes.text:
The common law procedure of an accused
cross-examining a witness to enable the accused
to adequately prepare and present a defence is
abolished.

This provision abolishes the procedure of holding a hearing
of the kind attributed to R v Basha (1989) 39 A Crim R 337.

nodes.heading: Procedure for pre-trial orders and other decisions
Court may make orders and other decisions before trial

nodes.text:
At any time before trial, the court may hear and
decide any issue with respect to the trial that the
court considers appropriate, including—

history.raw: Note to s. 199(1) inserted by No. 32/2024 s. 821.

nodes.text:
an issue of fact, or mixed law and fact, that
may be determined lawfully by a judge alone
without a jury, including an issue as to
admissibility of evidence;

an application for an order that may be made
in relation to the trial under this or any other
Act or at common law, including an
application to quash a charge in the
indictment;
any other issue with respect to the trial.

For a pre-trial determination of whether the presumption
against criminal responsibility is rebutted, see Division 5.

Subsection (1) applies despite sections 181, 183,
184 and 200.

An order or other decision made at a directions
hearing or other pre-trial hearing has the same
effect as if it had been made after the
commencement of the trial.

Nothing in this section limits the power of the
court to make any order or other decision that it
has power to make otherwise than under
subsection (1).

Section 192A of the Evidence Act 2008 provides for advance
rulings in relation to evidence proposed to be adduced in a
proceeding.

If a party intends to raise an issue referred to in
section 199(1)(a), (b), (c) or (d), whether before or
during trial, the party must—

first, notify the other party of the issue or the
order sought, in order to ascertain whether
the issue will be in dispute or the order will
be opposed; and

secondly, notify the court of the issue or the
order sought.

Notification under subsection (1)(b) must
include—

confirmation that the other party has been
notified of the issue or the order sought; and

information, if available, as to whether the
issue is in dispute or the order is opposed.
Notification under subsection (1) must occur—

as soon as possible after the party becomes
aware of the issue and at least 14 days before
the day on which the trial of the accused is
listed to commence; or

if the party is not aware of the issue within
the period referred to in paragraph (a), as
soon as possible after the party becomes
aware of it.

nodes.heading: Court may decide pre-trial issue without a hearing

nodes.text:
This section applies if the court is notified of an
issue under section 200(1) at least 14 days before
the day on which the trial of the accused is listed
to commence.

The court may decide the issue without an oral
hearing and entirely on the basis of written
submissions and without the appearance of the
parties—

if the court is satisfied that it is in the
interests of justice to do so; and

whether or not the parties consent to the
court doing so.

For the purposes of subsection (1A), in deciding
whether it is in the interests of justice to decide
the issue without an oral hearing, the court must
have regard to—
the right of an accused to a fair hearing; and
the nature of the issue; and

whether the accused or the offender (as the
case requires) has had the opportunity to
obtain legal advice; and

whether the parties consent to the court
doing so.

If the court decides to decide the issue on the basis
of written submissions, at least 10 days before the
day on which the trial of the accused is listed to
commence, the party who raised the issue must
file in court and serve on all other parties a copy
of that party's submission.

Within 5 days after a party is served with a copy
of a submission under subsection (2), that party
must file in court and serve on all other parties a
copy of a written submission in reply.

Within 3 days after a party is served with a written
submission in reply under subsection (3), that
party must file in court and serve on all other
parties a copy of a written submission in response
to the reply.

nodes.heading: Hearing of application for exclusion of evidence
nodes.text:
On the hearing of an application by the accused
for the exclusion of evidence, the court may hear
evidence called on behalf of the accused before it
hears evidence called on behalf of the prosecution.

nodes.heading: Judge at pre-trial hearing need not be trial judge
nodes.text:
The judge who constitutes the court at a
directions hearing or other pre-trial hearing held
in connection with the trial of an accused need not
be the trial judge on the trial of the accused.

nodes.heading: Pre-trial orders and other decisions generally binding on trial judge

history.raw: S. 204 amended by No. 32/2024 s. 822 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text:
An order or other decision made at a directions
hearing or other pre-trial hearing by a judge who
is not the trial judge is binding on the trial judge
unless the trial judge considers that it would not
be in the interests of justice for the order or other
decision to be binding.

This section does not apply to a pre-trial
determination of whether the presumption against
criminal responsibility is rebutted.
See section 206E.

nodes.heading: Pre-trial orders and other decisions may be applied in new trial

nodes.text:
If a new trial is held, the court may treat any order
or other decision made at a directions hearing or
other pre-trial hearing held in connection with the
earlier trial as if it had been made at a directions
hearing or other pre-trial hearing held in
connection with the new trial.

Despite subsection (1), the court need not treat an
order or other decision in the manner set out in
subsection (1) if the court considers that to do
so—

would be inconsistent with any order or
decision made or direction given on an
appeal; or

would otherwise not be in the interests of
justice.

nodes.heading: Procedure if prosecution proposes not to lead evidence

nodes.text:
This section applies if, before the trial of an
accused commences, the accused is arraigned and
pleads not guilty to a charge in respect of which
the prosecution proposes not to lead evidence.

The prosecution must inform the court that the
prosecution proposes not to lead evidence on the
charge.

The court must direct that an entry of not guilty
be made on the record in respect of the charge.

An entry of not guilty under subsection (3) has
the same effect as if it were the verdict of a jury
on the trial of the accused on that charge.

This section does not limit the power to
discontinue a prosecution under section 177.

nodes.heading: Procedure for pre-trial hearing about presumption against criminal responsibility
Application for pre-trial hearing about presumption against criminal responsibility

nodes.text:
At any time before trial of an accused for an
offence allegedly committed at 12 or 13 years of
age, the court may order that the issue of whether
the presumption against criminal responsibility is
rebutted be determined by a judge alone, without a
jury, if—

the offence is an indictable offence under an
Act; and

the charge for the offence will not be heard
and determined summarily; and

the court is satisfied that the accused has
obtained legal advice on the effect of the
issue being determined by a judge alone,
without a jury, before the trial of the
accused; and

the court considers that it is in the interests of
justice to determine the issue before the trial
of the accused.

The court may make an order under subsection (1)
on the application of the accused.

If the accused intends to raise the issue of whether
the presumption against criminal responsibility is
rebutted before trial, the accused must give notice
to the court and the prosecution in accordance
with section 200.

In determining whether to make an order under
subsection (1), the court is to have regard to the
submissions, if any, of the prosecution and the
accused.

The court may make an order under subsection (1)
whether or not the prosecution consents to the
making of the order.

Subsection (1) applies despite sections 181, 183
and 184.

To avoid doubt, this section does not limit the
application of section 199(1) in relation to any
other issue that the court considers appropriate to
hear and decide before a trial.

nodes.heading: Issue to be determined expeditiously
nodes.text:
A pre-trial determination of the issue of whether
the presumption against criminal responsibility is
rebutted must be conducted at the earliest possible
opportunity before the arraignment of a person
accused of committing an offence at 12 or
13 years of age.

nodes.heading: Conduct of pre-trial hearing about presumption against criminal responsibility

nodes.text:
Despite section 201, if a court is determining the
issue of whether the presumption against criminal
responsibility is rebutted before the trial of the
accused, the court is to conduct an oral hearing to
determine the issue.

On the application of the accused, the court may
excuse the accused from attending the hearing
if—
the accused is a child; and

the court is satisfied that it is in the interests
of justice to conduct the hearing without the
attendance of the accused.

For the purposes of subsection (2), in determining
whether it is in the interests of justice, the court is
to have regard to—
the right of an accused to a fair hearing; and

any information from the prosecution and the
accused about the nature of any evidence that
is proposed to be adduced; and

whether the prosecution consents to the
determination of the issue without the
attendance of the accused.

nodes.heading: Court to be constituted by the same judge who made pre-trial determination
nodes.text:
Despite section 203, as far as practicable, in the
trial of a person who is accused of committing an
offence at 12 or 13 years of age, the court is to be
constituted by the same judge who constitutes the
court in the pre-trial hearing of the issue of
whether the presumption against criminal
responsibility is rebutted.

nodes.heading: Determination at pre-trial hearing as to whether presumption is rebutted

nodes.text:
At a pre-trial hearing of the issue of whether the
presumption against criminal responsibility is
rebutted in respect of a charge for an offence, the
court—

may determine that the prosecution has not
rebutted the presumption and direct that an
entry of not guilty be made on the record in
respect of the charge; or

may determine that the prosecution has
rebutted the presumption and order that the
matter proceed to trial or to the
determination of other pre-trial issues (as the
case requires).

An entry of not guilty under subsection (1)(a) has
the same effect as if it were the verdict of a jury
on the trial of the accused on the charge.

A determination under subsection (1)(b) has the
same effect as if it had been made after the
commencement of the trial of the accused on the
charge.

nodes.heading: Judgment in pre-trial hearing of presumption against criminal responsibility
nodes.text:
In a pre-trial hearing of the issue of whether the
presumption against criminal responsibility is
rebutted, the reasons for judgment or decision
must include—

the principles of law applied by the court;
and
the facts on which the court relied.

In a pre-trial hearing of the issue of whether the
presumption against criminal responsibility is
rebutted, the court, if satisfied that it is in the
public interest to do so, may order that any of the
following must not be published except in the
manner and to the extent (if any) specified in the
order—

a report of the whole or any part of the
hearing;
evidence given in the pre-trial hearing;

the content of any report or other document
put before the court in the pre-trial hearing;

information that might enable an accused or
any person who has appeared or given
evidence in the pre-trial hearing to be
identified.
An order under this section may be made—

on the application of a party or on the court's
own motion; and

at any time, including at the time an order is
made under section 206A(1).

A person must not publish or cause to be
published any material in contravention of an
order under this section.
Penalty: in the case of an individual, Level 6
imprisonment (5 years maximum);
in the case of a body corporate,
3000 penalty units.

At any time after the indictment is filed but before
the trial commences, the court may indicate that,
if the accused pleads guilty to any charge on the
indictment at that time or another charge, the court
would be likely to impose on the accused—
a sentence of a specified type; or

a specified maximum total effective
sentence.
See section 210 for when a trial commences.

A sentence indication is given in relation to any
charges specified in the application under
section 208, not an individual charge.

The Open Courts Act 2013 enables the court to close a
proceeding or part of a proceeding to the public.
A sentence indication under section 207—

history.raw: Note to s. 208(1) inserted by No. 1/2022 s. 112(2).

nodes.text:
may be given only on the application of the
accused; and

may be given only once during the
proceeding, unless subsection (3A) applies.

See section 9B of the Victims' Charter Act 2006 for
obligations of the DPP to a victim in relation to an
application for a sentence indication.

If an application under subsection (1)(a) is made
in respect of a charge that is not on the indictment,
the accused must specify the charge in the
application.

A second or subsequent sentence indication may
be given if there has been a change in
circumstances since the previous sentence
indication that is likely to materially affect the
sentence indication previously given.

The court may refuse to give a sentence indication
under section 207.

Without limiting subsection (4), the court may
refuse to give a sentence indication under
section 207 if the court considers there is
insufficient information before it of the impact
of the offence on any victim of the offence.

Under section 5(2)(daa) of the Sentencing Act 1991, in
sentencing an offender a court must have regard to the
impact of the offence on any victim of the offence.

If—
the court, when sentencing the accused for the
offence, must not impose a more severe sentence
than the sentence type or maximum total effective
sentence indicated.

the court gives a sentence indication under
section 207; and

the accused pleads guilty to any charge to
which the sentence indication relates at the
first available opportunity—

A sentence indication does not bind the court on
any hearing before the court constituted by a
different judge.

A decision to give or not to give a sentence
indication is final and conclusive.

An application for a sentence indication and
the determination of the application are not
admissible in evidence against the accused in
any proceeding.

This section does not affect any right to appeal
against sentence.

nodes.heading: Review of amendments—Justice Legislation Amendment (Criminal Procedure Disclosure and Other Matters) Act 2022

nodes.text:
The Attorney-General must review the operation
of the amendments made to Part 5.6 and
section 9B of the Victims' Charter Act 2006 by
the Justice Legislation Amendment (Criminal
Procedure Disclosure and Other Matters)
Act 2022 to determine—

their effectiveness in reducing delay in the
courts; and
their impact on victims; and

the availability of information before the
courts of the impact of an offence on any
victim of the offence at the time that the
court is considering an application for a
sentence indication.

A review under subsection (1) must be conducted
not later than 2 years after the amendments are
made to Part 5.6 by the Justice Legislation
Amendment (Criminal Procedure Disclosure
and Other Matters) Act 2022.

A trial commences when the accused pleads not
guilty on arraignment in the presence of the jury
panel in accordance with section 217.

If a jury panel is split into 2 or more parts under
section 30(5) of the Juries Act 2000, the trial
commences when the accused pleads not guilty
on arraignment in the presence of the first part of
the jury panel that is present in court.
Section 215 sets out how and when arraignment occurs.

nodes.heading: Time limit for commencing trial for offences other than sexual offences
nodes.text:
The trial of a person for an offence (other than a
sexual offence) must commence—

within 12 months after the day on which the
person is committed for trial in respect of the
offence; or

if no committal proceeding in respect of the
offence is held, within 12 months after the
day on which the indictment against the
person is filed; or

if a new trial is ordered by the Court of
Appeal, within 6 months after the day on
which the order is made; or

if the period referred to in paragraph (a), (b)
or (c) or any extension of that period is
extended under section 247, within the
extended period.

nodes.heading: Time limits for commencing trials for sexual offences
nodes.text:
The trial of a person for a sexual offence must
commence—

within 3 months after the day on which the
person is committed for trial in respect of the
offence; or

if no committal proceeding in respect of the
offence is held, within 3 months after the day
on which the indictment against the person is
filed; or

if a new trial is ordered by the Court of
Appeal, within 3 months after the day on
which the order is made; or

if the period referred to in paragraph (a), (b)
or (c) or any extension of that period is
extended under section 247, within the
extended period.

nodes.heading: Powers of trial judge not affected

nodes.text:
Subject to section 204, a trial judge may make any
order or other decision during trial that could have
been made under Division 3 or 4 of Part 5.5.

Nothing in this Act removes or limits any powers
of a trial judge that existed immediately before the
commencement of this Act.

nodes.heading: Non-appearance of corporate accused at trial

nodes.text:
If a corporate accused does not appear on the
date and at the time specified in an order under
section 144(2)(d), the court, may, in its absence,
proceed with the trial and, if applicable, proceed
to hear and determine a summary offence under
Division 1 of Part 5.8 if—

the court is satisfied that a notice under
section 148 or 173 has been served on the
accused; and

the court considers that it is appropriate to do
so.

If the court conducts a trial in the absence of a
corporate accused, the court may dispense with or
vary any requirement imposed by or under this
Part.
An accused is arraigned when the court—

asks the accused whether the accused is the
person named on the indictment; and

reads out each charge on the indictment and
asks the accused whether the accused pleads
guilty or not guilty to the charge.

An accused may be arraigned or re-arraigned at
any time.

nodes.heading: Written pleas of guilty may be accepted

nodes.text:
If an accused pleads guilty to one or more charges
in the indictment and indicates an intention to
plead guilty to one or more remaining charges—

it is not necessary for those remaining
charges to be read to the accused; and

the court may accept pleas of guilty to the
remaining charges in the indictment by
written notice signed by the accused.

A court must not accept pleas of guilty under
subsection (1)(b) unless—
the prosecution consents; and

the court considers that it is appropriate to do
so, having regard to the number of charges in
the indictment.

A plea of guilty accepted under this section has
the same effect as if it were entered on
arraignment.

nodes.heading: Arraignment in presence of jury panel
nodes.text:
If an accused has not pleaded guilty to all of the
charges on an indictment—

the accused must be arraigned in the
presence of the jury panel or, if a jury panel
is split into 2 or more parts under
section 30(5) of the Juries Act 2000, the
first part of the jury panel that is present in
court; and

a jury for the trial must be empanelled from
that jury panel.

A trial commences when arraignment under this section
occurs: see section 210.
The Juries Act 2000 sets out the process for empanelling a
jury.

nodes.heading: Special pleas in addition to plea of not guilty
nodes.text:
On arraignment, an accused may enter a special
plea in addition to pleading not guilty.

nodes.heading: Plea of guilty to alternative offence

nodes.text:
On arraignment, an accused may plead not guilty
to the offence charged but guilty to another
offence of which the accused might be found
guilty.

The consequences of pleading guilty to another
offence under subsection (1) are the same as if the
other offence had been charged in the indictment.

nodes.heading: Form of plea of previous conviction or previous acquittal

nodes.text:
In a plea of previous conviction, it is sufficient
for an accused to state that the accused has been
lawfully convicted of the offence charged in the
indictment.

In a plea of previous acquittal, it is sufficient for
an accused to state that the accused has been
lawfully acquitted of the offence charged in the
indictment.

Subject to Chapter 7A, the rules of common law
with respect to autrefois convict and autrefois
acquit continue in force in respect of pleas of
previous conviction and previous acquittal,
respectively.

If, on arraignment, an accused will not answer
directly to a charge on the indictment, the court
may order that a plea of not guilty be entered on
behalf of the accused.

A plea of not guilty entered under subsection (1)
has the same effect as if the accused in fact had
pleaded not guilty.

See the Crimes (Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be
Tried) Act 1997 when an accused is or may be unfit to
stand trial.

nodes.heading: Judge may address jury
nodes.text:
At any time during a trial, the trial judge may
address the jury on—

the issues that are expected to arise or have
arisen in the trial;

the relevance to the conduct of the trial of
any admissions made, directions given or
matters determined prior to the
commencement of the trial;

any other matter relevant to the jury in
the performance of its functions and its
understanding of the trial process, including
giving a direction to the jury as to any issue
of law, evidence or procedure.

nodes.heading: Jury documents relating to trial issues and evidence

nodes.text:
For the purpose of helping the jury to understand
the issues or the evidence, the trial judge may
order, at any time during the trial, that copies of
any of the following are to be given to the jury in
any form that the trial judge considers
appropriate—
the indictment;
the summary of the prosecution opening;

the response of the accused to the summary
of the prosecution opening and the response
of the accused to the notice of pre-trial
admissions of the prosecution;
any document admitted as evidence;
any statement of facts;

the opening and closing addresses of the
prosecution and the accused;

any address of the trial judge to the jury
under section 222;
See sections 29(4) and 50 of the Evidence Act 2008.
the transcript of the evidence in the trial;

transcripts of evidence or audio or
audiovisual recordings of evidence;

transcripts of any audio or audiovisual
recordings;

the trial judge's directions to the jury under
section 238;
a jury guide specific to the trial;

history.raw: S. 223(1)(ka) inserted by No. 12/2013 s. 29(2), amended by No. 37/2017 s. 11(2).

nodes.text:
any other document that the trial judge
considers appropriate.

A jury guide referred to in subsection (1)(ka) may
contain any of the following—

a list of questions to assist the jury in
