the presumption against criminal responsibility
has been rebutted in respect of a charge for an
offence allegedly committed by a person at 12 or
13 years of age.

The appeal is to be determined on the evidence, if
any, given in the proceeding to which the appeal
relates, unless the Court of Appeal gives leave to
adduce additional evidence.
Despite section 300(2), the Court of Appeal—

may affirm the decision that the presumption
against criminal responsibility is rebutted; or

may set aside the decision and enter a
judgment of acquittal of the relevant offence.

On affirming a decision that the presumption
against criminal responsibility is rebutted, the
Court of Appeal may order that the matter proceed
to trial or to the determination of other pre-trial
issues (as the case requires).

A judgment of acquittal of the relevant offence
under subsection (3)(b)—

has the same effect as if it were a verdict of
not guilty by the jury on the trial of the
accused for the charge for the offence; and

is to be entered on the record of the court
that made the decision as a decision of not
guilty.

nodes.heading: Determination of interlocutory appeal to be entered on record
nodes.text:
The Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme
Court must transmit the decision of the Court of
Appeal to the court which made the interlocutory
decision and that court must enter the decision on
the court record.

nodes.heading: Case stated for Court of Appeal

nodes.text:
This section applies to a proceeding in the County
Court or the Trial Division of the Supreme Court
for the prosecution of an indictable offence.

In a proceeding referred to in subsection (1), if
a question of law arises before or during the
trial, the court may reserve the question for
determination by the Court of Appeal if the
court is satisfied that it is in the interests of
justice to do so, having regard to—

the extent of any disruption or delay to the
trial process that may arise if the question of
law is reserved; and

whether the determination of the question of
law may—
render the trial unnecessary; or

substantially reduce the time required
for the trial; or

resolve a novel question of law that is
necessary for the proper conduct of the
trial; or

reduce the likelihood of a successful
appeal against conviction in the event
that the accused is convicted at trial.

The court must not reserve a question of law after
the trial has commenced, unless the reasons for
doing so clearly outweigh any disruption to the
trial.

Section 33 of the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities
Act 2006 also provides for the referral to the Supreme Court of
questions of law that relate to the application of the Charter or the
interpretation of a statutory provision in accordance with the
Charter.

nodes.heading: Reservation of question of law on appeal to County Court
nodes.text:
If on the hearing of an appeal under Part 6.1 to
the County Court from the Magistrates' Court
a question of law arises, the County Court may
reserve the question for determination by the
Court of Appeal if the court is satisfied that it is in
the interests of justice to do so, having regard to—

the extent of any disruption or delay to the
hearing that may arise if the question of law
is reserved; and

whether the determination of the question of
law may—
render the hearing unnecessary; or

substantially reduce the time required
for the hearing; or

resolve a novel question of law that is
necessary for the proper conduct of the
hearing.

nodes.heading: Adjournment if question of law reserved

history.raw: S. 303 amended by No. 48/2012 s. 19 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text:
If a court reserves a question of law under
section 302 after the trial has commenced, the
court must adjourn the trial without discharging
the jury, if reasonably practicable, until the
question of law has been determined.

If a court reserves a question of law under
section 302A, the court must adjourn the hearing,
if reasonably practicable, until the question of law
has been determined.

nodes.heading: Refusal to reserve question of law

nodes.text:
If the Supreme Court or the County Court refuses
an application under section 302 or 302A to
reserve a question of law, the applicant may apply
to the Court of Appeal for an order calling on—
to show cause why the question of law should not
be reserved for determination by the Court of
Appeal.

the court which dismissed the application;
and
the respondent—

On an application under subsection (1), the Court
of Appeal may order that the question of law be
reserved for its determination or refuse the
application with or without costs.

If the Court of Appeal orders that the question of
law be reserved, the court to which the order is
directed must reserve the question for
determination by the Court of Appeal.

nodes.heading: Case to be stated if question of law reserved

nodes.text:
If a court reserves a question of law under
section 302, 302A or 304, it must state a case,
setting out the question and the circumstances in
which the question has arisen.

The court must sign the case stated and transmit it
within a reasonable time to the Court of Appeal.

The Court of Appeal may return a case stated
transmitted to it under subsection (2) for
amendment and the court that stated the case must
amend it as required.

nodes.heading: General powers of Court of Appeal on case stated

nodes.text:
The Court of Appeal may hear and finally
determine a question of law set out in a case
stated.

In the case of a question of law reserved under
section 302, 302A or 304, the Court of Appeal
may remit the question and the determination of
the Court of Appeal back to the court which
reserved the question.

The applicant is not required to attend the hearing
under subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Judgment to be entered on record
nodes.text:
The Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme
Court must transmit the judgment and order
(if any) of the Court of Appeal to the court that
reserved the question of law and that court must
enter the judgment and order (if any) on the court
record.

nodes.heading: DPP may refer point of law to Court of Appeal

nodes.text:
If a person is acquitted in respect of all or any
charges—
the DPP may refer to the Court of Appeal any
point of law that has arisen in the proceeding.

in a trial on indictment before the Supreme
Court or the County Court; or

on an appeal to the County Court from the
Magistrates' Court or, if the Magistrates'
Court was constituted by the Chief
Magistrate who is a dual commission holder,
to the Court of Appeal—

For the avoidance of doubt, if a point of law arises
in an appeal proceeding, and that appeal is from
the Magistrates' Court constituted by the Chief
Magistrate who is a dual commission holder,
subsection (1)(b) does not apply.

The Court of Appeal is to consider a point of law
referred to it under subsection (1) and give its
opinion on it.

An acquitted person who appears in court in
person or by a legal practitioner is entitled to
reasonable costs as settled by the Costs Court.

A reference under this section does not affect the
trial or hearing in relation to which the reference
is made or an acquittal in that trial or hearing.

nodes.heading: Status of sentences and orders during appeal period
Sentence not stayed during appeal period

nodes.text:
A sentence is not stayed during the appeal period
unless—

this Act or any other Act otherwise provides;
or
an order is made under subsection (2).

The trial judge or, if a notice of appeal or notice of
application for leave to appeal is filed, the Court
of Appeal may stay a sentence if satisfied that it is
in the interests of justice to do so.
See the definition of sentence in section 3.

A prisoner within the meaning of the Corrections
Act 1986 who appeals, or applies for leave to
appeal, to the Court of Appeal may apply to the
Court of Appeal to be granted bail.

On an application under subsection (1), the Court
of Appeal may grant the prisoner bail pending the
appeal.
See section 323 for bail following appeal.

nodes.heading: Stay of certain orders during appeal period

nodes.text:
This section applies to an order under section 84,
85B or 86 of the Sentencing Act 1991 made by
the Supreme Court or the County Court.

See section 83G(1) of the Sentencing Act 1991 in relation
to superannuation orders.

Unless the Supreme Court or the County Court
otherwise directs, an order referred to in
subsection (1) is stayed during the appeal period.

If an order is stayed under subsection (2) and the
conviction is set aside on appeal, the order does
not take effect unless the Court of Appeal
otherwise orders.

The Court of Appeal may set aside or vary an
order made by the Supreme Court or the County
Court under subsection (2).

Rules of court may provide for securing the safe
custody during the appeal period of any property
the subject of an order referred to in
subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Execution of order for forfeiture or destruction of property

nodes.text:
If a court orders the forfeiture or destruction of
any property in relation to an offence, the property
must not be forfeited or destroyed during the
appeal period unless earlier forfeiture or
destruction is permitted by any other law.

This section does not apply to orders made under
the Confiscation Act 1997.

Rules of court may provide for securing the
safe custody during the appeal period of any
property the subject of an order referred to in
subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Extension of time for filing or serving notice of appeal or notice of application for leave to appeal

nodes.text:
The Court of Appeal or, in accordance with the
rules of court, the Registrar of Criminal Appeals
of the Supreme Court at any time may extend the
time within which—

a notice referred to in paragraph (a) may be
served.

If the Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the
Supreme Court refuses an application to extend
time under subsection (1), the applicant is entitled
to have the Court of Appeal determine the
application.

nodes.heading: Abandonment of appeal
nodes.text:
An appeal to the Court of Appeal may be
abandoned in accordance with the rules of court.

nodes.heading: Powers which may be exercised by Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal

nodes.text:
The Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge
of Appeal may exercise the following powers—
to give leave to appeal;
to review a refusal to certify;

to extend the time within which notice of
appeal may be filed and served;
to grant the appellant bail;
to order stays of sentence;

to call on a court and a respondent to show
cause why a question of law should not be
reserved for determination by the Court of
Appeal.

If the Court of Appeal constituted by a single
Judge of Appeal refuses an application to exercise
a power referred to in subsection (1) in relation to
any ground of appeal, the applicant is entitled to
have the application determined by the Court of
Appeal constituted by 2 or more Judges of
Appeal.

An order under section 280(3) or 284A(3) made
by the Court of Appeal constituted by a single
Judge of Appeal is stayed on the filing of an
application to have the application for leave to
appeal determined by the Court of Appeal
constituted by 2 or more Judges of Appeal.
An order stayed under subsection (3)—

is of no effect if the application for leave to
appeal is granted by the Court of Appeal
constituted by 2 or more Judges of Appeal.

nodes.heading: Trial judge may be required to provide report on appeal

nodes.text:
For the purposes of this Part, the Registrar of
Criminal Appeals of the Supreme Court may
require a trial judge to provide to the Registrar a
report on a case tried by the judge, giving the
opinion of the trial judge on the case or on any
point arising in the case.

A trial judge must comply with a requirement
under subsection (1) in accordance with the rules
of court.

nodes.heading: Production of documents, exhibits or other things
nodes.text:
For the purposes of this Part, the Court of Appeal
may order the production of any document,
exhibit or other thing connected with the
proceeding if the Court of Appeal considers that
it is in the interests of justice to do so.

nodes.heading: Order for examination of compellable witness

nodes.text:
For the purposes of this Part, if the Court of
Appeal considers that it is in the interests of
justice to do so, the Court of Appeal may order
any witness who would have been a compellable
witness at the trial to attend and be examined
before the court, whether or not the witness was
called at the trial.

If the Court of Appeal makes an order under
subsection (1), it may order that the examination
of the witness be conducted, in accordance with
the rules of court, before any person appointed by
the Court of Appeal for that purpose.

The Court of Appeal may admit as evidence any
deposition of a witness taken in an examination
under subsection (2).

nodes.heading: Evidence of competent but not compellable witness
nodes.text:
For the purposes of this Part, if the Court of
Appeal considers that it is in the interests of
justice to do so, the Court of Appeal may receive
the evidence of any witness (including the
appellant) who is a competent but not compellable
witness.

As to competence and compellability of witnesses, see Division 1
of Part 2.1 of Chapter 2 of the Evidence Act 2008.

nodes.heading: Court of Appeal may refer issue or matter for reference determination

nodes.text: This section applies to—
an appeal under this Part or Part 6.4; and

an application for leave to appeal under this
Part or Part 6.4.

The Court of Appeal may refer, for the making of
a reference determination, any specified issue or
matter arising on an appeal or an application for
leave to appeal to which this section applies—

to the Trial Division of the Supreme Court
constituted by a Judge of the Court within
the meaning of the Supreme Court
Act 1986; or

to the County Court constituted by a judge
within the meaning of the County Court
Act 1958.

The Court of Appeal may make any directions it
considers appropriate in a referral under
subsection (2), including directions about—

the form any reference determination should
take; or
procedural matters.

The Trial Division of the Supreme Court or the
County Court (as the case requires) to which a
referral for a reference determination is made—

must hear and determine the issue or matter
in accordance with any directions in the
referral; and

may otherwise conduct the hearing and
determine the procedure for the hearing as it
considers appropriate; and

on the determination of the issue or matter,
must provide its reference determinations to
the Court of Appeal.

If the Court of Appeal gives leave, the Court of
Appeal may hear and determine an appeal against
a reference determination as part of the appeal or
application for leave to appeal to which the
reference determination relates.

Unless the Court of Appeal otherwise determines
in accordance with subsection (5), a reference
determination is taken to be a determination of the
Court of Appeal in the appeal or application for
leave to appeal to which the reference
determination relates.

A referral under subsection (2) must not be made
to—

the Trial Division of the Supreme Court
constituted by a Judge of the Court who was
also the trial judge in the proceeding which
is the subject of the appeal or application for
leave to appeal; or

the County Court constituted by a judge who
was also the trial judge in the proceeding
which is the subject of the appeal or
application for leave to appeal.

Nothing in this section limits any powers of the
Court of Appeal.

nodes.heading: Reference of question to special commissioner

nodes.text:
The Court of Appeal may appoint a special
commissioner to inquire into and report on any
question referred to the special commissioner by
the court if—

the question arises on an appeal under this
Part or an application for leave to appeal
under this Part; and
the question involves—

prolonged examination of documents or
accounts; or
any scientific or local investigation; and

the court considers that the examination or
investigation cannot conveniently be
conducted before the court; and

the court considers that it is in the interests of
justice to do so.

The Court of Appeal may act on the report of a
special commissioner to the extent that the court
considers appropriate to adopt the report.

The Court of Appeal may determine the
remuneration of a special commissioner.

Subject to subsections (2) and (3), on an appeal
under this Part, including an appeal by the DPP,
the Court of Appeal must not increase a sentence
by reason of any evidence that was not given at
the trial or sentencing hearing.

On an appeal under section 291, the Court of
Appeal may increase a sentence by reason of
evidence of the failure to fulfil an undertaking
referred to in section 291(a).

On an appeal under this Part, including an appeal
by the DPP, the Court of Appeal may increase a
sentence, by reason of any evidence that was not
given at the trial or sentencing hearing, if the court
considers that—

the originating court was misled at the
sentencing hearing as to a material fact; and

an increase in sentence is necessary in the
interests of justice.

On an appeal under section 290A, the Court of
Appeal may increase a sentence, by reason of any
evidence that was not given in the hearing of an
appeal under section 254 (an initial appeal), if the
court considers that—

the County Court or the Trial Division of the
Supreme Court, as the case requires, was
misled in the initial appeal as to a material
fact; and

an increase in sentence is necessary in the
interests of justice.

history.raw: S. 322 amended by No. 48/2012 s. 8 (ILA s. 39B(1)).
Note to s. 322 amended by No. 65/2011 s. 107(Sch. item 4.6).

nodes.text:
The Court of Appeal may impose a sentence on a
person under this Part even though the person
does not attend the hearing of an appeal or an
application to the Court of Appeal.

The Court of Appeal cannot impose a sentence that requires
the consent of the person, for example a community
correction order, in the absence of the person.

For the purposes of this section, the making of an
order under section 280(3) or 284A(3) is an
imposition of a sentence.

nodes.heading: Bail following appeal
nodes.text:
If on an appeal the Court of Appeal orders a new
trial or remits a matter to the Trial Division of
the Supreme Court or to the County Court, the
Court of Appeal may remand the appellant in
custody or grant the appellant bail pending the
commencement of the new trial or the remitted
matter.

history.raw: Note to s. 323 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 35.

nodes.text:
Section 277(2) requires the Court of Appeal to order that the
appellant appear on a specified date for the new trial.

nodes.heading: Warrants
nodes.text:
For the purposes of this Part, the Court of Appeal
may issue any warrant necessary for enforcing the
orders of the court.

In this section—
ancillary order means an order (other than the
order that is the subject of the appeal) made
by the originating court in the proceeding
or the County Court or the Trial Division
of the Supreme Court on an appeal under
section 254, as the case requires.

history.raw: S. 325(1) def. of ancillary order amended by No. 48/2018 s. 38(2).

nodes.text:
On an appeal under this Part, the Court of Appeal
may set aside or vary an ancillary order, if the
court is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice
to do so.

On an appeal against conviction from the County Court, the Court
of Appeal may set aside or vary an order made by the County
Court for the suppression of a name.

nodes.heading: Expenses of assessors and special commissioners
nodes.text:
Subject to any prescribed rates and scales of
payment, the Attorney-General must pay out of
money provided by Parliament all expenses of and
incidental to—

a reference of a question to a special
commissioner under section 320.

Chapter 8 contains general provisions that apply to all criminal
proceedings.

nodes.heading: Second or subsequent appeal to Court of Appeal
Right of second or subsequent appeal against conviction

nodes.text:
A person convicted of an indictable offence by an
originating court who—
may appeal to the Court of Appeal against the
conviction if the Court of Appeal gives the person
leave to appeal.

has exhausted the person's right to appeal
against conviction under Division 1 of
Part 6.3; or

has previously appealed under this Part but
leave to appeal was not granted or the appeal
was dismissed, in whole or in part—
See the definition of originating court in section 3.

An appeal under subsection (1) may also include
an appeal against a conviction for a related
summary offence.

An application for leave to appeal under
section 326A is commenced by filing a notice of
application for leave to appeal in accordance with
the rules of court.

The Registrar of Criminal Appeals of the Supreme
Court must provide to the respondent a copy of
the notice of application for leave to appeal within
7 days after the day on which the notice of
application is filed.

nodes.heading: Determination of application for leave to appeal under section 326A

nodes.text:
The Court of Appeal may grant leave to appeal
under section 326A if it is satisfied that there is
fresh and compelling evidence that should, in the
interests of justice, be considered on an appeal.

The Court of Appeal may grant leave to appeal
under section 326A against a conviction for a
related summary offence only if it grants leave to
appeal under subsection (1) in relation to the
indictable offence.

In this section, evidence relating to an offence of
which a person is convicted is—
fresh if—

it was not adduced at the trial of the
offence; and

it could not, even with the exercise of
reasonable diligence, have been
adduced at the trial; and
compelling if—
it is reliable; and
it is substantial; and
either—

it is highly probative in the
context of the issues in dispute at
the trial of the offence; or

it would have eliminated or
substantially weakened the
prosecution case if it had been
presented at trial.

Evidence that would be admissible on a second or
subsequent appeal is not precluded from being
fresh or compelling only because it would not
have been admissible in the earlier trial of the
offence that resulted in the conviction.

nodes.heading: Determination of second or subsequent appeal against conviction

nodes.text:
On an appeal under section 326A, the Court of
Appeal must allow the appeal against conviction if
it is satisfied that there has been a substantial
miscarriage of justice.

In any other case, the Court of Appeal must
dismiss an appeal under section 326A.

If the Court of Appeal allows an appeal under
section 326A, it must set aside the conviction of
the offence (offence A) and must—
order a new trial of offence A; or
enter a judgment of acquittal of offence A; or

if—
enter a judgment of conviction of offence B
and impose a sentence for offence B that is
no more severe than the sentence that was
imposed for offence A; or

the appellant could have been found
guilty of some other offence
(offence B) instead of offence A; and

the court is satisfied that the jury or, in
the case of a plea of guilty to offence A,
the trial judge must have been satisfied
of facts that prove the appellant was
guilty of offence B—

if the appellant could have been found guilty
of some other offence (offence B) instead of
offence A and the court is not satisfied as
required by paragraph (c)(ii), order a new
trial for offence B; or

if the court is satisfied that the appellant
should have been found not guilty of
offence A because of mental impairment,
enter a finding of not guilty because of
mental impairment and make an order or
declaration under section 23 of the Crimes
(Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be
Tried) Act 1997; or

if the appellant could have been found guilty
of some other offence (offence B) instead of
offence A and the court is satisfied—
enter a finding of not guilty of offence B
because of mental impairment and make an
order or declaration under section 23 of the
Crimes (Mental Impairment and
Unfitness to be Tried) Act 1997.

that the jury must have been satisfied of
facts that prove the appellant did the
acts or made the omissions that
constitute offence B; and

that the appellant should have been
found not guilty of offence B because
of mental impairment—

If the Court of Appeal orders a new trial, the court
must order that the appellant attend on a specified
date before the court in which the new trial will be
conducted.

Section 326K enables the Court of Appeal to remand the
appellant in custody or grant bail pending a new trial.

If the Court of Appeal sets aside the conviction of
offence A, it may vary a sentence that—

was imposed for an offence other than
offence A at or after the time when the
appellant was sentenced for offence A; and
took into account the sentence for offence A.

A power of the Court of Appeal under this section
to impose a sentence in substitution for the
sentence imposed by the originating court may
still be exercised even if the sentence imposed by
the originating court is an aggregate sentence of
imprisonment.

If at the conclusion of an appeal the appellant
remains convicted of more than one offence, the
Court of Appeal may either—

impose a separate sentence in respect of each
offence; or

impose an aggregate sentence of
imprisonment in respect of all offences or
any 2 or more offences.

nodes.heading: Stay of sentence and bail pending appeal

nodes.text:
If a notice of application for leave to appeal is
filed under section 326B, the Court of Appeal may
stay a sentence if satisfied that it is in the interests
of justice to do so.

A prisoner within the meaning of the Corrections
Act 1986 who applies for leave to appeal to the
Court of Appeal under this Part may apply to the
Court of Appeal to be granted bail.

On an application under subsection (2), the Court
of Appeal may grant the prisoner bail pending the
appeal.

nodes.heading: Abandonment of appeal
nodes.text:
An appeal under this Part may be abandoned in
accordance with the rules of court.

nodes.heading: Powers which may be exercised by Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal

nodes.text:
The Court of Appeal constituted by a single Judge
of Appeal may exercise the following powers in
this Part—
to give leave to appeal;
to grant the appellant bail;
to order stays of sentence.

If the Court of Appeal constituted by a single
Judge of Appeal refuses an application to exercise
a power referred to in subsection (1) in relation to
any ground of appeal, the applicant is entitled to
have the application determined by the Court of
Appeal constituted by 2 or more Judges of
Appeal.

nodes.heading: Application of sections 316 to 320 and 326
nodes.text:
Sections 316 to 320 and 326 apply with any
necessary modification to a proceeding under this
Part.

nodes.heading: Sentence in absence of offender
nodes.text:
The Court of Appeal may impose a sentence on a
person under this Part even though the person
does not attend the hearing of an appeal or an
application to the Court of Appeal.

The Court of Appeal cannot impose a sentence that requires the
consent of the person, for example a community correction order,
in the absence of the person.

nodes.heading: Bail following appeal
nodes.text:
If on an appeal under this Part the Court of Appeal
orders a new trial, the Court of Appeal may
remand the appellant in custody or grant the
appellant bail pending the commencement of the
new trial.

Section 326E(2) requires the Court of Appeal to order that the
appellant attend on a specified date for the new trial.

nodes.heading: Warrants
nodes.text:
For the purposes of this Part, the Court of Appeal
may issue any warrant necessary for enforcing the
orders of the court.

On an appeal under this Part, the Court of Appeal
may set aside or vary an ancillary order, if the
court is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice
to do so.

In this section—
ancillary order means an order (other than the
order that is the subject of the appeal) made
by the originating court in the proceeding or
by the Court of Appeal on an earlier appeal.

nodes.heading: Reference to Court of Appeal on petition for mercy

history.raw: Note to s. 327 substituted by No. 68/2009 s. 36.

nodes.text:
If a person convicted on indictment or found unfit
to stand trial or found not guilty because of mental
impairment petitions for the exercise of
His Majesty's mercy in relation to the conviction
or finding, or the sentence imposed on the person,
the Attorney-General—

history.raw: S. 327(1) amended by No. 25/2023 s. 7(Sch. 1 item 7).

nodes.text:
may refer the whole case to the Court of
Appeal; or

may refer any point arising in the case to the
judges of the Trial Division of the Supreme
Court for their opinion.

If the Attorney-General refers the whole case to
the Court of Appeal, the Court of Appeal must
hear and determine the case as if it were an appeal
by the person.

If the Attorney-General refers a question to the
judges of the Trial Division of the Supreme Court,
those judges or any 3 of them must consider the
point and provide the Attorney-General with their
opinion.

Nothing in this Chapter affects the prerogative of
mercy.

Chapter 8 contains general provisions that apply to all
criminal proceedings.
Clause 11 of Schedule 4 contains transitional provisions.

nodes.heading: Limitations on rules relating to double jeopardy

nodes.text:
This Chapter extends to an acquittal in a place
outside Victoria if the law of that place permits
the acquitted person to be retried.

Subject to subsection (3), this Chapter does not
apply if a person is acquitted of the offence
charged but is convicted of a lesser offence arising
out of the same set of circumstances that gave rise
to the charge.

This Chapter applies in the circumstances set out
in subsection (2) if the acquittal was tainted.

nodes.heading: Definitions
nodes.text: In this Chapter—

nodes.heading: acquittal
nodes.text: includes—

a verdict of not guilty (other than a
verdict of not guilty because of mental
impairment); and

an entry of not guilty made on the
record on the direction of the trial
judge; and

a judgment of acquittal entered by the
Court of Appeal on an appeal;

nodes.heading: administration of justice offence
nodes.text: means—
perjury or subornation of perjury; or

perverting, or attempting to pervert, the
course of justice or conspiracy to
pervert the course of justice; or

bribery of a public official, being a
judge of the County Court or the
Supreme Court; or

a substantially similar offence against
the law of a place outside Victoria
corresponding to an offence referred to
in paragraph (a), (b) or (c).

nodes.heading: Meaning of fresh and compelling evidence

nodes.text:
For the purposes of this Chapter, evidence relating
to an offence of which a person is acquitted is—
fresh if—

it was not adduced at the trial of the
offence; and

it could not, even with the exercise of
reasonable diligence, have been
adduced at the trial; and
compelling if—
it is reliable; and
it is substantial; and

it is highly probative in the context of
the issues in dispute at the trial of the
offence.

Evidence that would be admissible on a new trial
under this Chapter is not precluded from being
fresh or compelling only because it would not
have been admissible in the earlier trial of the
offence that resulted in the acquittal.

To avoid doubt, a reference in this Chapter to
evidence relating to an offence includes a
reference to evidence relating to the issue of
whether the presumption against criminal
responsibility is rebutted in respect of the offence.

nodes.heading: Meaning of tainted acquittal
nodes.text:
For the purposes of this Chapter, if at the trial of
an offence a person is acquitted of the offence, the
acquittal will be tainted if—

the person or another person has been
convicted (whether or not in Victoria) of
an administration of justice offence in
connection with the trial resulting in the
acquittal; and

it is more likely than not that, had it not been
for the commission of the administration of
justice offence, the person would have been
convicted of the first mentioned offence at
the trial.

nodes.heading: Circumstances in which police may reinvestigate offence after acquittal

nodes.text:
In this section—
an offence of which a person has previously
been acquitted includes—

nodes.heading: Bail following filing of direct indictment
nodes.text:
If an accused is in custody following the filing of
a direct indictment under this Chapter, it is to be
presumed that the accused is to be released on
bail, regardless of the offence charged, pending
determination of the DPP's application under
section 327H or discontinuance of the prosecution
under section 327K.
Sections 331(2) and 411(4) provide further for bail.

nodes.heading: DPP may apply to Court of Appeal

nodes.text:
The DPP may apply to the Court of Appeal for an
order—

setting aside the previous acquittal of the
accused or removing the previous acquittal
as a bar to the accused being tried on the
direct indictment (as the case requires); and

authorising the continuation of the
prosecution of the charge in the indictment.

An application must specify whether it is based
on—
a tainted acquittal; or
fresh and compelling evidence; or
an administration of justice offence.

An application based on fresh and compelling
evidence cannot be made in relation to an
acquittal resulting from a new trial authorised
under this Chapter.

An application under subsection (1) is
commenced by filing a notice of application in
accordance with the rules of court within 28 days
after the day on which a direct indictment is filed
under section 327F.

A notice of application under subsection (4) must
be signed by the DPP personally.

A copy of the notice of application must be served
personally on the accused in accordance with
section 391 within 7 days after the day on which
the notice of application is filed.

The DPP must provide a copy of the notice of
application to the legal practitioner who last
represented the accused in the criminal proceeding
which resulted in the previous acquittal, if that
legal practitioner can reasonably be identified.

An accused is entitled to appear at the hearing of
an application under this section and may be
represented by a legal practitioner.

nodes.heading: Extension of time for filing or serving notice of application

nodes.text:
The Court of Appeal or, in accordance with the
rules of court, the Registrar of Criminal Appeals
of the Supreme Court at any time may extend the
time within which—
if the court or Registrar considers that it is in the
interests of justice to do so.

a notice of application under section 327H
may be filed; or

a notice referred to in paragraph (a) may be
served—

The power of the Court of Appeal to extend time
under this section may be exercised by the Court
of Appeal constituted by a single Judge of Appeal.

If the Court of Appeal constituted by a single
Judge of Appeal or the Registrar of Criminal
Appeals of the Supreme Court refuses an
application to extend time under subsection (1),
the DPP is entitled to have the Court of Appeal
constituted by 2 or more Judges of Appeal
determine the application.

nodes.heading: DPP may apply only once in relation to particular acquittal
nodes.text:
The DPP may make an application to the Court of
Appeal under section 327H only once in relation
to a particular acquittal.

nodes.heading: DPP must discontinue prosecution if fails to make application
nodes.text:
If the DPP fails to make an application under
section 327H within 28 days after filing a direct
indictment under section 327F, or any extension
of that period granted under section 327I, the DPP
must discontinue the prosecution (in accordance
with Part 5.4) within 14 days after the expiry of
the 28 days or the extension (as the case requires).

nodes.heading: Determination of application where acquittal tainted
nodes.text:
On an application under section 327H, the Court
of Appeal may make any order referred to in
section 327O in relation to a person who has been
acquitted of an offence if the court is satisfied
that—

at the time the offence is alleged to have
been committed, the offence was punishable
by level 4 imprisonment (15 years
maximum) or more (however the penalty is
described); and
the acquittal was tainted; and

it is likely that a new trial for that offence
would be fair, having regard to—

the length of time since the offence is
alleged to have been committed; and

whether there has been a failure on the
part of the police or the prosecution to
act with reasonable diligence or
expedition with respect to the making
of the application; and

any other matter that the court
considers relevant.

nodes.heading: Determination of application where fresh and compelling evidence

nodes.text:
On an application under section 327H, the Court
of Appeal may make any order referred to in
section 327O in relation to a person who has been
acquitted of an offence if the court is satisfied
that—

the offence is referred to in subsection (2);
and

any circumstances referred to in
subsection (2) in respect of the offence were
present in the commission of the offence;
and

it is likely that a new trial for that offence
would be fair, having regard to—

the length of time since the offence is
alleged to have been committed; and

whether there has been a failure on the
part of the police or the prosecution to
act with reasonable diligence or
expedition with respect to the making
of the application; and

any other matter that the court
considers relevant.
Subsection (1) applies to the following offences—
murder;

conspiracy to commit murder (section 321 of
the Crimes Act 1958);

incitement to commit murder (section 321G
of the Crimes Act 1958);

attempting to commit murder (section 321M
of the Crimes Act 1958);
manslaughter;

an offence against section 144(1) of the
Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004
arising in respect of a contravention of
section 39G(1) of that Act;

child homicide (section 5A of the Crimes
Act 1958);

homicide by firearm (section 5B of the
Crimes Act 1958);

arson causing death (section 197A of the
Crimes Act 1958);

trafficking in a drug or drugs of
dependence—large commercial quantity
(section 71 of the Drugs, Poisons and
Controlled Substances Act 1981);

cultivation of narcotic plants—large
commercial quantity (section 72 of the
Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances
Act 1981);

rape (section 38 of the Crimes Act 1958),
rape by compelling sexual penetration
(section 39 of the Crimes Act 1958) or
armed robbery (section 75A of the Crimes
Act 1958) if the offence is committed in
circumstances where—

torture (being the deliberate and
systematic infliction over a period of
time of severe pain on the victim) was
involved in the commission of the
offence; or

the offender caused really serious
injury to the victim; or

the offender threatened to cause death
or really serious injury to the victim;

a substantially similar offence against a
previous enactment or the law of a place
outside Victoria corresponding to an offence
referred to in this subsection.

nodes.heading: Determination of application where administration of justice offence
nodes.text:
On an application under section 327H, the Court
of Appeal may make any order referred to in
section 327O in relation to a person who has been
acquitted of an offence if the court is satisfied
that—

at the time the offence is alleged to have
been committed, the offence was an
indictable offence; and

there is fresh evidence against the acquitted
person of the commission of an
administration of justice offence in relation
to the previous acquittal; and

it is likely that a trial for the administration
of justice offence would be fair, having
regard to—

the length of time since the
administration of justice offence is
alleged to have been committed; and

whether there has been a failure on the
part of the police or the prosecution to
act with reasonable diligence or
expedition with respect to the making
of the application; and

any other matter that the court
considers relevant.

On an application under section 327H, if the Court
of Appeal is satisfied of the matters in
section 327L or 327M, the court may order that—

the previous acquittal of the accused of an
offence charged in the direct indictment be
set aside or removed as a bar to the accused
being tried on the direct indictment (as the
case requires); and

the prosecution of the charge in the direct
indictment may continue.

On an application under section 327H, if the Court
of Appeal is satisfied of the matters in
section 327N, the court may order that—

the previous acquittal of the accused be
removed as a bar to the accused being tried
for the administration of justice offence
alleged to have been committed in relation to
the previous acquittal; and

the prosecution of the charge in the direct
indictment may continue.

In addition to subsections (1) and (2), the Court of
Appeal may make any other order that it considers
appropriate.

If the Court of Appeal is not satisfied that
section 327L, 327M or 327N applies or that a fair
trial is likely, the court must order that the charge
in the direct indictment is permanently stayed.

If more than one offence is charged in the direct
indictment, the Court of Appeal must make an
order under subsection (1), (2) or (4) in relation to
each charge.

If the Court of Appeal makes an order under
subsection (1) or (2), the court may make any
order for or in relation to the bail of the accused
that the court considers appropriate.

nodes.heading: DPP must elect which offence to prosecute
nodes.text:
If the DPP satisfies the Court of Appeal under
sections 327L, 327M and 327N, or any 2 of those
sections, the DPP must elect to prosecute either—
and may proceed only on that basis.
the administration of justice offence; or

the offence of which the accused has been
acquitted or a related offence—

nodes.heading: Amendment of indictment
nodes.text:
If the Court of Appeal makes an order under
section 327O(1) or (2) in relation to an offence
charged in a direct indictment, the trial court must
not amend the indictment to significantly change
the offence charged.

nodes.heading: Prohibition on making certain references in new trial
nodes.text:
At a new trial that has been authorised under this
Chapter, the prosecution must not refer to the fact
that the Court of Appeal has been satisfied that—

there is fresh evidence, or fresh and
compelling evidence, against the accused in
relation to the offence charged; or

it is more likely than not that, had it not been
for the commission of an administration of
justice offence, the accused would have been
convicted of the offence charged at the
earlier trial.

Section 18 of the Supreme Court Act 1986 permits the court to
make an order prohibiting the publication of the whole or part of a
proceeding.

nodes.heading: Appeal and review rights unaffected
nodes.text:
This Chapter does not affect any right to appeal or
review the acquittal of a person.

nodes.heading: When accused etc. is required to appear at hearing

history.raw: Note 2 to s. 329 amended by Nos 69/2009 s. 54(Sch. Pt 2 item 18.2), 38/2016 s. 9(3).

nodes.text:
An accused must appear at every hearing in the
criminal proceeding against the accused, unless
otherwise provided by this Act or the rules of
court.

A party to an appeal who was the accused in the
criminal proceeding to which the appeal relates
must appear at every hearing in the appeal, unless
otherwise provided by this Act or the rules of
court.

The court may excuse a person from appearing at
a hearing.

See section 328 for the ways in which an accused may
appear.
Division 3 of Part IIA of the Evidence (Miscellaneous

Provisions) Act 1958 authorises or requires the appearance
of an accused before the court by audio visual link in certain
circumstances.

nodes.heading: When accused etc. is required to attend hearing

nodes.text:
An accused must attend a hearing in the criminal
proceeding against the accused if—

this Act or the rules of court require the
attendance of the accused at the hearing; or

the accused has been remanded in custody or
granted bail to attend the hearing; or

the court requires the attendance of the
accused at the hearing.

A party to an appeal who was the accused in the
criminal proceeding to which the appeal relates
must attend a hearing in the appeal if—

this Act or the rules of court require the
attendance of the party at the hearing; or

the party has been remanded in custody or
granted bail to attend the hearing; or

the court requires the attendance of the party
at the hearing.

The court may excuse a person from attending a
hearing.

If a person fails to attend when required under
subsection (1)(a), (1)(b), (2)(a) or (2)(b), the court
may issue a warrant to arrest the person.

If a person fails to attend when required under
subsection (1)(c) or (2)(c), the court may issue a
warrant to arrest the person if the court is satisfied
that the person has had reasonable notice of the
requirement to attend.

Section 246 provides for the attendance of an accused

proceeding before the court—

If a court has adjourned the hearing of a criminal

If a court has adjourned the hearing of a criminal

the accused be brought at any time before then—
in order that the hearing may be held or continued.
before the court; or

The officer in charge of the prison or youth justice

nodes.heading: Transfer of accused between place of detention and court

nodes.text:
A person who has the legal custody of an accused
in detention must cause the accused to be brought
to and from court whenever necessary so that the
accused may be tried, sentenced or otherwise dealt
with according to law.

If a court considers it in the interests of justice that
an accused in detention should be present in court
otherwise than for trial, hearing or sentence, the
court may order that the accused be brought
before the court.

If a court makes an order under subsection (2), the
responsible person, on receiving a copy of the
order, must cause the accused to be brought before
the court in accordance with the order.

See the definitions of in detention and responsible person in
section 3.

nodes.heading: Power to return accused to youth justice centre

nodes.text:
Despite anything in the Bail Act 1977, if—
the court may, subject to subsection (3), instead of
remanding the accused in custody—

the accused in a criminal proceeding in the
Magistrates' Court is undergoing a sentence
of detention in a youth justice centre; and

the Magistrates' Court adjourns the
proceeding or commits the accused for
trial—

direct that the accused be returned to the
custody of the Secretary to the Department
of Human Services until the end of the
sentence of detention or the resumption of
the hearing or the commencement of the trial
(whichever is the sooner); and
either—

grant the accused bail on a condition
that bail is not to be entered until the
end of the sentence of detention; or

refuse bail and direct that the accused
be brought before the Magistrates'
Court at a later date for it to consider
the granting of bail.

For the purposes of this section, the end of the
sentence of detention means the time when the
accused is released from custody, whether on
parole or otherwise.

Section 5A of the Bail Act 1977 provides equivalent powers
to the Supreme Court and the County Court.

If the Secretary to the Department of Justice and
Regulation in a criminal proceeding objects to the
accused being returned to a youth justice centre
under subsection (1), the court may only order that
the accused is to be returned to the youth justice
centre if the court has considered—

the age and maturity of the accused; and

any evidence of the behaviour of the accused
in custody; and

whether an application has been made to the
Youth Parole Board regarding the custody of
the accused; and
any other relevant factor.

nodes.heading: Interpreter
nodes.text:
If—
the court must not hear and determine the
proceeding without a competent interpreter
interpreting it.

a person is charged with an offence

the court is satisfied that the person does not

nodes.heading: Subpoenas and witness summonses
nodes.text:
A party to a criminal proceeding may apply for
the issue of a subpoena in accordance with the
rules of court or a witness summons in accordance
with the Magistrates' Court Act 1989, as the
case requires.

nodes.heading: Victim who is a witness entitled to be present in court

history.raw: S. 336A(2) repealed by No. 48/2018 s. 33. S. 337 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 38 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text:
In a criminal proceeding where a victim of the
offence is a witness in the proceeding, the court
may order the victim to leave the courtroom until
required to give evidence only if the court
considers it appropriate to do so.

nodes.heading: Court may act on application or on own motion

nodes.text:
Unless the context otherwise requires, a power or
discretion conferred on a court by or under this
Act may be exercised by the court on the
application of a party or on its own motion.

Unless the context otherwise requires, a power or
discretion referred to in subsection (1) includes a
power or discretion to revoke or vary a decision or
order made in the exercise of that power or
discretion.

nodes.heading: Court may determine issue in criminal proceeding without oral hearing

nodes.text:
In addition to, and without limiting, section 201, a
court may determine any issue (other than
determining whether an accused is guilty or not
guilty) in any criminal proceeding without an oral
hearing and entirely on the basis of written
submissions and without the appearance of the
parties—

if the court is satisfied that it is in the
interests of justice to do so; and

whether or not the parties consent to the
court doing so.

Section 201 provides for issues to be decided before trial on
the basis of written submissions and without the appearance
of the parties.

For the purposes of subsection (1), in determining
whether it is in the interests of justice to determine
an issue in a criminal proceeding without an oral
hearing, the court must have regard to—

the right of an accused to be present at the
accused's trial; and
the right of an accused to a fair hearing; and
the nature of the issue; and

whether the accused or the offender (as the
case requires) has had the opportunity to
obtain legal advice; and

whether the parties consent to the court
doing so.

Nothing in this section affects any other power of
the court to determine an issue in a criminal
proceeding without an oral hearing.

nodes.heading: Guiding principles
nodes.text:
It is the intention of Parliament that in interpreting

that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a

This Division applies to all complainants in a
