nodes.text:
This Division applies despite anything in this or
any other Act or any rule of law to the contrary.

nodes.heading: Definition
nodes.text: In this Division—

history.raw: New s. 340 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 340 renumbered as s. 392 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(d).
S. 340(3)(da) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 39(1), renumbered as s. 392(3)(da) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(d).
S. 340(4) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 39(2), renumbered as s. 392(4) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(d).

nodes.heading: sexual history evidence
nodes.text:
means evidence that
relates to or tends to establish the fact that
the complainant—

was accustomed to engaging in sexual
activities; or

had freely agreed to engage in sexual
activity (other than that to which the
charge relates) with the accused person
or another person.

nodes.heading: Prohibition on questions and evidence concerning sexual reputation of complainant
nodes.text:
The court must not allow any questions as to, or
admit any evidence of, the sexual reputation of the
complainant.

history.raw: New s. 341 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50, amended by No. 38/2022 s. 73(2).
S. 341 renumbered as s. 393 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(e).

nodes.heading: Restriction on questions and evidence concerning complainant's sexual activities
nodes.text:
The complainant must not be cross-examined,
and the court must not admit any evidence, as
to the sexual activities (whether consensual or
non-consensual) of the complainant (other than
those to which the charge relates), without the
leave of the court.

history.raw: New s. 342 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 342 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 39(4) (ILA s. 39B(1)), renumbered as s. 394 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(f).
S. 342(ba) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 39(3), renumbered as s. 394(1)(ba) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(f).
S. 342(2) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 39(4), renumbered as s. 394(2) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(f).

nodes.heading: Admissibility of sexual history evidence
nodes.text:
Sexual history evidence is not admissible to
support an inference that the complainant is the
type of person who is more likely to have
consented to the sexual activity to which the
charge relates.

history.raw: New s. 343 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 343 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zx), renumbered as s. 395 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(g).

nodes.heading: Application for leave
nodes.text: An application for leave under section 342—

history.raw: New s. 344 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 344 renumbered as s. 396 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(h).

nodes.text:
in the case of a summary proceeding, must
be filed with the Magistrates' Court and
served on the informant in accordance with
section 392 at least 7 days before the
summary hearing;

in the case of a pre-trial cross-examination
under an order made under section 198A or a
limited preparatory cross-examination under
an order made under section 198B, must
be—

in the case of a trial, must be filed with the
County Court or the Supreme Court (as the
case requires) and served on the DPP in
accordance with section 392—

at least 14 days before the day on which
the trial is listed to commence; or

if a special hearing is to be held, at least
14 days before that hearing;

in the case of a sentencing hearing, must be
filed with the relevant court and served on
the informant or the DPP (as the case
requires) in accordance with section 392 at
least 7 days before the sentencing hearing is
listed to commence.

nodes.heading: Application for leave out of time
nodes.text:
If it is in the interests of justice to do so, the court
may hear and determine an application for leave
under section 342 after the expiry of the relevant
time limit specified in section 344.

history.raw: New s. 345 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 345 renumbered as s. 397 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(i), amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 38.5).
New s. 346 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 346 renumbered as s. 398 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(j).

nodes.text:
An application for leave under section 342 must
be in writing and set out the matters required by
subsection (2) or (3), as the case requires.

An application for leave to cross-examine the
complainant as to the sexual activities of the
complainant must set out—

the initial questions sought to be asked of the
complainant; and

the scope of the questioning sought to flow
from the initial questioning; and

how the evidence sought to be elicited from
the questioning has substantial relevance to
facts in issue or why it is proper matter for
cross-examination as to credit.

An application for leave to admit evidence as to
the sexual activities of the complainant must—

identify the evidence that is sought to be
admitted; and

set out how the evidence has substantial
relevance to facts in issue.

nodes.heading: Waiver of requirement to apply for leave in writing
nodes.text:
If it is in the interests of justice to do so, the court
may waive the requirement that an application for
leave under section 342 be made in writing.

history.raw: New s. 347 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 347 renumbered as s. 399 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(k).

nodes.heading: Hearing of application for leave
nodes.text:
An application for leave under section 342 must
be heard in the absence of the jury (if any) and, if
the accused so requests, in the absence of the
complainant.

history.raw: New s. 348 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 348 renumbered as s. 400 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(m).

nodes.heading: Determination of application for leave during summary hearing or trial
nodes.text:
In the course of a summary hearing or trial, the
court must not grant leave under section 342
unless it is satisfied that the evidence has
substantial relevance to a fact in issue and that it is
in the interests of justice to allow the cross-
examination or to admit the evidence, having
regard to—

history.raw: New s. 349 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50, amended by No. 5/2025 s. 19(2).
S. 349 renumbered as s. 401 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(n).

nodes.text:
whether the probative value of the evidence
outweighs the distress, humiliation and
embarrassment that the complainant may
experience as a result of the cross-
examination or the admission of the
evidence, in view of the age of the
complainant and the number and nature of
the questions that the complainant is likely to
be asked; and

the risk that the evidence may arouse in the
jury discriminatory belief or bias, prejudice,
sympathy or hostility; and

the need to respect the complainant's
personal dignity and privacy; and

the right of the accused to fully answer and
defend the charge.
Section 352 limits the relevance of sexual history evidence.

nodes.heading: Determination of application for leave during sentencing hearing

history.raw: New s. 350 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50, amended by No. 30/2010 s. 65 (ILA s. 39B(1)).
S. 350 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 40 (ILA s. 39B(1)), renumbered as s. 402 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(o).

nodes.text:
In the course of a sentencing hearing, the court
must not grant leave under section 342 unless
it is satisfied that the evidence has substantial
relevance to the issue of appropriate sentence and
the offender—

has pleaded guilty to all sexual offences
charged against the offender; or

has been found guilty of all sexual offences
charged against the offender.

In determining, under subsection (1), whether the
evidence has substantial relevance to the issue of
appropriate sentence, the court must have regard
to—

history.raw: S. 350(2) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 40, renumbered as s. 402(2) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(o), amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 41.8).

nodes.text:
whether the probative value of the
evidence outweighs the distress,
humiliation and embarrassment that the
complainant may experience as a result of
the cross-examination or the admission of
the evidence, in view of the age of the
complainant and the number and nature of
the questions that the complainant is likely
to be asked; and

the need to respect the complainant's
personal dignity and privacy.
Section 352 limits the relevance of sexual history evidence.

nodes.heading: Court must state reasons if leave granted

history.raw: New s. 351 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 351 renumbered as s. 403 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(p).

nodes.text: If the court grants leave under section 342 it—

must state in writing the reasons for granting
leave; and

cause those reasons to be entered in the
records of the court.

The failure of a court to comply with
subsection (1) does not invalidate any order made
by it.

nodes.heading: Limitation on sexual history evidence
nodes.text: Sexual history evidence is not to be regarded—

history.raw: New s. 352 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 352 renumbered as s. 404 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(q).

nodes.text:
as having a substantial relevance to the facts
in issue by virtue of any inferences it may
raise as to general disposition; or

as being proper matter for cross-examination
as to credit unless, because of special
circumstances, it would be likely materially
to impair confidence in the reliability of the
evidence of the complainant.

history.raw: New s. 353 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 353 amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zz), renumbered as s. 405 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(r).

nodes.text:
This Division applies to a criminal proceeding
that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for—
a sexual offence; or
a family violence offence; or

history.raw: S. 353(1)(b) substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 39, amended by No. 1/2026 s. 72(a).

nodes.text:
an offence against section 21A(1) of the
Crimes Act 1958 (stalking).

This Division applies to a protected witness in a
criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Definitions
nodes.text: In this Division—

history.raw: New s. 354 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 354 renumbered as s. 406 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(s).

nodes.heading: family member
nodes.text:
, in relation to the complainant or
the accused, includes—

a person who is or has been married to
the complainant or the accused; and

a person who has or has had an intimate
personal relationship with the
complainant or the accused; and

a person who is or has been the parent
or step-parent of the complainant or the
accused; and

a child who normally or regularly
resides with the complainant or the
accused; and

a guardian of the complainant or the
accused; and

nodes.heading: protected witness
nodes.text: means—
the complainant; or
a family member of the complainant; or
a family member of the accused; or

any other witness whom the court
declares under section 355 to be a
protected witness.

nodes.heading: Court may declare witness to be protected witness
nodes.text:
The court may at any time declare a witness to be
a protected witness.

history.raw: New s. 355 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 355 renumbered as s. 407 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(t).
Note to s. 355(2) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 51(zza), renumbered as note to s. 407(2) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(t).

nodes.heading: Protected witness not to be cross-examined by accused in person
nodes.text:
A protected witness must not be cross-examined
by the accused in person.

history.raw: New s. 356 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 356 renumbered as s. 408 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(u).

nodes.heading: When accused is not legally represented

history.raw: New s. 357 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 357 renumbered as s. 409 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(v).

nodes.text:
If the accused is not legally represented, the court
must—

inform the accused and the jury (if any) that
the accused is not permitted personally to
cross-examine a protected witness; and

ask the accused whether the accused
has sought legal representation for the
cross-examination of a protected witness;
and

if satisfied that the accused has not had a
reasonable opportunity to obtain legal
representation, grant an adjournment if so
requested by the accused.

If the accused does not obtain legal representation
for the cross-examination of a protected witness
(after being given a reasonable opportunity to do
so), the court must order Victoria Legal Aid to
provide legal representation for the accused for
that purpose.

Despite anything in the Legal Aid Act 1978,
Victoria Legal Aid must provide legal
representation in accordance with an order under
subsection (2).

A legal practitioner provided by Victoria Legal
Aid must act in the best interests of the accused if
the accused does not give any instructions to that
legal practitioner.

Subject to any direction given under section
389E(2)(f), if the accused refuses the legal
representation provided under subsection (3), or
otherwise refuses to co-operate, the court must
warn the accused that the accused will not be
permitted to adduce evidence in relation to a fact
in issue in order to contradict the evidence of a
protected witness unless the evidence on which
the accused intends to rely has been put to the
protected witness during cross-examination.

nodes.heading: Jury warning concerning legal representation for cross-examination
nodes.text:
If the accused is only legally represented for the
cross-examination of a protected witness, the trial
judge must warn the jury—

history.raw: New s. 358 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 358 renumbered as s. 410 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(w).

nodes.text:
that it is routine practice for an unrepresented
accused to obtain or be provided with legal
representation for the cross-examination of a
protected witness; and

that no adverse inference may be drawn
against the accused as a result of the
cross-examination not being conducted
by the accused in person; and

that the evidence given under
cross-examination is not to be given any
greater or lesser weight as a result of the
cross-examination not being conducted
by the accused in person.

history.raw: New s. 359 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 359 renumbered as s. 411 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(y).
S. 359(4) amended by No. 68/2009 s. 41, renumbered as s. 411(4) by No. 68/2009 s. 52(y).

nodes.text:
This Division applies to a criminal proceeding
that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for—
a sexual offence; or

an offence against section 195N(1) or
195O(1) of the Crimes Act 1958; or
a family violence offence; or

history.raw: S. 359(1)(b) amended by No. 30/2010 s. 66(1), substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 40.

nodes.text:
an offence against section 21A(1) of the
Crimes Act 1958 (stalking); or

an offence against section 17(1) or 19 of the
Summary Offences Act 1966.

This Division applies to all witnesses (including
complainants) in a criminal proceeding referred to
in subsection (1).

This Division applies at any stage of the criminal
proceeding, including an appeal or rehearing.

nodes.heading: Alternative arrangements for giving evidence
nodes.text:
The court may direct that alternative arrangements
be made for the giving of evidence by a witness,
including arrangements—

history.raw: New s. 360 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 360 renumbered as s. 412 by No. 68/2009 s. 52(z).

nodes.text:
permitting the evidence to be given from a
place other than the courtroom by means of
closed-circuit television or other facilities
that enable communication between that
place and the courtroom;

using screens to remove the accused from the
direct line of vision of the witness;

permitting a person, chosen by the witness
and approved by the court for this purpose,
to be beside the witness while the witness is
giving evidence, for the purpose of providing
emotional support to the witness;
requiring legal practitioners not to robe;

requiring legal practitioners to be seated
while examining or cross-examining the
witness.

Section 337(1) enables this direction to be made by the court
on the application of a party or on its own motion.

Section 337(2) provides that this direction may be varied or
revoked.

nodes.heading: Evidence given by closed-circuit television or other facilities

history.raw: New s. 362 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 362 renumbered as s. 415 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(a).

nodes.text:
This section applies to arrangements referred to in
section 360(a) that are directed to be made under
that section.

Any place outside the courtroom where the
witness is permitted to give evidence is taken to
be part of the courtroom while the witness is there
for the purpose of giving evidence.

The court must direct that any evidence given by
the witness is recorded.

The court may make any order it considers
appropriate to enable the witness to view any
place or thing, or identify any person or thing, for
the purposes of the proceeding or the evidence of
the witness.

nodes.heading: When court must direct use of closed-circuit television or other facilities for complainant

history.raw: New s. 363 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50, amended by Nos 30/2010 s. 68, 1/2022 s. 124 (ILA s. 39B(1)).
S. 363 renumbered as s. 416 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(b).

nodes.text:
If the witness is a complainant in a criminal
proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a
charge for a sexual offence, the court must direct
that an arrangement referred to in section 360(a)
be made unless—

the prosecution applies for the complainant
to give evidence in the courtroom; and
the court is satisfied that the complainant—

is aware of the right of the complainant
to give evidence in another place by
closed-circuit television or other
facilities; and

is able and wishes to give evidence in
the courtroom.

Subject to subsection (3), if the witness is a
complainant in a proceeding that relates (wholly
or partly) to a charge for a family violence
offence, the court must direct that an arrangement
referred to in section 360(a) be made if—

history.raw: S. 363(2) inserted by No. 1/2022 s. 124, amended by No. 5/2025 s. 41.

nodes.text:
closed-circuit television or other facilities
that enable communication between the
courtroom and the other place are available;
and
it is practicable to do so.

The court is not required to direct that an
arrangement referred to in section 360(a) be made
under subsection (2) if—

the prosecution applies for the complainant
to give evidence in the courtroom; and
the court is satisfied that the complainant—

is aware of the complainant's right to
give evidence in another place by
closed-circuit television or other
facilities; and

is able and wishes to give evidence in
the courtroom.

nodes.heading: When court must direct use of screens for complainant
nodes.text:
If the witness is a complainant in a criminal
proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a
charge for a sexual offence and is to give evidence
in the courtroom, the court must direct that an
arrangement referred to in section 360(b) be made
unless the court is satisfied that the complainant—

history.raw: New s. 364 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50, amended by No. 30/2010 s. 69.
S. 364 renumbered as s. 417 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(c).

nodes.text:
is aware of the right of the complainant to
give evidence while screens are used to
remove the accused from the direct line of
vision of the complainant; and
does not wish a screen to be so used.

nodes.heading: When court must direct presence of support person for complainant

history.raw: New s. 365 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 365 renumbered as s. 418 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(d), amended by No. 1/2022 s. 78 (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text:
If the witness is a complainant in a criminal
proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a
charge for a sexual offence, the court must direct
that an arrangement referred to in section 360(c)
be made unless the court is satisfied that the
complainant—
does not wish to have a support person.

Subsection (1) applies whether the witness is to
give evidence in the courtroom or in another
place.

nodes.heading: Use of recorded evidence-in-chief of children and cognitively impaired witnesses in sexual offence, assault and family violence matters

history.raw: New s. 366 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 366 renumbered as s. 419 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(e).

nodes.text:
This Division applies to a criminal proceeding
(other than a committal proceeding) that relates
(wholly or partly) to a charge for—

history.raw: S. 366(1)(c) inserted by No. 48/2012 s. 21(b), amended by No. 42/2015 s. 22, repealed by No. 47/2016 s. 37(10)(b).

nodes.text: a sexual offence; or
a family violence offence; or

history.raw: S. 366(1)(ab) inserted by No. 19/2017 s. 57, substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 42.

nodes.text:
an offence against section 21A(1) of the
Crimes Act 1958 (stalking); or

an indictable offence which involves an
assault on, or injury or a threat of injury
to, a person; or

any offences against section 23 or 24 of
the Summary Offences Act 1966 if those
offences are related offences to an offence
specified in paragraph (a), (ab), (ac) or (b),
despite whether any such related offences
are withdrawn or dismissed before an
offence against section 23 or 24 of the
Summary Offences Act 1966 is heard
and determined.
For committal proceedings see Chapter 4.

This Division applies to a witness in a criminal
proceeding referred to in subsection (1) if the
witness is—
a person under the age of 18 years; or
a person with a cognitive impairment.

In this Division, witness means a witness referred
to in subsection (2).

nodes.heading: Use of recorded evidence-in-chief
nodes.text:
A witness may give evidence-in-chief (wholly or
partly) in the form of an audio or audiovisual
recording of the witness answering questions put
to him or her by a person prescribed by the
regulations for the purposes of this section.

history.raw: New s. 367 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.
S. 367 renumbered as s. 420 by No. 68/2009 s. 54(f).
S. 367(1)(ea) inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 43, renumbered as s. 420(1)(ea) by No. 68/2009 s. 54(f), amended by No. 30/2010 s. 72, substituted by No. 5/2018 s. 30(b), amended by No. 1/2022 s. 12(1).
New s. 368 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
Subject to subsection (3), a recording referred to
in section 367 is admissible as evidence in a
summary hearing, special hearing or trial in the
proceeding as if its contents were the direct
testimony of the witness if—

a transcript of it was served personally on the
accused in accordance with section 391, or
on the legal practitioner representing the
accused in accordance with section 394—

in the case of a summary proceeding, at
least 14 days before the contest mention
hearing or, if a contest mention hearing
is not held, the summary hearing;

in the case of a trial, at least 14 days
before the day on which the trial is
listed to commence or, if a special
hearing is to be held, at least 14 days
before that hearing; and

the court is satisfied that the accused and
the legal practitioner of the accused were
given, in accordance with the regulations, a
reasonable opportunity to listen to and, in the
case of an audiovisual recording, view the
recording; and

at the summary hearing, special hearing or
trial, the witness—

identifies himself or herself and attests
to the truthfulness of the contents of the
recording; and

is available for cross-examination and
re-examination.

The admissibility of a recording of the evidence of
a person under the age of 18 years is not affected
only because the person attains the age of 18 years
before the evidence is presented in a proceeding.

The court may rule as inadmissible the whole or
any part of the contents of a recording and, if so,
the court may direct that the recording be edited or
altered to delete any part of it that is inadmissible.

Subject to this section, a recording referred to in
section 367 is admissible in evidence as if its
contents were the direct testimony of the
witness—
in the proceeding; and

unless the relevant court otherwise orders,
in—

any new trial of, or appeal from, the
proceeding; or

another proceeding in the same court
for the charge for an offence specified
in section 366(1) or a charge for a
related offence; or

a civil proceeding arising from the
same facts as those on which the charge
for an offence specified in
section 366(1) is founded.

The court, by order, may abridge any time fixed—
if the court considers that it is in the interests of
justice to do so.
by or under subsection (1)(a); or

by any order abridging time made under this
subsection—

nodes.heading: Court may order production of recording made under this Division in certain circumstances

nodes.text:
A court may order that a recording referred to in
section 367 be produced for use in a proceeding
(other than a proceeding referred to in
section 368) before that court if the court is
satisfied that it is in the best interests of the
witness to do so.

If a court makes an order under subsection (1), it
must also specify—

the persons who may view or listen to the
recording; and

when and where the recording is required to
be produced; and

if necessary, any requirements as to the
destruction of the recording.

In making an order under subsection (1), the court
must have regard to the need to protect the privacy
of the witness.

In this section, court includes a tribunal if the
complainant is the applicant in a proceeding
before the tribunal.

nodes.heading: Procedure and rules for children and cognitively impaired complainants

history.raw: New s. 369 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
This Division applies to a trial in a criminal
proceeding that relates (wholly or partly) to a
charge for—
a sexual offence; or
a family violence offence; or

an offence against section 21A(1) of the
Crimes Act 1958 (stalking).

This Division applies to a complainant in a
criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1)
if, at the time at which the proceeding
commenced, the complainant—
was under the age of 18 years; or
had a cognitive impairment.

In this Division, complainant means a
complainant referred to in subsection (2).

history.raw: S. 369(3) amended by No. 29/2011 s. 3(Sch. 1 item 24).
New s. 370 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
Subject to subsection (2), the whole of the
evidence (including cross-examination and
re-examination) of a complainant must be—

in the case of a special hearing before the
trial, presented to the court in the form of
that recording.

The court must direct that a special hearing under
this Division is to be held—
before the trial; or
during the trial.

Section 337 enables the court to vary its direction on the
application of a party or on its own motion.

In making a direction under subsection (1A), the
court must have regard to—

if the complainant is a child, the age and
maturity of the child; and

if the complainant is cognitively impaired,
the severity of that impairment; and

any preference expressed by the complainant
to give their evidence before the trial or
during the trial; and

whether conducting the special hearing
during the trial is likely—

to intimidate the complainant when
giving his or her evidence; or

to have an adverse effect on the
complainant; and

the need to complete the evidence of the
complainant expeditiously; and

the likelihood that the evidence given by
the complainant will include inadmissible
evidence that may result in the discharge of
the jury; and

any other matter that the court considers
relevant.

On the application of the prosecution, the court
may direct that subsection (1) is not to apply and
that the complainant is to give direct testimony in
the proceeding if the court is satisfied that the
complainant—

is aware of the right of the complainant to
have his or her evidence taken at a special
hearing under this Division and
audiovisually recorded; and

is able and wishes to give direct testimony in
the proceeding.

Division 4 provides that the court may make alternative
arrangements for the giving of direct testimony.

history.raw: New s. 371 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: If a special hearing is to be held, it must be held—

history.raw: Note to s. 371(1) substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 21(2).

nodes.text:
within the applicable period after the accused
is committed for trial; and

before the court at which the indictment is
filed.

Sections 211 and 212 impose time limits for commencing
trials for offences.

Subject to subsection (1B), the applicable period
is—

for a trial in a criminal proceeding that
relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a
sexual offence, a period of 3 months; or

for a trial in a criminal proceeding that
relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a
family violence offence, a period of 12
months; or

for a trial in a criminal proceeding that
relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for an
offence against section 21A(1) of the
Crimes Act 1958 (stalking), a period of
12 months.

If a trial in a criminal proceeding relates partly to
a charge for a sexual offence and partly to a
charge for a family violence offence or an offence
against section 21A(1) of the Crimes Act 1958
(stalking), the applicable period is a period of
3 months.

history.raw: S. 371(1B) inserted by No. 5/2025 s. 21(3), amended by No. 1/2026 s. 76(2).

nodes.text:
The court may extend the time for holding a
special hearing if the court considers that it is in
the interests of justice to do so, having regard to—

if the complainant is a child, the age and
maturity of the child; and

if the complainant is cognitively impaired,
the severity of that impairment; and

the period of time since the complaint was
first made; and

the period of time since the offence was
allegedly committed; and

any other matter that the court considers
relevant.

The court may extend time under subsection (2)
before or after the time expires.

More than one extension of time may be granted
under subsection (2).

nodes.heading: Timing arrangements for special hearing during trial
nodes.text:
If the court directs that a special hearing be held
during the trial, the court must—

history.raw: Note to s. 371A substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 22.

nodes.text:
as far as possible, commence the special
hearing on the date specified under
section 181(2)(d)(iii); and

ensure that the complainant's evidence is
disrupted to the least extent possible.

An application to discharge the jury may be heard and
determined after the special hearing is completed.

Sections 211 and 212 impose time limits for commencing trials for
offences.

history.raw: New s. 372 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: At a special hearing—

the accused and his or her legal practitioner
are to be present in the courtroom;
the accused—

is entitled to see and hear the
complainant while the complainant is
giving evidence and to have at all times
the means of communicating with his
or her legal practitioner;

no person, other than a person authorised by
the court, is to be present in the courtroom or
the same room as the complainant when the
complainant's evidence is being taken;

the evidence of the complainant is to be
given by means of closed-circuit television
or other facilities that enable communication
between the room in which the complainant
is present and the courtroom;

except as provided by this Division, the
usual rules of evidence apply.

The room in which the complainant gives
evidence is taken to be part of the courtroom
while the complainant is there for the purpose of
giving evidence.

nodes.heading: Form in which recording of special hearing is to be tendered

history.raw: New s. 373 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
A recording of a special hearing that is tendered
as evidence by the prosecution must be the best
available record, or be comprised of the best
available records, of the evidence of the
complainant.

In subsection (1)—
the best available record of the evidence, or any
part of the evidence, means an audiovisual
recording of the evidence.

In exceptional circumstances and having regard to
whether the accused would be unfairly prejudiced,
the court may admit as evidence an audio
recording of the evidence, or any part of the
evidence, if an audiovisual recording of the
evidence is not available.

nodes.heading: Admissibility of evidence from special hearing

history.raw: New s. 374 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
In this section—
recording means a recording of a special hearing.

Subject to subsection (3), a recording is
admissible in evidence as if its contents were the
direct testimony of the complainant—
in the proceeding; and

unless the relevant court otherwise orders,
in—

any new trial of, or appeal from, the
proceeding; or

another proceeding in the same court
for—

the charge for the sexual offence,
the family violence offence or the
offence against section 21A(1) of
the Crimes Act 1958 (stalking)
(as the case requires); or
a charge for a related offence; or

a civil proceeding arising from the
same facts as those on which the charge
for the sexual offence, the family
violence offence or the offence against
section 21A(1) of the Crimes Act 1958
(stalking) is founded.

history.raw: S. 374(2)(b)(iii) substituted by No. 5/2025 s. 23, amended by No. 1/2026 s. 77.

nodes.text:
The court may rule as inadmissible the whole or
any part of the contents of a recording and, if so,
the court may direct that the recording be edited or
altered to delete any part of it that is inadmissible.

A party may apply for a ruling under subsection (3):
section 337.

Subject to subsection (3), the whole of a recording
must be heard by the court.

The admissibility of a recording of the evidence of
a person under the age of 18 years is not affected
only because the person attains the age of 18 years
before the evidence is presented in a proceeding.

Subject to section 376(3), if under this section a
recording is admitted into evidence in a
proceeding, the complainant is not required to
attend the proceeding unless required to do so for
cross-examination or re-examination.

history.raw: New s. 376 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
A complainant whose evidence is recorded under
section 370 cannot be cross-examined or
re-examined without leave.

A court must not grant leave to cross-examine a
complainant referred to in subsection (1) unless
the court is satisfied that—

the accused is seeking leave because of
becoming aware of a matter of which the
accused could not reasonably have been
aware at the time of the recording; or

if the complainant were giving direct
testimony in the proceeding, the complainant
could be recalled, in the interests of justice,
to give further evidence; or

it is otherwise in the interests of justice to
permit the complainant to be cross-examined
or re-examined.

If leave is granted under subsection (2), the
complainant must attend the proceeding to be
cross-examined or re-examined.

Section 377 previously provided an exception to the hearsay rule
in relation to previous representations made by a complainant
under 18 years in certain circumstances. This matter is now
provided for in section 66 of the Evidence Act 2008.

nodes.heading: Admission of recorded evidence of complainant given in trial for sexual offences

history.raw: New s. 378 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
This Division applies to a criminal proceeding that
relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for a sexual
offence.

This Division applies to a complainant in a
criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1),
other than a complainant whose evidence has been
taken at a special hearing under Division 6.

This Division applies to a recording of the
evidence (including cross-examination and
re-examination) of a complainant given during a
trial in a criminal proceeding referred to in
subsection (1).

If the jury is discharged without verdict before a
complainant completes his or her evidence, this
Division applies to a recording of the partial
evidence of the complainant.

In this Division—
complainant means a complainant referred to in
subsection (2);
recording means a recording referred to in
subsection (3) or (4).

nodes.heading: Admissibility of recording of complainant's evidence
nodes.text:
Subject to section 381, a recording is admissible
in evidence as if its contents were the direct
testimony of the complainant—

history.raw: New s. 379 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text: in the proceeding; and

unless the relevant court otherwise orders,
in—

any new trial of, or appeal from, the
proceeding; or

another proceeding in the same court
for the charge for a sexual offence or a
charge for a related offence; or

a civil proceeding arising from the
same facts as those on which the charge
for a sexual offence is founded.

nodes.heading: Prosecution to give notice of intention to tender recording

history.raw: New s. 380 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
If the prosecution intends to apply to tender a
recording as evidence in a proceeding referred to
in section 379, the prosecution must serve on the
accused and file in court written notice of that
intention at least 21 days before the day on which
the trial or hearing is listed to commence.

The court may dispense with or vary a
requirement imposed by subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Admission of recording of evidence of complainant

history.raw: New s. 381 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
Subject to this section, the court may admit a
recording of the evidence of the complainant.

There is a presumption in favour of admitting the
recording.

The presumption in favour of admitting the
recording is rebutted if the court considers that it
is in the interests of justice that the recording not
be admitted, having regard to—

the effect of editing any inadmissible
evidence from the recording;

subject to subsection (1A), any other matter
that the court considers relevant.

The availability or willingness of the complainant
to give further evidence is irrelevant to the
question of whether it is in the interests of justice
not to admit the recording.

The court may admit the whole or any part of the
contents of a recording and may direct that the
recording be edited or altered to delete any part of
it that is inadmissible.

nodes.heading: Attendance of complainant
nodes.text:
Subject to sections 384 and 385, if a recording is
admitted into evidence in a proceeding, the
complainant is not required to attend the
proceeding unless required to do so to give further
evidence.

history.raw: New s. 383 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.heading: Direct testimony in addition to recording

history.raw: New s. 384 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
On the application of the prosecution, the court
may direct that the complainant is to give direct
testimony additional to a recording admitted into
evidence if the court is satisfied that—

the complainant is able and wishes to give
direct testimony; and
it is in the interests of justice to do so.

A complainant may be cross-examined and
re-examined in relation to any direct testimony
given by the complainant in response to a
direction under subsection (1).
Any other cross-examination requires leave under section 385.

history.raw: New s. 385 inserted by No. 68/2009 s. 50.

nodes.text:
Subject to section 384(2), if a recording of the
evidence of the complainant is admitted into
evidence in a proceeding, the complainant cannot
be cross-examined or re-examined without leave.

A court must not grant leave to cross-examine a
complainant unless the court is satisfied that—

the accused is seeking leave because of
becoming aware of a matter of which the
accused could not reasonably have been
aware at the time of the recording; or

if the complainant were giving direct
testimony in the proceeding, the complainant
could be recalled, in the interests of justice,
to give further evidence; or

it is otherwise in the interests of justice to
permit the complainant to be cross-examined
or re-examined.

If leave is granted under subsection (2), the
complainant must attend the proceeding to be
cross-examined or re-examined.

nodes.heading: Form in which recording of complainant's evidence is to be tendered

nodes.text:
A recording that is tendered as evidence by the
prosecution under this Division must be the best
available record, or be comprised of the best
available records, of the evidence of the
complainant.

In subsection (1)—
the best available record of the evidence, or any
part of the evidence, means an audiovisual
recording of the evidence.

In exceptional circumstances and having regard to
whether the accused would be unfairly prejudiced,
the court may admit as evidence an audio
recording of the evidence, or any part of the
evidence, if an audiovisual recording of the
evidence is not available.

In this section—
hearsay rule has the same meaning as in the
Evidence Act 2008.
The hearsay rule does not prevent—

the admission of a recording in accordance
with this Division; or

the use of the recording to prove the
existence of a fact that the complainant
intended to assert by a representation made
in the recorded evidence.

nodes.heading: Admission of recorded evidence of complainant given in summary hearing by Children's Court of certain sexual offences

history.raw: Pt 8.2 Div. 7A (Heading and ss 387A, 387B inserted by No. 28/2016 s. 9.

nodes.text:
This Division applies to a criminal proceeding that
relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for—

history.raw: S. 387A(1) amended by No. 28/2016 s. 12, substituted by No. 5/2018 s. 14.

nodes.text:
an offence against any of the following
provisions of the Crimes Act 1958—
section 38 (rape);

section 39 (rape by compelling sexual
penetration);

section 49A (sexual penetration of a
child under the age of 12);

section 49B (sexual penetration of a
child under the age of 16);

section 49D (sexual assault of a child
under the age of 16);

section 49I (causing a child aged 16
or 17 under care, supervision or
authority to be present during sexual
activity);

section 49J (persistent sexual abuse
of a child under the age of 16);

section 50C (sexual penetration of a
child or lineal descendant);

section 50D (sexual penetration of a
step-child);

section 50E (sexual penetration of a
parent, lineal ancestor or step-parent);

section 50F (sexual penetration of a
sibling or half-sibling); or

an offence of attempting to commit, or
of incitement or conspiracy to commit,
an offence referred to in paragraph (a).

This Division applies to a complainant
in a criminal proceeding referred to in
subsection (1).

This Division applies to a recording of the
evidence (including cross-examination and
re-examination) of a complainant given during
a summary hearing by the Children's Court in a
criminal proceeding referred to in subsection (1).

nodes.heading: Admissibility of recording of complainant's evidence
nodes.text:
Division 7 (other than section 378) applies to this
Division as if—

history.raw: S. 387B inserted by No. 28/2016 s. 9, amended by No. 37/2017 s. 13(2).

nodes.text:
a reference to a sexual offence were a
reference to an offence referred to in
section 387A(1); and

a reference to a complainant were a reference
to a complainant referred to in
section 387A(2); and

a reference to a trial were a reference to a
summary hearing of the charge by the
Children's Court.

nodes.heading: Use of recorded evidence-in-chief of complainant in family violence offence proceedings

history.raw: Pt 8.2 Div. 7B (Heading and ss 387C– 387P) inserted by No. 33/2018 s. 116.

nodes.text: In this Division—

nodes.heading: family violence offence
nodes.text: means—

an offence against section 37(2),
37A(2), 123(2), 123A(2) or 125A(1)
of the Family Violence Protection
Act 2008; or

nodes.heading: recorded statement
nodes.text:
means an audiovisual or audio
recording of a complainant answering
questions put to the complainant by a trained
police officer;

nodes.heading: trained police officer
nodes.text:
means a police officer who
has successfully completed a training course
approved by the Chief Commissioner of
Police under subsection (2).

The Chief Commissioner of Police may approve
one or more training courses for police officers for
the purposes of this Division.

This Division applies to a criminal proceeding
(including a summary hearing, a committal
proceeding and a trial) that relates (wholly or
partly) to a charge for a family violence offence.
Sections 387J and 387K apply to other proceedings.

However, this Division does not apply if the
accused was under the age of 18 years at the time
the family violence offence is alleged to have
been committed.

nodes.heading: Use of recorded statement as complainant's evidence-in-chief

nodes.text:
A complainant may give evidence-in-chief
(wholly or partly) in the form of a recorded
statement in accordance with this Division.

In determining whether or not to have a
complainant give evidence wholly or partly in the
form of a recorded statement, the prosecution
must take into account—
the wishes of the complainant; and

any evidence of intimidation of the
complainant by the accused; and

the purpose of the Family Violence
Protection Act 2008.

The purpose of the Family Violence Protection Act 2008 is
set out in section 1 of that Act.

Subject to this Division, a recorded statement
referred to in section 387E is admissible in
evidence as if its contents were the direct
testimony of the complainant—
in the proceeding; and

unless the relevant court otherwise orders, in
any new trial of, or appeal from, the
proceeding.

Subject to subsection (4), a recorded statement is
admissible under subsection (1) if—

the recorded statement complies with
section 387G; and

subject to subsection (3), a copy or transcript
of the recorded statement was served in
accordance with section 387H; and

subject to subsection (3), the court is
satisfied that, if the accused is not
represented by a legal practitioner,
the accused was given a reasonable
opportunity to—

view the recorded statement if it is in
the form of an audiovisual recording; or

listen to the recorded statement if it
exists only in the form of an audio
recording and the accused has not been
served with a copy of it; and

at the hearing of the proceeding, the
complainant—

identifies himself or herself and attests
to the truthfulness of the contents of the
recorded statement; and

is available for cross-examination and
re-examination.

A recorded statement is admissible under
subsection (1) despite non-compliance with
subsection (2)(b) or (c) if the parties consent to its
use as the complainant's evidence-in-chief.

The court may rule as inadmissible the whole or
any part of the content of a recorded statement
and, if so, the court may direct that the recorded
statement be edited or otherwise altered to delete
any part that is inadmissible.

Without limiting what is a reasonable opportunity
for the purposes of subsection (2)(c), a reasonable
opportunity is taken to have been given if—

the accused was given an opportunity to
view or listen to the recorded statement, as
referred to in subsection (2)(c), while being
questioned in relation to the alleged family
violence offence; or

the informant notified the accused in writing
that the accused had the right to view or
listen to the recorded statement, as referred
to in subsection (2)(c), on a day arranged
with the informant.

To be admissible as evidence-in-chief under
section 387F, a recorded statement—
must be made—

as soon as practicable after the events
constituting the alleged family violence
offence to which the statement relates
occurred; and

with the complainant's informed
consent; and

must include, at the end of the recording, an
attestation by the complainant as to the truth
of the content of the statement; and

subject to subsection (2), must be in the form
of an audiovisual recording.

In exceptional circumstances and having regard to
whether the accused would be unfairly prejudiced,
the court may admit as evidence-in-chief a
recorded statement in the form of an audio
recording, if an audiovisual recording of the
statement is not available.

A recorded statement is made with informed
consent if—

the trained police officer informs the
complainant that—

the recorded statement may be used in
evidence in a criminal proceeding, a
proceeding for a family violence
intervention order or, if a court or
tribunal orders, another proceeding; and

the complainant may be required to
give further evidence in the proceeding,
including further evidence-in-chief and
evidence on cross-examination and
re-examination; and

the complainant indicates in the recorded
statement that the complainant—

understands the matters referred to in
paragraph (a); and

consents to the making of the recorded
statement.

If any part of a recorded statement is in a language
other than English—

the recorded statement must contain an oral
translation of the part into English; or

a separate written English translation of the
part must accompany the recorded statement.

A recorded statement must be served on the
accused or the accused's legal practitioner in
accordance with Part 3.2, Part 4.4 or Part 5.5, as
the case requires, subject to the following
modifications—

if the accused is represented by a legal
practitioner, the legal practitioner must be
served with an audiovisual copy of the
recorded statement (or an audio copy if the
statement is in audio form) but must not give
a copy of the recorded statement to the
accused or allow the accused to be given, or
take a copy of, the recorded statement;

if the accused is not represented by a legal
practitioner, the accused must be served
with—

an audio copy of the recorded statement
(whether the recorded statement is in
audio or audiovisual form); or

in the circumstances described in
subsection (2), a transcript of the
recorded statement.

For the purposes of subsection (1)(b)(ii),
an accused is to be served with a transcript rather
than an audio copy only if the informant or
prosecutor believes that—

serving an audio copy on the accused
would be likely to present a reasonably
ascertainable risk that the accused would
commit an offence under section 387L(1) or
in relation to the recorded statement; or

in the particular circumstances of the
accused, a transcript is required.

An example for subsection (2)(b) is where an accused
is hearing impaired and would not be able to listen to
an audio copy of the recorded statement.

In addition to subsection (1), if a recorded
statement is to be used in a committal proceeding
or a trial on indictment, a transcript of the
recorded statement must be served on the accused
or the accused's legal practitioner in the same
manner as the recorded statement is served under
Part 4.4 or Part 5.5, as the case requires.

nodes.heading: Editing or otherwise altering recorded statement
nodes.text:
A recorded statement may be edited or otherwise
altered only—

with the consent of the parties to the
proceeding; or

if editing or altering the statement is
required—

so as to avoid disclosure of material
that is not required to be disclosed, or
must not be disclosed, to the accused;
or

to comply with a direction of the court
under section 387F(4); or

for the purpose referred to in
section 387L(4)(h).

Examples for paragraph (b)(i) include editing a recorded
statement—
to avoid disclosure of a confidential source of information to
•
the accused—see section 45(1)(c);
to avoid disclosure of certain law enforcement methods or
•
procedures to the accused—see section 45(1)(d);
to avoid disclosure of child abuse material to the accused—
•
see section 185A;
to avoid disclosure of addresses or telephone numbers to the
•
accused—see section 186.

If a recorded statement is edited or altered to avoid the
disclosure of material, certain notice requirements may apply—
see section 41(1)(f).

nodes.heading: Court or tribunal may order production of recorded statement in certain circumstances

nodes.text:
A court or tribunal may order that a recorded
statement be produced for use in a proceeding
(other than the proceeding in which the statement
was used as evidence-in-chief under section 387E
or a proceeding referred to in section 387K)
before that court or tribunal if the court or tribunal
is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do
so.

Subsection (1) applies whether or not the
proceeding relates to a charge for a family
violence offence.

If a court or tribunal makes an order under
subsection (1), it must also specify—

the persons who may view or listen to the
recording; and

when and where the recording is required to
be produced; and

if necessary, any requirements as to the
destruction of the recording.

In making an order under subsection (1), the court
or tribunal must have regard to the need to protect
the privacy of the complainant.

nodes.heading: Use of recorded statement in family violence intervention order proceeding

nodes.text: This section applies if—

an application for a family violence
intervention order under the Family
Violence Protection Act 2008 arises from
the circumstances of the alleged family
violence offence in relation to which a
recorded statement has been made (whether
or not the statement has been used in
proceedings referred to in section 387D(1) or
whether or not any such proceedings have
commenced); or

in a proceeding for a family violence
intervention order under the Family
Violence Protection Act 2008 an affected
family member is the complainant who made
a recorded statement and the respondent is
the person accused of the family violence
offence to which the statement relates
(whether or not the statement has been used
in proceedings referred to in section 387D(1)
or whether or not any such proceedings have
commenced).

Without limiting section 65(1) of the Family
Violence Protection Act 2008, the recorded
statement may be used as evidence in the
proceeding for the family violence intervention
order.

Section 387L sets out the circumstances in which
the respondent may be given, or is not permitted to possess,
a copy of the recorded statement and the form in which
that statement may be given—see section 387L(3), (4), (5)
and (6).

In this section, affected family member, family
violence intervention order and respondent have
the same meaning as in the Family Violence
Protection Act 2008.

nodes.heading: Offences in relation to recorded statements

nodes.text:
Unless permitted to do so by this section, a person
must not publish a recorded statement.
Penalty: Level 7 imprisonment (2 years
maximum).

Unless permitted to do so by this section, a
person, other than the complainant, must not
knowingly—
Penalty: Level 7 imprisonment (2 years
maximum).
copy a recorded statement; or

supply a recorded statement or a copy of a
recorded statement to another person.

Unless permitted to do so by this section, a
person, other than the complainant, must not
knowingly possess a recorded statement.
Penalty: Level 8 imprisonment (1 year
maximum).

A person may possess, publish or copy a recorded
statement, or supply a recorded statement or a
copy of a recorded statement to another person—

for the purpose of investigating the family
violence offence to which the recorded
statement relates; or

for the purpose of preparing for the
proceeding in which the recorded statement
is proposed to be used in evidence, including
a proceeding for a family violence
intervention order referred to in
section 387K; or

for the purpose of complying with a court
order or tribunal order under section 387J or
for preparing for a proceeding to which such
an order relates; or

for the purpose of the performance of official
functions by—

a member of Victoria Police personnel;
or

a member of staff of the Office of
Public Prosecutions; or

a judicial officer, member or member
of staff of a court or tribunal; or

for the purpose of an investigation or inquest
under the Coroners Act 2008; or

for purposes connected with disciplinary
action against a police officer under the
Victoria Police Act 2013; or

for purposes connected with an investigation
into the proper exercise of power by a public
official, including an investigation by the
Independent Broad-based Anti-Corruption
Commission; or

for the purpose of training or teaching a
prescribed person or testing recording
equipment if—

the accused to whom the recorded
statement relates has been convicted or
found guilty of the charge to which the
statement relates; and

all legal proceedings in relation to the
subject matter in the recorded statement
have been concluded; and

either the complainant consents to the
use of the recorded statement for the
purpose or the recorded statement is
edited or otherwise altered so as to
prevent the identification of the
complainant and any person referred to
in the statement; or

for a purpose, or in the circumstances,
prescribed by the regulations.

A person may possess a recorded statement
(whether in audiovisual form or audio form) if the
statement was—

served on that person in accordance with this
Act; or

subject to subsection (6), otherwise lawfully
supplied to that person.
Subsection (5)(b) does not apply in relation to—

the supply of a recorded statement in
audiovisual form, or a copy of it, to the
accused or respondent; or

if the accused or respondent was served only
with a transcript of a recorded statement in
accordance with section 387H(2), the supply
of the recorded statement in audio form, or a
copy of it, to the accused or respondent.

For the purposes of Subdivision (1) of Division 1
of Part II of the Crimes Act 1958, the
complainant is not involved in the commission of
an offence against this section by the accused or
respondent, and is not punishable as a principal
offender, only because the complainant supplied a
recorded statement, or a copy of a recorded
statement, to the accused or respondent.

This section does not apply to the publication or
supply of a recorded statement as part of the
publication or supply of an official court recording
of proceedings.

In this section—
member of Victoria Police personnel has the
same meaning as in the Victoria Police
Act 2013;
prescribed person means—
publish means disseminate or provide access to
the public or a section of the public by any
means, including by—
respondent has the same meaning as in the
Family Violence Protection Act 2008.

a member of Victoria Police personnel
other than a protective services officer;

a person or body engaged to provide
services to Victoria Police in relation to
the installation or maintenance of
recording equipment;

a legal practitioner or a person training
to become a legal practitioner;

an investigating official (as defined in
section 464(2) of the Crimes Act 1958)
or a person acting under an
investigating official's direction;
broadcast by radio or television; or
public exhibition; or
broadcast or electronic communication;

nodes.heading: Division does not affect other provisions
nodes.text:
This Division is in addition to the other provisions
of this Part and of the Evidence Act 2008 and
does not, unless the contrary intention appears,
affect the operation of those provisions or that
Act.

This Division does not affect—
Division 2, which provides for restrictions on the
•
admissibility of evidence about a complainant in criminal
proceedings for sexual offences;
section 65 of the Evidence Act 2008, which is an exception
•
to the hearsay rule if a person is not available to give
evidence;
Part 3.10 of the Evidence Act 2008, which deals with various
•
privileges in relation to evidence.

nodes.heading: Relationship with Surveillance Devices Act 1999
nodes.text:
Despite anything to the contrary in the
Surveillance Devices Act 1999, a recorded
statement made for the purposes of this Division
is not protected information for the purposes of
Division 1 of Part 5 of that Act.

nodes.heading: Evidence of specialised knowledge in certain cases
nodes.text:
Despite any rule of law to the contrary, in a
criminal proceeding that relates (wholly or partly)
to a charge for a sexual offence, the court may
receive evidence of a person's opinion that is
based on that person's specialised knowledge
(acquired through training, study or experience)
of—
the nature of sexual offences; and

the social, psychological and cultural factors
that may affect the behaviour of a person
who has been the victim, or who alleges that
he or she has been the victim, of a sexual
offence, including the reasons that may
contribute to a delay on the part of the victim
to report the offence.

nodes.heading: Audiovisual link evidence from overseas in certain proceedings

nodes.text:
This section applies to a criminal proceeding
that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for
an offence against—
section 49S(1) of the Crimes Act 1958; or

section 49A(1) of the Crimes Act 1958
as in force before the commencement of
section 16 of the Crimes Amendment
(Sexual Offences) Act 2016.

The court may, on the application of a party to
the criminal proceeding, direct that a witness give
evidence by audiovisual link if—

the witness will give the evidence from
outside Australia; and

the witness is not an accused in the
proceeding; and

the facilities required by subsection (3) are
available or can reasonably be made
available; and

the court is satisfied that attendance of the
witness at the court to give the evidence
would—

cause unreasonable expense or
inconvenience; or

cause the witness psychological harm
or unreasonable distress; or

cause the witness to become so
intimidated or distressed that his or her
reliability as a witness would be
significantly reduced; and

the court is satisfied that it is consistent with
the interests of justice that the evidence be
taken by audiovisual link.

A witness can give evidence under a direction
under this section only if the courtroom or
other place in Victoria where the court is sitting
(the Victorian point) and the place where the
evidence is given (the overseas point) are
equipped with audiovisual facilities that—

enable all persons at the Victorian point that
the court considers appropriate, to see and
hear the witness give the evidence; and

enable all persons at the overseas point that
the court considers appropriate, to see and
hear appropriate persons at the Victorian
point.

The place where a witness gives evidence under a
direction under this section is taken to be part of
the courtroom or other place in Victoria where the
court is sitting while the witness is there for the
purpose of giving evidence.

An oath or affirmation to be sworn or made by a
witness who is to give evidence under a direction
under this section may be administered either—

by means of the audiovisual link, in as nearly
as practicable the same way as if the witness
were to give the evidence at the courtroom or
other place in Victoria where the court is
sitting; or

at the direction of, and on behalf of, the court
at the place where the witness is to give the
evidence by a person authorised by the court.

A court may make any orders that are just for the
payment of expenses incurred in connection with
the giving of evidence under a direction by the
court under this section.

This section does not prevent any other law, or
any rule or regulation made under any other law,
about taking evidence of a witness outside
Australia from applying for the purposes of a
proceeding to which this section applies.

Nothing in this section limits the application of
this Part to a charge for an offence referred to in
subsection (1).

This Division applies to a criminal proceeding
that relates (wholly or partly) to a charge for—
a sexual offence; or
a family violence offence; or

an offence against section 21A(1) of the
Crimes Act 1958 (stalking); or

an indictable offence which involves an
assault on, or injury or a threat of injury
to, a person; or

any offences against section 23 or 24 of
the Summary Offences Act 1966 if the
offences are related offences to an offence
specified in paragraph (a), (ba) or (c), despite
whether any such related offences are
withdrawn or dismissed before an offence
against section 23 or 24 of the Summary
Offences Act 1966 is heard and determined.

This Division applies at any stage of the criminal
proceeding, including an appeal or rehearing.
This Division applies to—

a witness (including a complainant) other
than the accused in a criminal proceeding
referred to in subsection (1) if the witness
is—
a person under the age of 18 years; or

a person with a cognitive impairment;
and

a witness who is a complainant in relation to
a charge for a sexual offence.

In this Division, witness means a witness referred
to in subsection (3).

nodes.heading: Ground rules hearings
nodes.text:
A ground rules hearing is a hearing at which the
court—

considers the communication, support or
other needs of witnesses; and

decides how the proceeding is to be
conducted to fairly and effectively meet
those needs.

nodes.heading: Ground rules hearing to be held

nodes.text:
The court may direct that a ground rules hearing is
to be held.

Section 337(1) enables this direction to be made by the court
on the application of a party or on its own motion.

An application for the court to direct that a ground
rules hearing is to be held may be made orally or
in writing.
A ground rules hearing must be held if—

an intermediary is appointed under
Division 2; or

a witness is a complainant in relation to a
charge for a sexual offence.

nodes.heading: Time limits for ground rules hearing

nodes.text:
If a ground rules hearing is to be held, it must be
held before the commencement of any hearing at
which a witness is to give evidence.

The court may extend the time for holding a
ground rules hearing if the court considers that
it is in the interests of justice to do so.

The court may extend time under subsection (2)
before or after the time expires.

More than one extension of time may be granted
under subsection (2).

The following persons must attend a ground rules
hearing—
a person acting for the prosecution;

the intermediary appointed for a witness,
if any.

A witness is not required to attend a ground rules
hearing.

The court may make an order that a witness for
whom an intermediary is appointed not attend a
ground rules hearing.

At a ground rules hearing, the court may make or
vary any direction for the fair and efficient
conduct of the proceeding.

Without limiting subsection (1), the court may
give one or more of the following directions—

a direction about the manner of questioning
a witness;

a direction about the duration of questioning
a witness;

a direction about the questions that may or
may not be put to a witness;

if there is more than one accused, a direction
about the allocation among the accused of
the topics about which a witness may be
asked;

a direction that if a party intends to lead
evidence that contradicts or challenges the
evidence of a witness or that otherwise
discredits a witness, the party is not obliged
to put that evidence in its entirety to the
witness in cross-examination.

nodes.heading: Participating venues of courts
nodes.text:
The Minister may, by notice published in the
Government Gazette, declare a venue of a court
to be a participating venue for the purposes of
this Division.

The Secretary to the Department of Justice and
Regulation must establish a panel of persons who
the Secretary is satisfied are suitable persons to be
appointed as intermediaries.

A person must not be on the panel unless the
person—

has a tertiary qualification in psychology,
social work, speech pathology or
occupational therapy; or

has other prescribed qualifications, training,
experience or skills.

The Secretary to the Department of Justice and
Regulation must remove a person from the panel
if the Secretary is no longer satisfied that the
person is a suitable person to be appointed as an
intermediary.
The functions of an intermediary are—

to communicate or explain to a witness
for whom an intermediary is appointed,
questions put to the witness to the extent
necessary to enable them to be understood
by the witness; and

to communicate or explain to a person
asking questions of a witness for whom
an intermediary is appointed, the answers
given by the witness in reply to the extent
necessary to enable them to be understood
by the person; and

to provide recommendations to the court
regarding effective communication with the
witness; and

to otherwise assist the court and any legal
representative of a party to the proceeding to
communicate with the witness.

An intermediary may provide the
recommendations referred to in subsection (1)(c)
in the form of a written report.

An intermediary may perform the function
referred to in subsection (1)(d) at a hearing or as
the court otherwise directs.

An intermediary is an officer of the court and
has a duty to act impartially when assisting
communication with the witness.

A court may appoint an intermediary for a witness
from the panel established under this Division.

Section 337(1) enables this appointment to be made by
the court on the application of a party or on its own
motion.

Section 337(2) provides that this appointment may be
varied or revoked.

An application for a court to appoint an
intermediary may be made orally or in writing.

A court must not appoint an intermediary for a
witness if the court is satisfied that the witness—

is aware of the right of the witness to make
an application for an intermediary to be
appointed; and

is able and wishes to give evidence in the
criminal proceeding without the assistance
of an intermediary.

A court must not appoint a person as an
intermediary for a witness if the person—

is a relative, friend or acquaintance of
the witness or the accused; or

has assisted the witness (other than as
an intermediary) or the accused in a
professional capacity; or

is a party or potential witness (other
than by reason of the person's role as an
intermediary) in the relevant proceeding.

nodes.heading: Witness to give evidence in presence of intermediary

nodes.text:
In a proceeding in which an intermediary has been
appointed, the evidence of the witness must be
given in the presence of the intermediary.

Subject to any direction of the court and rules of
court, the evidence of the witness given in the
presence of the intermediary must be given in
circumstances in which—

the court and any legal practitioner appearing
in the proceeding are able to see and hear the
witness giving evidence and to communicate
with the intermediary; and

the jury (if any) is able to see and hear the
witness giving evidence (including any
assistance given by the intermediary), other
than evidence given in accordance with an
arrangement made under section 360(a) as
directed by the court.

The provisions of Division 2 (other than
section 22(2)) of Part 2.1 of the Evidence
Act 2008 which apply to interpreters are
taken to apply to an intermediary.

Section 22(2) of the Evidence Act 2008 requires
interpreters to take an oath or make an affirmation
in accordance with a form in Schedule 1 to that Act
or a similar form.

A person must not act as an intermediary in
a particular proceeding unless the person has
taken an oath or made an affirmation in the
prescribed form.

nodes.heading: Service on company, registered body, incorporated association or other body corporate

nodes.text:
If the person to be served is a company within the
meaning of the Corporations Act, service of a
document on the person may be effected in
accordance with section 109X of that Act or in
accordance with subsection (4).

If the person to be served is a registered body
within the meaning of the Corporations Act,
service of a document on the person may be
effected in accordance with section 601CX of
that Act or in accordance with subsection (4).

If the person to be served is an incorporated
association within the meaning of the
Associations Incorporation Reform Act 2012,
service of a document on the person may be
effected in accordance with section 217 of that
Act or in accordance with subsection (4).

If the person to be served is a body corporate
and service is not effected in accordance with
subsection (1), (2) or (3), service of a document
on the person must be effected—

by leaving a copy of the document at the
registered office or principal place of
business of the body corporate; or

by sending a copy of the document by
prepaid ordinary post to the registered office
or principal place of business of the body
corporate; or

if the body corporate is represented by a
legal practitioner, by sending a copy of the
document by prepaid ordinary post addressed
to the legal practitioner at the ordinary
business address of the legal practitioner; or

by serving a copy of the document on a
representative of the body corporate within
the meaning of section 334 in a manner
nominated in writing by the representative.

The Electronic Transactions Act 1999 of the Commonwealth or
the Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000 applies to
enable a document to be served electronically, including fax

Unless this Act or any other Act or the rules of
court otherwise provide, ordinary service of a
document is effected—

nodes.text:
If this Act requires or permits service of a
document to be effected in accordance with
section 394 or by ordinary service, the document
may be served in accordance with section 391.

nodes.heading: Last known place of residence or business
nodes.text:
Rules of court may prescribe how the last known
place of residence or business of an accused is to
be ascertained in specified circumstances.

nodes.heading: Order for substituted service
nodes.text:
If it appears to a court by sworn or affirmed
evidence, whether oral or by affidavit, that service
cannot be promptly effected, the court may make
an order for substituted service.

nodes.heading: Who may effect service

If by or under this Act a person is required or
permitted to serve a document, the person may
serve the document by causing it to be served by
another person.

nodes.heading: Costs in summary proceedings and committal proceedings

nodes.text:
Unless otherwise expressly provided by this or
any other Act or by the rules of court, the costs of,
and incidental to, all criminal proceedings in the
Magistrates' Court are in the discretion of the
court and the court has full power to determine by
whom, to whom and to what extent the costs are
to be paid.

In exercising its discretion under subsection (1)
in a criminal proceeding, the Magistrates' Court
may take into account any unreasonable act or
omission by, or on behalf of, a party to the
proceeding that the court is satisfied resulted in
prolonging the proceeding.

If the Magistrates' Court strikes out a charge under
section 14(3), the court may award costs against
the informant.

This section and section 410 apply to a purported
proceeding in the Magistrates' Court which is
beyond the jurisdiction of the court as if the
purported proceeding were within jurisdiction.

If the Magistrates' Court determines to award
costs against an informant who is a police officer,
the order must be made against the Chief
Commissioner of Police.
